The works of Anatoly Klyosov, biochemist, doctor of chemical sciences, professor and founder of a new scientific discipline called "DNA genealogy", scientifically substantiate the historical origin of peoples, and the Slavic people in particular, but, unfortunately, they are of little demand in their homeland, causing pain In his interview for the Novorossiya news agency, Professor Klyosov spoke about the discoveries of a new scientific discipline that relate to the genealogy of the once united Slavic people, as well as about the migration routes of the ancient Slavs. Novorossiya news agency: It is known that DNA genealogy is a new and young science. As a result of the symbiosis of what disciplines did it arise and what is its essence? Anatoly Klyosov: DNA genealogy was formed at the intersection, first of all, of physical chemistry, since it is based on mathematical calculations, as well as a number of historical sciences - anthropology, archeology. The basis of DNA genealogy, one might say, its methodological base is the definition of mutations, or changes (Latin mutatio - change), in DNA, which are transmitted exclusively by inheritance. It is known that the male Y-chromosome, or Y-chromosomal DNA, is passed from father to son, and this has been going on for hundreds of thousands and even millions of years. In the same way, mutations that form from time to time are inherited, averaging about one mutation per generation. The same thing happens in the female line, from mother to daughter, then to her daughter, etc. And a lot can be determined from these changes (mutations). For example, they found the bones of a person who died about five thousand years ago, extracted fossil DNA from them. Then we look where there are other similar mutations, that is, where the “relatives” of this person live. And thus, if generations had not been destroyed, thousands of his descendants could be found that have exactly the same mutations that were originally found in ancient bones. If all this is depicted graphically, it will take the form of an ideal family tree, similar to those that our ancestors hung on the walls of houses. IA Novorossiya: In other words, can DNA genealogy be defined as a science that studies the “pedigree” of DNA mutations? A.K.: Quite right. Genealogy is genealogy. If you write the name of a science in Russian, you get a DNA genealogy. But there is one subtlety here. The study of DNA mutations is always carried out along the male line as a clearer, more straightforward one, since with female mutations the picture is somewhat different, there is no straight line. It can be said that they diverge like circles on water, and over vast territories. The second important aspect of science is the presence of a calculation apparatus, with the help of which historical facts and patterns are clarified, ancient migrations are tracked. For example, it is mathematically calculated from the pattern of mutations how many thousands of years ago the ancestors of a particular group of people lived. That is, one common ancestor is established, from which this “branch”, or group of people, went. In them, these people, root mutations inherited from this ancestor should be identified. This can be compared to a growing tree, in which its “trunk” is a common ancestor, and the “branches” coming from it are mutations. Although there is only one trunk. According to indigenous mutations, it is calculated when and in what period the common ancestor lived. As an example, if we take the southern, or Danubian, Slavs, then their common ancestor lived only 2200 years ago. Although in fact the line of the genus is very ancient, but almost all of them were destroyed about four to five thousand years ago. That is, for several thousand years the remaining Slavs survived, and only went into growth at the end of the last era, 2200 years ago. The South Slavs include Serbs, Croats, Bosnians. In Ukraine, there are about 20% of them, which is more than in Russia (11-12%), since the Danube is nearby. With the help of DNA genealogy, you can track who went where and where they came from. Now, for example, it has already been established that the American Indians, the ancient Maya, are in fact the descendants of Siberians. They left Siberia somewhere around 15-18 thousand years ago and created a completely unique civilization on the Yucatan Peninsula. And we know this thanks to DNA genealogy, which allows us to track the resettlement of people and, on this basis, build the true history of ancient peoples. IA Novorossiya: According to some ancient texts, the ancestral home of the Russian ethnic group was in the north and was called Arctida or Hyperborea. Is it possible to establish with the help of DNA genealogy how true this is, that is, did people who can be considered the ancestors of Russians lived in the north, and when did they live? А.К.: The fact is that myths and legends are not a scientific concept, since it can be difficult to distinguish fiction from real historical facts. Similarly, Hyperborea was taken from ancient Greek myths and transferred to the Kola Peninsula. But people really lived on the Kola Peninsula many thousands of years ago, then, when the glacier happened, everyone who survived went to other places. So far, the root mutations of P1a, which are found in half of modern Russians, have been found in only two places in the north. In the settlement of Veretye, Arkhangelsk region (400 kilometers north of Yaroslavl), a mutation with an “age” of 13 thousand years was found, which indicates with a certain degree of probability that these people could be the ancestors of modern Russians. Also in Karelia, on Deer Lake, similar mutations were found with an average dating of 8375 years ago, or 6850–6000 BC. However, this question must be worked out scientifically, and only then an exact answer can be given to it. I will add that the found root mutation P1a is present in half of modern Russians, Ukrainians, Belarusians, and also Poles. These are the Slavic peoples of the northern or middle zone, they are all related precisely due to the presence of a radical mutation in them. Novorossiya news agency: When did the P1a mutation form? А.К.: Approximately 24 thousand years ago in the Altai region. It is from there that the path of migration towards Europe can be traced. They came there about 10 thousand years ago, which means that the migration process continued for about 15 thousand years. After all, they not only walked, they lived all the way, the climate and habitat changed, and this was a new impetus for the next transition. Naturally, on this "road" they left their descendants. Therefore, P1a exists among the Uighurs, and among the Chinese, and among the Mongols, and in Kazakhstan ... It is impossible to single out some isolated group, people or ethnic group with only one P1a, but it is possible to determine the ethnic group where P1a is most present. This is the majority of the inhabitants of the Slavic countries: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Poland. This is one people. The division occurred for political and religious reasons, as, for example, in the case of Poland, which adopted Catholicism many centuries ago, which rejected the Poles from Orthodoxy. We can say that the Poles have mentally, religiously, customs moved away from other Slavs, although at the same time they remain Slavs, they speak the language of the Slavic group. That is, according to the genealogy, this is the same people as the Belarusians, Ukrainians and Russians. But religion divided them in the same way as Jews and Arabs in their time. Novorossiya news agency: And when were the Slavs: Russians, Ukrainians, Belarusians and Poles one whole, one people? А.К.: Approximately 5 thousand years ago, but, I repeat, at first religion made its contribution, separating the Poles. Then there were other shifts of a political nature, since 1918 new state borders were established. Poland, as you know, having left the Russian Empire, acquired its new borders. As for Ukraine, which was part of the USSR, it also seceded politically in 1991. Therefore, it is only the study of DNA genealogy that can clearly determine who these peoples are by origin, find out their ancient history. It is the most stable, everything else is superficial. News Agency “Novorossiya: Now in Ukraine, Russians are denied the right to be an indigenous people. There are only two of them - these are actually Ukrainians and Crimean Tatars. Is it possible to confirm the right to be an “indigenous people” using DNA genealogy? A.K.: Of course, you can. It is only necessary to define what "indigenous people" are. That is, this is the people whose ancestors lived in this territory for thousands of years. In this regard, the Crimean Tatars can hardly be an indigenous people. They are very diverse, because Crimea is a crossroads of civilizations, everyone was there - Greeks, Byzantines, and Turks. The Crimean Tatars are so diverse that they cannot be singled out as a separate group. Therefore, you can call them an indigenous people, realizing that they are united only by speech that was developed, for example, 1000 years ago. This is important, of course, so there are no objections to the Crimean Tatars being an indigenous people. As for Ukrainians and Russians, they are generally one people. To apply here the concept of "indigenous people" in the sense of which of them is "more indigenous" is complete illiteracy. They have the same common ancestors, the division occurred in language. We all know how the Ukrainian language was created. Gogol wrote in Russian, although he was a Little Russian, Shevchenko did not write at all in the local Surzhik. Therefore, in this case, the language is a conditional indicator. Belarusians are the same, the same indigenous people as Russians and Ukrainians. Novorossiya News Agency: About ten years ago, genetic studies were carried out in Ukraine, during which they concluded that supposedly the inhabitants of Galicia (the center is Lvov) are genetically close to the inhabitants of Donbass? How true is this according to DNA genealogy? A.K.: That's right. Moreover, both the residents of Russia and the residents of Kyiv are very close to the residents of Donbass. In fact, they are all the same people. In Galicia, of course, there are certain enclaves, for example, the Hungarian enclave, there are other haplogroups. It's like in a village, for example, there is the Smirnov family and the Frolov family. According to DNA genealogy, the Frolov family means that their ancestors descended from a certain Frolov. And his descendants will inherit the same mutations, if translated into scientific language, and therefore the Frolov family is one DNA genealogical line. Although the Smirnov family is descended from Smirnov, it may turn out that he only changed his last name. That is, in fact, these are the same people who geographically lived, on the one hand, somewhat apart, and secondly, there may have been tributaries of the Hungarians. It's just that Galicia is somewhat different politically. But this policy has nothing to do with origin. For example, if we take the period of the Civil War in Russia, there were the same people by origin - both red and white. You probably know why the White Army did not award orders for participation in the Civil War. But because it's a shame to kill your own! Because it is unworthy and shameful to kill our own, but only because otherwise they will kill us, we have to conduct military operations. But it was impossible to reward for a fratricidal war. It was in the Red Army that they handed out orders, because they were not guided by these concepts of honor. Novorossiya News Agency: In Ukraine, information is now being spread that supposedly Russians are Finno-Ugric peoples. What can DNA genealogy say in this regard? A.K .: This is complete nonsense, I even wonder how people do not understand this. Firstly, Slavs are people who speak the language of the Slavic group. Poles, Russians, Belarusians, Ukrainians, Serbs, Croats - they all speak languages of the Slavic group, so by definition they are all Slavs. Except for those whose native language is different, say, for example, the Mari, Komi, Chuvash or Tatars. They are not Slavs, their native language is Turkic. The Russians have a native Russian, which means they are Slavs, the question is closed. Finno-Ugric peoples, or Finno-Ugric peoples, their native language is Ugric. These are Estonians, Karelians, Finns, Mari. Ugric is the Uralic languages, they are not Slavs. They are part of the Russian Federation, but not Slavs, just as the Tatars are not Slavs. Therefore, when Russians are classified as Finno-Ugric, it is simply ridiculous. Among Russians, 14% of people belong to the haplogroup (or genus) of Ural origin. But their native language is Russian, and they are Slavs, albeit of Uralic origin, especially since they usually don’t know about it. For example, the writer Ivan Bunin, Nobel Prize winner in literature, he would be very surprised that his distant ancestors were of Ural origin. And those for whom the native language of the Finno-Ugric group are not Russians, they are Mari, Chuvash, Udmurts, Komi, etc. Therefore, here you just need to understand, since the Slavic language is the Slavs. IA Novorossiya: Some people confuse DNA genealogy with genetics. Are these two sciences different from each other? А.К.: Completely different. They have completely different methodologies. Genetics studies genes, but DNA genealogy does not contain genes. Therefore, geneticists could not create a DNA genealogy, they do not have a calculation apparatus, and their conclusions are not of a historical nature. DNA genealogy is actually a historical science, it is aimed at studying history. Those who say about me that “he is not a geneticist,” so I don’t want to be a geneticist. Because, if I were a geneticist, I would never apply the formulas and equations of physical chemistry, of which I am a specialist, to DNA mutations. And the DNA genealogy would have remained undiscovered. IA Novorossiya: Thank you for the interview. We hope to see you soon. Full access, special status and immunity Serbia demands explanations from Ukraine about secret US laboratories on its territory A key player representing US interests in this region is the Science and Technology Center in Ukraine (STCU), through which most of the biosafety projects in the region are implemented. The history of cooperation between the Moldovan authorities and the STCU dates back to 2003, when it was decided to join the Agreement on the Establishment of the Scientific and Technological Center. By that time, the STCU, in the status of an intergovernmental organization, had been working on the territory of a neighboring country for 10 years and began to actively expand its activities within the former post-Soviet space. Today, the parties to the Agreement are Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova, Ukraine, Uzbekistan, as well as the United States and the European Union. In total, the STCU has about 180 partner companies, within the framework of various projects, the center has distributed over 300 million dollars. , in case of their interest, in other states of the former USSR. The Center engages weapons scientists and engineers in its work, especially those with knowledge and skills related to weapons of mass destruction or missile systems. Among its goals, STCU declares assistance through its projects in solving national or international technical problems, supporting fundamental and applied research and technology development, as well as integrating scientists from the former USSR into the international scientific community. In addition to governments and international structures, STCU cooperates with civil society and the private sector , if necessary, can open branches in different territories. Over the past 14 years, the foreign staff of the center has a special status in Moldova and enjoys a number of benefits. The staff of the center is exempt from any taxation and other fees, as well as immigration restrictions and procedures for the registration of foreigners. In Moldova, as in other countries of the former USSR that have acceded to the Agreement, STCU staff have the right to study the situation related to projects and available materials on the spot. Text In Sweden, the international exercise Aurora was recently concluded. Even in Russia, there has been a lot of talk about "Aurora" lately, albeit in a completely different context. It will soon be 100 years since the October Revolution. It began, as you know, with the shots from the cruiser Aurora, which has since become one of the main symbols of this disputed era. Strangely enough, it was precisely this tragic period for our country that became the starting point for a new chapter of Russian-Swedish relations, and drove a unprecedentedly put their development forward. We remember well that Sweden, which had played a minor role as a trading partner to the Russian Empire, was the first in the West to establish trade relations with the internationally isolated Soviet Russia and towards 1920 became its largest importer. The neutral Sweden showed thereby on the importance of building a mutually beneficial and constructive cooperation with the neighbor in the East, regardless of the political situation, and became a role model for the whole world. The relationship between our countries was also later during the Soviet era essentially good, and not even the protracted Cold War with all its "submarine drama" could change that. Against this background, it appears even more strange that Russia and Sweden for some reason find it much more difficult to find points of contact now than in the past. I ask myself this question not least based on my own diplomatic career, which for roughly 37 years (apart from shorter intervals) was in one way or another devoted to neighboring Sweden. When I compare the tense 1970s and 1980s with today's situation, I come to a paradoxical conclusion. Despite the fact that our country has changed its state and taken a huge step forward in terms of openness and democratization, the Swedish view of Russia has obviously not changed for the better. The bilateral relations can hardly be said to be flourishing either. Honestly, I have never before felt such a fear of Russia in Sweden as I do today. In the country where the descendants of Axel Oxenstierna, Karl XIV Johan and Olof Palme live, it has become commonplace to fuel the "Russian threat" in every way and demonize Russia. It sometimes seems that Western politicians, no matter how Russia behaves, would still mechanically complain about its "guilt". This has its explanation in the fact that, while in the 1990s, after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the fall of the Iron Curtain, our country diligently fulfilled all "diplomatic settlements" , many in the West could not overcome their "victory complex" and held on to old ideological stereotypes. A paradoxical situation arose whereby NATO not only refrained from following the example of the disbanded Warsaw Pact but, on the contrary, continued to expand its borders by persistently expanding eastwards. What did it ultimately result in? Every state that does not have its position heard is forced to firmly assert its national interests. No one who is cornered acts differently, do they? But it turned out that Russia was once again considered guilty because she would have disturbed the European security order. But what then should one call what NATO, led by the United States, did in the Balkans by bombing Serbia and without any "national referendums" establishing a "independent" Kosovo? What did the highly renowned European politicians do at that moment and what happened to their "principled support" for international law and the supremacy of the law? So far this year, after all, we have been able to observe some glimmers of light in the relations between our countries. We look positively on Foreign Minister Margot Wallström's and EU and Trade Minister Ann Linde's visit to Russia, and on the bilateral contacts between our foreign ministers that took place in connection with, among other things, OSCE meeting, UN General Assembly session and regional forums. The direct line between the military commands in Russia and Sweden, which has been operating since July, has served us well, not least during the exercises "Aurora" and "Zapad". Bilateral trade, which during 2014-2016 more than halved, increased during the first half of the year by 35 percent. However, it is still too early to talk about a full-fledged revival of Russian-Swedish relations. This requires a breakthrough in overcoming the artificial obstacles that are sometimes raised. And we have a lot to do: we need to restore trust and political dialogue, restore the greatly reduced trade and economic exchange, take on global challenges and reconnect our humanitarian and cultural contacts. When I meet Swedish businessmen and scientists, cultural figures and regional politicians in my work, I feel their incomprehension and disappointment at the lack of constructive dialogue between Moscow and Stockholm, which makes it difficult for their activities in Russia. The relations between Russia and Sweden have never been completely painless. But in 1814 we made our fateful choice and drew a line over the long-standing military dilemma. I will think of what the Swedish chancellor Axel Oxenstierna said long before that, during the Thirty Years' War: "I freely confess and admit, nothing would be more convenient, more useful, safer, yes, more necessary for our state and fatherland than peace with Russia..."I I think it is high time to make peace not only on the battlefield but also in the minds. Having said that, I would like to express my wish that the upcoming election campaign, in accordance with the proud traditions of Swedish democracy, will remain free from the notorious "external influence", and will be conducted honorably, without dirty measures. The General Assembly overwhelmingly adopted a resolution demanding that Russia cease hostilities in Ukraine. Only four dictatorships voted against with Moscow and 35 countries abstained. A historic vote to increase diplomatic pressure. By Carrie Nooten (New York, United Nations, correspondent) Reading Time 5 min.Seven days after the outbreak of war, Vladimir Putin's Russia was banned from the international community on Wednesday March 2 in New York, during the adoption of the resolution "Aggression against Ukraine". The text asks Moscow to "stop using force in Ukraine" and condemns its decision "to accentuate the alerting of its nuclear forces". It was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly, where all member states are represented, in order to circumvent the veto imposed by Russia on the Security Council six days earlier. The vote, which was held after two days and a half speech, lasted less than a minute; the results were immediately displayed on the giant screens of the hemicycle: 141 countries, out of 193 members, approved the resolution, 5 opposed it and 35, including China, abstained. The result confirmed, a large majority of diplomats stood up and applauded a vote that many described as "historic". "The message of the General Assembly is loud and clear", reacted Secretary General Antonio Guterres after the ballot. “End hostilities in Ukraine – now. Open the door to dialogue and diplomacy – now. "A huge majority of nations recognize that Putin is attacking not just Ukraine, but the very foundations of peace and security in the world," added US President Joe Biden in a statement. "The international community has shown its unity," said Emmanuel Macron, Wednesday evening, during a televised intervention devoted to the conflict. Russia appeared even more isolated than in 2014, during a similar condemnation in the Assembly General Assembly for the annexation of Crimea: instead of the ten countries which had voted in favor of it then, only four dictatorships did so yesterday – Belarus, Syria, North Korea and Eritrea. "Vladimir Putin's Russia is joining the club of the worst pariahs", analyzes a European diplomat, who underlines that such mobilization is very rare for this kind of resolution "pointing the finger at a country". For him, “the brutality with which the events have unfolded over the past ten days has made even the countries geographically most distant from Ukraine react. Vladimir Putin certainly underestimated the power of social media.” Showing Russia's isolation is crucial in Western strategy. Even if this resolution has no binding value, unlike those voted by the Security Council, diplomats are counting on its symbolic value and the pressure it could exert on the holding of talks with a view to an uncertain cease fire. Le Monde with AFP Reading Time 4 min. The General Assembly of the United Nations (UN) adopted, on Wednesday March 2, by an overwhelming majority, a resolution which “demands that Russia immediately cease the use of force against Ukraine”. A vote hailed as "historic" and greeted by a round of applause. Of the 193 members of the UN, 141 countries approved the text, five - Russia, Belarus, North Korea, Eritrea and Syria - are there opposed and thirty-five abstained, including China. of Ukraine and "condemns Russia's decision to increase the alerting of its nuclear forces". Led by the European Union (EU) in coordination with Ukraine, the text also "deplores" "in the terms Russia's aggression against Ukraine" and affirms "its commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity" of this country. The President of the United States, Joe Biden, judged that the vote “exposed in broad daylight the isolation” of his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin. "An overwhelming majority of nations recognize that Putin is attacking not just Ukraine, but the very foundations of world peace and security," he said in a statement. General Assembly is loud and clear, responded UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres. End hostilities in Ukraine – now. Open the door to dialogue and diplomacy – now. "For the head of European diplomacy, Josep Borrell, the result of the vote is "historic", a point of view shared by the British Prime Minister, Boris Johnson, for whom "rarely has the contrast between good and evil been so titled “Aggression against Ukraine”, the resolution also calls for unhindered humanitarian access and “deplores the involvement of Belarus” in the attack on Ukraine.In the room of the General Assembly, many countries had placed on the table of their delegation soft toys of giraffes, bears or rabbits to underline their support for the younger generations. The Ambassador of Ukraine to the United Nations, Sergiy Kyslytsya , had denounced just before the tribune a "genocide" in progress in his country, perpetrated by Russia. “It is already clear that Russia's goal is not just an occupation. It's genocide," he said, while US Ambassador to the UN Linda Thomas-Greenfield said Russia intended to use "cluster munitions" and "thermobaric weapons. “, banned by the Geneva Convention. North America and Europe, the resolution benefited from the favorable vote of many African States, but not that of South Africa, which abstained, like Algeria, the Central African Republic and Mali, two countries currently developing their ties with Russia. Burkina Faso, where there was a recent coup, did not vote; Senegal opted for a surprising abstention. A majority of Latin American countries, although far removed from the Ukrainian theatre, voted in favor of the resolution. For the Middle East, the United Arab Emirates – suspected of having concluded a more or less tacit agreement with Russia in exchange for a favorable vote on Monday by this country in the Security Council to designate the Yemeni Houthis as "terrorists" - voted in favor, breaking with a position followed since last week in the Council. Iran, in negotiations on its nuclear program with Russia in particular, abstained, a position also adopted by Iraq. Saudi Arabia and Israel voted in favor of the resolution. The population of Russia has been declining since the fall of the USSR, a decline that has not been halted by the measures taken by Vladimir Putin By Frank Tétart (Doctor in geopolitics), Floriane Picard, Flavie Holzinger, Delphine Papin and Victor Simonnet Time de Lecture 2 min.Since the fall of the Soviet Union, the population has continued to decline in Russia. The year 1992 marked a turning point: for the first time in a large developed country, the death rate greatly exceeded the birth rate. With 147 million inhabitants in 1989, the country will only have 145.47 million in 2021, according to the Russian State Federal Statistics Service (Rosstat). This figure includes the 2.4 million inhabitants of the Crimean peninsula, annexed in 2014. According to forecasts, the country's demography could stagnate between 130 and 140 million people in 2050. Moreover, the share of ethnic Russian has shrunk from 81.5% of the total population in 1989 to 77.7% today. The rate of the working population is also falling, at the risk of causing major social problems. decade – and its consequences (cardiovascular diseases and road accidents caused more than 30,000 annual deaths in the 2000s; and another 18,000 in 2018). However, this decline is only slightly offset by the birth rate, despite the measures taken by the State from 2007. Although the birth rate has risen to 1.6 children per woman since 2010 (compared to 1.16 in 1999 ), it remains far from the generation renewal rate, statistically fixed at 2.05. Between October 2020 and September 2021, the Covid-19 epidemic also claimed the lives of nearly one million inhabitants or indirectly, according to Russian demographer Alexei Rakcha. The health measures have been little followed by the population, and the vaccination campaign has proved laborious: at the beginning of March 2022, only one inhabitant in two had received two doses in Russia. This decline is hampering the projects of Vladimir Putin, who , as soon as he came to power in 2000, had bet on population growth as a factor in the return of Russian power on the international scene. At the national level, it also thwarts the desired rebalancing between the weight of the Russians – and more generally of the Slavs (mainly Christians) – and that of the Muslim populations, whose fertility rate remains higher. Not only are migrations from the countries of the former USSR, initially encouraged by Moscow, no longer sufficient to offset the demographic decline, but they are decried by the Russian majority, when the country already has 2 million Caucasians. 11 mins. Story "Russia-Ukraine, the war of stories" (2/3). "Le Monde" returns to the way in which the memories of the two countries clash. Second part, the famine which decimated millions of Ukrainian peasants, an emblematic drama, concealed by the Soviet power and minimized by Vladimir Putin. There was a crowd, Brotteaux station, to welcome President Herriot to his good city. It must be said that on September 13, 1933, the irremovable mayor of Lyon, leader of the Radical Party and former President of the Council, was returning from an unusual trip. A few days earlier, at the invitation of the Soviet government, he had crossed the USSR, from Odessa to the Baltic. Since the October Revolution of 1917, it was the first time that a political leader of this stature had the opportunity to visit the homeland of communism, about which disturbing rumors had circulated for months. As soon as he got off the train, the question that was on everyone's lips was asked: is there a famine in Ukraine? Edouard Herriot's response is anything but spontaneous: “I crossed Ukraine. Well ! I tell you that I saw it as a garden in full production, a beautiful garden with black and rich soil covered, over considerable areas, by magnificent harvests. It is assured, you will say to me, that this region lives at these times in a sad time? I can't talk about what I haven't seen. However, I had myself taken to places that were said to be tested. However, I have only seen prosperity. "In his account Tout passe (in Œuvres, Robert Laffont, 2006), the great Soviet writer Vassili Grossman made a devastating allusion to this episode: "One day, I remember, an old man brought the president of the kolkhoz a piece of newspaper, which he had picked up on the way. A Frenchman had come to our house, a well-known minister, and they had taken him to the Dnepropetrovsk region where the most appalling famine was raging, a famine even worse than ours. There, men eat man. So the minister was taken to a village, to the kindergarten of the kolkhoz, and there he asked: “What did you eat for lunch? And the children answered: “Chicken broth, pirozhki and rice croquettes.” To say that I read this with my own eyes. This piece of newspaper, I can still see it. But what is this ? We coldly kill millions of people and we abuse, we deceive the whole world! Chicken broth they write! Croquettes ! While they ate earthworms…” Edouard Herriot stayed two weeks in the USSR, including five days in rich Ukraine (from August 26 to 30, 1933) and, even though during the previous months, 3 to 5 million people were starving there, so he didn't see anything. In a meticulous and damning investigation (Le Voyage de monsieur Herriot, L'Harmattan, 2018), historian Iryna Dmytrychyn sheds light on the means deployed by Stalin to conceal the tragedy as well as the part of blindness that it took to French to accept, in the name of reason of state, to look away when what he saw did not fit with the official narrative. City streets "cleaned" of corpses and all traces of misery, shops suddenly full, hotels hastily repainted (to the point that the smell bothers visitors)... Nothing is missing, and the pinnacle is reached in Kiev , when Edouard Herriot enters the Sainte-Sophie cathedral, at the time of a service: “It's Sunday. The old archbishop, in a golden robe edged in red, motionless, (…) impassively presides over the ceremony, while chants rise, followed with reverence by a few poor women under dark arcades”, he will describe. later, still bewitched by the scene. 18 mins. ReportIn ten years, Ukraine has become one of the world's leading grain exporters. A formidable agricultural logistics seized by the Russian invasion launched on February 24th. The blockade of the Black Sea threatens the food security of many countries which obtain wheat, corn, rapeseed, sunflower, barley from Kiev...These grains of wheat that Boris Z. slips between his fingers, in the shadow of his warehouse in Velyka Mykhailivka, in the Odessa region, should have been sold and ended up, precious starch, precious calories, in the stomach of an Egyptian, a Tunisian or a Lebanese child, after having sailed through the holds of a giant freighter on the Black Sea, in the Bosphorus Strait, on the Mediterranean, and beyond. Because of the war, these wheats have remained in the steel sheds, by the hundreds of tons, and Boris Z. sadly lets his thoughts slip away like flowing grain. “Tomorrow?, he asks himself. I don't know what the future will hold. My horizon stops at the day after. The 38-year-old farmer, father of two children, who left to take refuge abroad with their mother, does not want to give his name, and it is easy to understand. With his hand, he points to his fields in the distance, which border the border with Transnistria, a pro-Russian separatist territory in Moldova, northwest of Odessa, where 1,500 soldiers are stationed under the orders of President Putin. A handful of grains in his hand, with this peasant gesture that weighs with gravity for millennia, Boris Z. says his fear of the future for his country and for the planet: "I had illusions before, like everyone world. War is hitting us Ukrainians, but Putin has declared a war against the whole world and food is a terrible weapon. “Under the April sun, the entrepreneur follows the seed drill as it advances with the regularity of a jewel of technology, controlled by GPS, on his land ready for spring sowing – 13 kilometers traveled per hour, a sunflower seed placed every 20 centimeters under 5 centimeters of soil. With its 3,000 hectares, a considerable area in France but average for Ukraine, the thirty permanent employees of Boris Z. produce more than 10,000 tonnes of wheat and sunflower. In times of peace, a noria of trucks comes to load the seeds, washed, dried, transported to the immense steel silos of Odessa, Youjné, Tchornomorsk or Mykolaiv, the ports of the Black Sea, where they will be embarked. The winter wheat, planted at the end of 2021, has already largely grown on this black soil, called "chernozem", among the most fertile in the world, rich in humus, potash, nitrogen and trace elements. By July, the fields will take on the yellow color, that of the Ukrainian flag, under the blue of the sky. This will mean that, sun-kissed, plants will have acquired those caloric values that have fed billions of humans since our species ceased to be hunter-gatherers. But can these wheats be harvested? In what proportion? At what cost? And, above all, how will they cross the thousands of kilometers that separate them from Africa, the Middle East or Asia, if Russia persists in blocking the ports of the Black Sea? By Marie Jégo, Faustine Vincent and Benoît Vitkine (Moscow, correspondent) Reading Time 5 min. They are thin, exhausted, but alive, and now free. Against all expectations, Kiev announced, on the night of Wednesday September 21 to Thursday September 22, the release of 215 Ukrainian prisoners, including 188 "heroes" of the battle of Azovstal in Mariupol, a port city in southern Ukraine razed by Russian bombings. Among them are 108 members of the Azov regiment, which the Kremlin nevertheless presents as the worst Nazi war criminals since the Second World War. Their fate remained uncertain since a missile hit the prison of Olenivka, in the pro-Russian separatist region of Donetsk, on July 29. About fifty Azovstal fighters, whose identity has not been revealed, were then killed. A symbolic defeat for Russian President Vladimir Putin, the five military commanders of Azovstal were also released. These men, whose fierce resistance held millions of people around the world in suspense during the siege of the factory in April and May, have been transferred to Turkey.Under an agreement reached with the Turkish President, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, these five soldiers – Azov commander Denys Prokopenko, Sviatoslav Palamar, Serhi Volynsky, Denys Shlega and Oleg Khomenko – will remain “in absolute security” in this country and will live “in comfortable conditions until the end of war," said the Ukrainian president. They are now placed "under the personal protection" of the Turkish number one. Upon their arrival in Turkey, the five officers, in camouflage uniforms, spoke by videoconference with the Ukrainian President, Volodymyr Zelensky. Taken to a place of residence kept confidential, they will, these days, “receive medical care, rest, see their families, who will soon join them”, explains a Ukrainian diplomat. The fate of the five Azovstal officers was the subject of particular attention from Russia, which insisted that they could not return to Ukraine, where they would certainly have taken up arms again. An arrangement has therefore been reached with Turkey, where they will have to stay until the end of the conflict. By Benoît Vitkine (Moscow, correspondent) Reading Time 3 min.Nearly eight months after its launch, the “special military operation” launched by Vladimir Putin on February 24 is once again changing in nature. The most obvious sign of this turning point: the missiles that fell on downtown Kiev, spared for several months. In all, according to the Russian authorities, more than 150 missiles were fired on Monday, October 10, throughout Ukrainian territory. Drones were also used. Energy or communication infrastructures, but also a playground for children and cars were affected. At least twelve people were killed and eighty others injured, according to Kiev. Certainly, the major Ukrainian cities had already been the target of massive bombardments, in the early days of the Russian invasion. The vocabulary used on Monday by the Russian Ministry of Defense and by Vladimir Putin was thus reminiscent of known formulations – it is always a question of “high-precision missiles”, attacks targeting “the Kiev regime” and not the population… However, the punitive, even vengeful nature of this latest bombing campaign is evident, two days after the attack attributed by Moscow to a truck bomb that damaged the Crimean bridge. Vladimir Putin barely concealed it when he spoke to his security council on Monday. After accusing Kiev of “atomic terrorism” or referring to unknown sabotage attempts on the Turkish Stream gas pipeline, the Russian president considered that “the Kiev regime is thus putting itself on the same level as the most repulsive terrorist groups in the world. planet”. "Leaving this unanswered is impossible," he concluded. Another telling sign is the missile dropped on the glass bridge that runs over St. Vladimir's Hill in central Kiev. Without even mentioning its non-existent military value, the building, used by tourists, does not play the slightest role in the functioning of the Ukrainian capital. Crimean bridge against pedestrian footbridge, the message is clear. 'chivalrous soul', according to the propagandist journalist Alexander Kots – is a myth that only lived for a few days, at the end of February. Washington, long reluctant to give up its most sophisticated military equipment, has confirmed the delivery to Ukraine of one of these batteries. By Cédric Pietralunga Reading Time 3 min. This is a new sign of the upgrading of the Ukrainian army. Long reluctant to give up their most sophisticated military equipment, for fear of an escalation with Russia, the United States confirmed, on Wednesday, December 21, the delivery of a Patriot air defense system to troops in Kiev. on the sidelines of the visit of the Ukrainian President, Volodymyr Zelensky, to Washington, and intended to reassure on the continuation of Western support, three hundred days after the invasion of Ukraine by Russia. "What we do, what we continue to do, is to ensure that the Ukrainians have the means to defend themselves effectively against Russian aggression", justified a senior American official. Designed in the 1960s , the Patriot is considered one of the best anti-aircraft defense devices in Western armies. It has been deployed many times in theaters of operations, by the United States but also by one of the seventeen countries to have it, notably Israel and Saudi Arabia. "The Patriot is the workhorse of the anti-aircraft and anti-missile defense of the American army, a key element of the projection of power of the United States”, recalls the American think tank CSIS, in a note published on December 16. It is Patriots who protect, for example, the Rzeszow-Jasionka airport in south-eastern Poland, through which a large part of Western military aid to Ukraine currently passes. Regularly modernized since its first commissioning service, in 1982, the Patriot system is reputed to be effective against aircraft but especially against ballistic and cruise missiles, which Russia makes intensive use of in Ukraine to destroy the country's energy infrastructure. It does, however, have more difficulty "engaging" low-flying drones, a weakness shared by many ground-to-air systems. Some 90 operators are required to operate a Patriot battery, which includes radar, a command center , an electric generator and up to eight launchers with four to sixteen missiles each, depending on their nature. Washington recognizes that "some time" of training, estimated at a minimum of three months by specialists, will be necessary before the Ukrainian military can use it. This Patriot battery complements the previous deliveries of ground-to-air defense equipment made by Westerners. This embarrassing discovery is added to that of classified documents, at the end of November, in a former office of the American president. Joe Biden claims to "cooperate fully" with American justice. By Sandra Favier (with AFP) Reading Time 3 min. The new year does not begin auspiciously for the White House. Two days after an initial revelation, Joe Biden's aides discovered another batch of classified documents at a residence of the president, according to a statement from a White House legal adviser on Thursday, January 12, confirming US media reports, including NBC News and New York Times. It is in this context that this second series of documents was found. Most were in "a storage space in the garage" of the Wilmington home, the statement said, with only one other, page-long item discovered among other documents in an adjacent room. was found in the Rehoboth Beach residence. As with the first discoveries, the documents have been handed over to the Department of Justice, the statement said, which also recalls that the "White House will continue to cooperate with the Justice Department's investigation". This second investigation closes the research. The American Minister of Justice, Merrick Garland, on Thursday appointed an independent prosecutor to investigate the documents found. “I have signed a document appointing Robert Hur as a special prosecutor” which “authorizes him to investigate any person or entity who may have violated the law” in this case, he said during a short speech. November, Mr. Biden's lawyers had found confidential documents - including briefing notes on foreign countries, according to the New York Times - in one of the offices he sometimes used as a workplace. These documents, like those found in his residence, date from when Joe Biden was Barack Obama's Vice President (2009-2017). Per government rules, access to classified documents is limited to accredited individuals and items should be kept in secure cabinets. According to the Presidential Records Act, official documents, classified or not, must also be deposited in the National Archives after the departure of an administration. The administration of the Democratic president had so far confirmed that a “small number of classified documents” – about ten – had been found in a “locked cupboard” at the Penn Biden Center, a think tank where Joe Biden once had an office. “I was surprised to learn that documents relating to the government had been taken from this office. But I don't know what's in the documents,” the president told reporters on Tuesday on the sidelines of a summit with the Mexican president and the prime minister of Canada in Mexico City. Thursday, Joe Biden assured, during a brief exchange with the press, "to fully cooperate" with American justice. On Tuesday, the CBS channel announced that the Minister of Justice, Merrick Garland, had appointed a magistrate to examine the first documents discovered at the Penn Biden Center. With this new twist, the case should still make noise and could serve as an argument for the Republican camp while justice is also investigating the numerous documents stored by former President Donald Trump in his Florida residence, after his departure from the White House in 2021. So far, the case of the billionaire is considered more serious, the federal police (FBI) having seized, during a spectacular search, thousands of documents, including a hundred classified secret-defense than the Republican refused to return. But the recent discoveries remain embarrassing for the Democratic president, who has long put forward his ethical standards as opposed to his predecessor. According to commentators, they could also introduce delicate political considerations into the investigation into Donald Trump, who immediately called that Joe Biden receives the same attention. “When will the FBI raid Joe Biden’s many residences, or even the White House? he reacted. Republicans call for the creation of a "special council" to investigate the Democratic president. On Twitter, Senator Josh Hawley shared the NBC News article, simply accompanied by the words "special advice". "Congress must investigate this matter," the Republican Speaker of the House of Representatives told reporters on Thursday. , Kevin McCarthy, denouncing “a new misstep by the Biden administration”. Even though the extent of the documents stored by President Biden is different, the embarrassment was palpable among the Democrats on Thursday and it did not escape their opposition. “Remember how the left reacted when President Trump took so-called 'confidential' documents home? She's awfully quiet today,” commented Republican House Representative Jim Jordan, a loyal aide to Donald Trump. The White House argues that if mistakes were made, the administration at least immediately rectified them. . As soon as the first documents were found, at the end of November, lawyers returned them to the National Archives, which manages this type of file, she defended herself. To defuse accusations of political interference, the attorney general assigned the case to a Chicago prosecutor appointed during the Trump administration. The secrecy of the investigation was mentioned by the spokesperson for the White House, Karine Jean-Pierre, to justify her refusal to answer questions from journalists on this subject on Wednesday. Which wasn't enough to stop them. "We're going to be limited in what we can say here," she said. European Union and its 450 million citizens. This text, negotiated since June 2016 and ratified by the Commission in October 2021, must still be validated by MEPs. Neither the monetary crisis nor the consequences of the February 6 earthquake once again got the better of the Turkish president's ability to stay in power. Given the loser in the polls before the first round of the presidential election, the head of state won on Sunday with 52% of the vote. By Marie Jégo Reading Time 6 min. After defying all predictions about his possible end to his reign, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan was re-elected on Sunday May 28 for a third five-year term. At 69, he remains the most popular politician since Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the father of modern Turkey, which he surpassed in terms of prerogatives and longevity at the head of the state. The dominant personality of the Turkish political scene, adored by his supporters – who see him as a father –, hated by his detractors, who protest to see him cultivate the stature of a sultan, leaves no one indifferent. the presidential election with 52% of the vote, he has until 2028 to build a "Second Republic", which he imagines to be more religious, more autocratic, more oriented towards the Gulf, Russia and China than the first, born there a hundred years on the rubble of the ottoman empire. After twenty years of exercise of power, nothing seems to be able to undermine his charisma, neither his frenzied authoritarianism (200,000 legal inquiries are opened for insulting the president) nor inflation ( 44% on annual average), which is hitting the population hard, barely recovering from the devastating earthquake of February 6, which was aggravated by the reaction deemed too slow by the government he leads. Paradoxically, the conservative and pious masses of Turkey – “my people”, as he says – did not hold it against him. His re-election for a third term, while the Constitution authorizes two, confirms his status as an unsinkable president. In twenty years, he has overcome everything: mass protests, corruption scandals, an attempted military coup, the abandonment of his former traveling companions. "The king is naked", said of him last year Bülent Arinç, with whom he founded the AKP. In decline perhaps. Certainly not naked. His age, his health no longer allow him to wet his shirt as he once did. Victim of discomfort and then falling asleep during two television interviews during his campaign, the president is no longer as alert but he has other strings to his bow. A populist leader with strong authoritarian roots, he has, in twenty years of reign, considerably strengthened his control over the country. This influence is also material. The democratic opposition parties put aside their differences for the time of a gigantic anti-government march in the capital. The initiative was launched by Donald Tusk, candidate for the post of Prime Minister, with the approach of the legislative elections of the fall. By Hélène Bienvenu (Warsaw, correspondence) Reading Time 5 min. A tidal wave of Polish and European flags swept through the streets of central Warsaw on Sunday, June 4, under a blazing sun. The crowd responded to the call of Donald Tusk, one of the leaders of the opposition, a few months before the legislative elections in the fall. This 66-year-old man, who was Prime Minister from 2007 to 2014, and who returned to Polish politics after chairing the European Council, called on April 15 for a march in Warsaw "against inflation, theft and lie and for free elections, democracy and a European Poland”. The leader of the Civic Platform (PO), the main democratic opposition formation, could hardly have dreamed of a better way to relaunch his electoral campaign. Warsaw City Hall estimated the number of demonstrators at nearly 500,000, a figure not reached for more than thirty years, in a country which has lost the habit of massive gatherings of the Solidarnosc years. young people, pensioners, families converged on the capital by their own means, in coaches or specially chartered trains, to express their fed up with the policy of the ultra-conservatives of the PiS (Law and Justice) party, in power since 2015, and accused of having restricted the freedoms of Polish citizens. In any case, this is what Romek Hryncewicz thinks, who left Sunday morning Dobre Miasto, a small town of 10,000 inhabitants, 240 kilometers north of Warsaw. This psychologist remembers very well the communist era and its hardships. “I was 17 in 1989 when communism fell. Today, we can travel freely within the European Union and the government is threatening to get us out of it”, protests this 50-year-old. “This autumn, we will be dealing with the most important elections since 1989. This government exceeds all bounds and if the PiS wins once again, it is not excluded that it falsifies the next elections, because it will have completely appropriated the courts and will not fail to silence the free media that we have again,” adds the protester, who is waving a European flag. The opposition may owe part of its success on Sunday to a government initiative. A decried law, which came into force on May 30, creates a commission of inquiry into Russian influence, likely to dismiss from any post involving public funds anyone who has been too close to the Kremlin. The commission was deemed unconstitutional by many jurists and was condemned by Brussels and Washington. Bao Choy, a freelance journalist, was fined in 2021 for "false reporting" in connection with an investigation into the 2019 assault on pro-democracy activists. Le Monde with AFP Reading Time 1 min. Hong Kong's Supreme Court on Monday (June 5) overturned the conviction of a journalist for an investigation into the July 2019 assault on pro-democracy activists by pro-Beijing. In 2021, a court convicted Bao Choy, an independent journalist , fined 6,000 HKD (700 euros) after convicting her of “misrepresentation” to obtain, in a public register, the records of ownership of a vehicle within the framework of an investigation she was carrying out .The online form for accessing this information provided three options for applicants: “for legal proceedings”, “for the sale and purchase of vehicles” and “for other traffic and traffic matters”. transportation ". Bao Choy had chosen the last option, which in the eyes of the trial court and also on appeal did not correspond to a journalistic purpose. But on Monday, a group of five Supreme Court judges unanimously decided to cancel condemnation, finding that “there was no reason (…) for good faith journalism to be excluded [in the definition of third choice]”. "'Other traffic and transport matters' may be taken in a broader sense to include serious investigative journalism undertaken here," the judges said in their decision. They added that this expansive interpretation was tied to the “constitutionally protected freedom of speech and press.” “Happy.” I can't think of another word to describe my state of mind right now,” reporter Bao Choy said after the decision. "I think that kind of happiness should be shared by everyone in our society," she added. that Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020. The journalist had carried out her research as part of a documentary she produced in 2020 for the Hong Kong public broadcaster RTHK. She was investigating the responsiveness of the police during of the July 2019 assault, a key event in the violent pro-democracy protests that year in Hong Kong. The award-winning documentary claims that on the evening of the assault, police failed to respond to the arrival en masse in special vehicles of men armed with sticks in Yuen Long district. Using vehicle ownership records, Bao Choy's documentary revealed new details about the alleged attackers, some of whom have ties to pro-Beijing and politically influential rural committees. The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) considers that the adjustments that have been made since have not changed the situation. It therefore demands that Warsaw take back its copy. Le Monde with AFP Reading Time 1 min. The reform of the Polish justice system, introduced by the nationalist populist government in 2019 and the subject of a standoff between Warsaw and Brussels, violates Community law, announced on Monday June 5, the Court of Justice of the European Union ( CJEU). And this in particular in its section relating to the disciplinary system of judges and their independence, specified the Court in its judgment, immediately welcomed by the European Commission which had seized it of this reform. “It is an important day for the restoration of an independent judiciary in Poland", commented the European Commissioner for Justice, Didier Reynders, explaining that the Polish law "undermines the independence of judges". "After today's decision, the law on the judiciary will have to be adapted accordingly", he added, stressing that the CJEU's decision "definitively settles the question". He urged the Polish authorities “to comply fully with the judgment”. The Polish justice minister denounced a decision unfavorable to Poland. "The EU's main court is corrupt", and the decision condemning Poland for its controversial justice reform "was not written by judges, but by politicians", in "violation of the treaties", said Zbigniew Ziobro, representative of an openly anti-European party, quoted by the PAP agency. In 2021, the CJEU sentenced Poland to fines of one million euros per day to stop the activities of the disciplinary chamber of the Supreme Court, a key institution in a controversial reform of the Polish judicial system. The amount of these fines has so far exceeded 550 million euros. Poland has always refused to pay these fines, but Brussels has taken part of them from the funds intended for Poland. The judgment of the European Court lifts the financial sanction as of June 5, but Poland must still settle the sums due for the past. Russian and Ukrainian authorities accuse each other of being behind strikes on the power plant dam. According to the Ukrainian Interior Ministry, 24 localities were flooded Tuesday at midday. The evacuation of civilians is underway. By Sandra Favier Reading Time 6 min. the front about forty kilometers to the north. The dam of the Kakhovka hydroelectric power station in southern Ukraine was partially destroyed on the night of Monday June 5 to Tuesday June 6. Several towns and villages were flooded in Ukraine, including the city of Kherson . Located about 60 kilometers to the east, it was the first major locality to fall into Russian hands in March 2022, before being taken over by the Ukrainian army in mid-November. Residents have begun to be evacuated, with Ukraine's railway company announcing that it has increased the frequency of its trains to help civilians leave. The Nova Kakhovka Dam, located in a Moscow-controlled area of Ukraine's Kherson region, was partially destroyed overnight after several explosions. The circumstances were not yet clear at midday, and the Russian and Ukrainian authorities accused each other of being behind strikes on the structure. According to the Ukrainian presidency, Russia "blew up" the dam in order to flood the area and thus curb the Ukrainian offensive in preparation. Denouncing a "war crime committed by Russian terrorists", the head of the Ukrainian presidential administration, Andriy Yermak, announced that Volodymyr Zelensky was convening a security council. Soon after, kyiv also called for an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council. In a press release, the Ministry of the Interior called on the European Union and the G7 “to impose new devastating sanctions on Russia”. “The world must react”, also launched Mr. Zelensky. “Russia is at war against life, against nature, against civilization,” he commented, accusing the Russians of having “mined” the dam before “exploding” it. In a videoconference speech to the "Nine from Bucharest", an organization bringing together nine countries of Central and Eastern Europe that are members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), he also affirmed that it "is [was] the biggest man-made environmental catastrophe in Europe for decades”. According to the Head of State, "it is physically impossible to blow up [the dam] in one way or another from the outside, with bombardments", the version put forward by Moscow to explain this destruction in the night. Le Monde with AFP Reading Time 2 min. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi spoke on the phone Tuesday, June 6 with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu following a rare deadly incident on the border between the two countries, the Egyptian presidency announced. Sisi received a call from Mr. Netanyahu “about the exchange of fire that took place at the border” on Saturday, and they stressed “the importance of coordination between the two countries to elucidate the circumstances” of this incident, the Egyptian presidential spokesman said in a statement. Mr. Sissi "presented his condolences" to Mr. Netanyahu, indicated for his part the office of the Israeli Prime Minister. Two Israeli soldiers were killed on Saturday by an "Egyptian policeman", "infiltrated" from Egypt into Israel. The assailant, tracked for several hours, was then shot dead during exchanges of fire which caused a third victim among the Israeli soldiers, according to an Israeli military spokesman. The incident took place near the Israeli military base in Harif, about 100 kilometers south of the Gaza Strip. According to the Egyptian army's version, a member of the "security forces chasing drug traffickers" crossed a checkpoint between the two countries. There followed an "exchange of fire that left three dead on the Israeli side" in addition to the death of the Egyptian. After the incident, the circumstances of which are still unclear, the Israeli and Egyptian authorities hastened to reaffirm their cooperation. The same day, Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday described the incident as "very serious and very unusual", promised a "full" investigation. On Sunday, thousands of Israelis paid their respects on Sunday to the three Israeli soldiers killed on Saturday, during a funeral in several cities in Israel, whose officials have promised to clarify the circumstances of their death. An Egyptian delegation including military officials arrived in Israel on Sunday as part of a joint investigation, according to an Israeli source familiar with the matter. . The assailant is not believed to be linked to Islamist groups but appears to have become radicalized, she added. Although his name has not been officially released, Egyptian media have identified him as Mohamad Salah, an elderly conscript 22 years old.Egypt was the first Arab country to sign a peace treaty with Israel in 1979. Many Egyptians, however, do not support this normalization.While the border between the two countries is generally calm, it remains the theater regular attempts to smuggle drugs, which in recent years have resulted in exchanges of fire between smugglers and Israeli soldiers stationed along the border. Hours before Saturday's attack, Israeli soldiers had thus thwarted an attempt to drug trafficking at the border. No link has yet been established between this event and the death of the three soldiers, according to an Israeli army spokesman. The UAE does not distinguish between items manufactured within the internationally recognized borders of the Jewish state and those originating from territories illegally occupied in 1967. By Ghazal Golshiri (Dubai, special correspondent) Reading time 2 min. in Dubai airport duty free, bottles of wine from the Golan Heights are offered for sale under the “Israeli product” label. However, under international law, the Golan, although conquered by Israel in 1967, remains Syrian territory. Its annexation by the Jewish state in 1981, which has so far only been recognized by one country, the United States, has been declared "null and void" by the United Nations. Under resolution 2334 of 2016, member countries of the UN are required to distinguish between Israel and the territories occupied in 1967. This principle, known as differentiation, implies excluding the Jewish colonies of the West Bank and the Golan from the benefit of any agreement signed with the Jewish state. In France, for example, goods coming from these territories must display special labels, mentioning their precise origin. They cannot take advantage of the preferential rates reserved for products made in Israel. The United Arab Emirates do not seem to want to bother with these rules of law. In December 2020, four months after the normalization of relations between the Gulf monarchy and the Jewish state, the president of the Dubai Chamber of Commerce, Hamad Buamim, declared that his country did not consider it necessary to make a distinction between the Israeli exports. A way of implying that the UAE would not take any measures to differentiate between items produced in Israel and those produced in Jewish settlements. so-called Hamad Buamim, convinced that this economic partnership will benefit the Palestinians who work in the settlements. Questioned by Le Monde on this subject, the Emirati political scientist Ebtesam Al-Ketbi, director of the Emirates Policy Center, a think tank close to the Emirati government, believes that the Emirates are “essentially concerned about the quality of imported products. If they meet the standards, there is no problem [with their importation].” This position is reflected in the standardization agreements signed between the two countries. “Two of the three agreements, the one on investment protection and the one on double taxation, are remarkable in their language, because they deliberately include Israeli settlements,” observes Hugh Lovatt, in charge of the Israeli-Palestinian dossier at the European Council. for International Relations (ECFR), a think tank. Israel is defined in these documents as "the territory over which the State of Israel exercises its sovereignty, sovereign rights or jurisdiction in accordance with international law and the laws of the State of Israel", which, according to Hugh Lovatt , includes occupied territories. Arrested in Poland more than a year ago while trying to cross to Ukraine, this freelancer, who also has a passport in the name of Pavel Rubtsov, is accused, according to Madrid, of "very serious and very serious facts ". By Sandrine Morel(Madrid, correspondent) Reading Time 4 min.LETTER FROM MADRIDJournalist Pablo Gonzalez will spend at least another two months in prison. At the end of May, his pre-trial detention was extended for the fifth time since he was arrested on February 28, 2022, 13 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, in the Polish town of Przemysl. Imprisoned for fifteen months and accused of spying, this massive 41-year-old man with dual Spanish and Russian nationality, with a shaved head and bushy eyebrows, is still waiting, in the Polish prison of Radom, 100 kilometers from Warsaw, for a date to be set for his eventual trial. And asks, in the meantime, to be able to at least speak with his three children, aged 8 to 15. Placed in solitary confinement until recently, classified among the "dangerous prisoners" and locked in a cell twenty-three hours a day -four, according to his family, Pablo Gonzalez has only been able to receive one visit from his wife, in November 2022. He can only speak to his lawyers, who complain that they have not yet been formally informed of the charges against their client and of not having had access to the documents seized and other evidential elements available to the Polish courts. This judgment marks the end of the first cycle of a legal battle launched several years ago for the recognition of marriage for all in Japan. Le Monde with AFP Reading Time 2 min. The Fukuoka court ruled the ban on same-sex marriage "unconstitutional" on Thursday, June 8. This judgment marks the end of the first cycle of a legal battle launched several years ago for the recognition of marriage for all in Japan. Its record, although mixed for the moment, is considered encouraging by activists for LGBT + rights in Japan. Coordinated legal actions were launched in 2019 by these activists to order the Japanese state to pay damages to same-sex couples deprived of the opportunity to marry and therefore enjoy the associated rights and benefits. Their larger goal was to put pressure on the state to legally recognize same-sex unions. Japan is the only G7 country not to recognize marriage for all at all. In total, a dozen couples had launched proceedings before five courts of first instance across the country. Each time, the judges rejected their claims for damages. But they were divided on the fundamental question posed by the ban on marriage for all opposed to Article 14 of the Japanese Constitution, which guarantees the equality of all before the law. For example, Judge Takebe Tomoko of the Sapporo Magistrate's Court, found in March 2021 that denying same-sex couples the rights associated with marriage is "discrimination without legal basis" that violates Article 14 of the Constitution. This Constitution, adopted in 1947 , merely mentions that "marriage can only take place with the mutual consent of both sexes", which gives rise to much debate and interpretation. All the courts approached "agree at least on the necessity of legislation that publicly endorses same-sex relationships and grants them legal protection equivalent to that of heterosexual couples,” said Takeharu Kato, a lawyer who filed one of these proceedings, on Thursday. June, the judges of the Nagoya court had recognized that same-sex couples were "excluded from access to important personal advantages granted to legally married couples". "The justification for the existence of these significant disparities and the absence of action to remedy them is now unconvincing", added this court. A year ago, the Osaka court had however argued that the differences between homosexual and heterosexual couples were already partially taken into account by the partnership certificates issued by municipalities. Indeed, a growing number of companies and municipalities in the country are offering same-sex couples benefits similar to those of married people. For their part, several surveys show that a majority of the Japanese population is favorable to the marriage for all. A timid bill aimed at "promoting understanding" with regard to the LGBT+ community should be approved in June by Parliament. Polish commission for place names has decided to ban the use of the Russian name of the city and the enclave of Kaliningrad – belonging to neighboring Russia – in favor of the historical Polish name of Krolewiec. By Hélène Bienvenu(Warsaw, correspondence) Reading Time 3 min.LETTER FROM WARSAWFor the past few days there has been a great commotion on the sides of the roads in north-eastern Poland, near the Russian border with enclave of Kaliningrad, where workers are busy replacing road signs. In a tweet from Poland's infrastructure ministry on May 31, two men in reflective clothing are seen unscrewing a road sign displaying "Kaliningrad" and writing "Krolewiec" instead. Since May 9, the name Kaliningrad - commonly used in Poland until then – gives way to the old Polish toponym of Krolewiec. Same treatment for the Kaliningrad oblast – its administrative region – which is now called “Obwod Krolewiecki” and no longer “Kaliningradzki”. This is what was decided last April by the Commission for the Standardization of Geographical Names outside the Republic of Poland, the Polish institution responsible for toponymy. Even though this is only a recommendation, it involves changing all the road signs bearing the mention of Kaliningrad, as well as future maps. "We do not want Russification in Poland, hence our decision to call Kaliningrad and its region in our own language,” Development and Technology Minister Waldemar Buda said in an official statement from his ministry. "The fact of naming a large town near our border after Mr. Kalinin, that is to say a criminal jointly responsible, among other things, for having taken the decision to carry out the mass murder of Polish officers in Katyn in 1940, evokes negative emotions among the Poles", continues the press release, which underlines the particularly sensitive context of the Russian invasion in Ukraine, on the pretext of a threatened "ruski mir" ("the Russian world"), and recalls a painful episode in the Polish history of the Second World War. Consider the execution of several thousand Polish officers by the Soviet political police of the NKVD, in 1940, validated by Mikhail Kalinin, head of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet. A fact long hidden by the USSR. However, the origin of the city, founded on the Baltic Sea by the Teutonic Knights in 1255, is rather German-speaking. Conigsberg or Königsberg ("the king's mountain") thus paid homage to King Ottokar II of Bohemia, who had taken part in the crusades in the region. The city was integrated into Prussia in the 18th century, which saw the birth of the philosopher Emmanuel Kant. It belonged until the end of the Second World War to Germany and returned to Russia in 1945, after the Yalta and Potsdam agreements. Moscow then hastens to rename the enclave after Mikhail Kalinin, Stalin's collaborator. At the fall of the USSR, an impossible consensus will make it keep its Soviet toponym. This was stated by the mayor of the Isonzo capital, Rodolfo Ziberna, addressing the president of the Slovenian jury, immediately after the proclamation. ''"'"Our goal is not just to carry out the 600 events scheduled - he added -, and it's not just to get to 2025: we want to get to 2035, 2045, 2055. '"'"If we succeeded here - concluded Ziberna -, where conditions were the worst due to the tragedies of the 20th century, without a doubt those other areas in Europe that suffer from 'being border territories' can also succeed" '".The governor of Friuli Venezia Giulia Massimiliano Fedriga commented: '"'"It is a deserved triumph that fills not only the cities of Gorizia and Nova Gorica with satisfaction, once again united in this common goal, but the whole of Friuli Venezia Giulia who will not fail to benefit and grow from this opportunity also with the support of the regional administration'"'".
