During his more than thirty-year career, Viktor Orbán lost a government election only once, after which he reorganized his party in 2002, not as party leader, but as prime minister who was forced to leave his position. The homeland can never be in the opposition, Orbán stated in one of his most quoted speeches in 2002. on May 7. After its first term in government, Fidesz believed in a revival: they believed that a campaign based on the country's improving economic situation would be enough to keep the left in opposition. Thus, only a few weeks after the election result that shocked the right, Orbán had to give faith to the crowd gathered at Dísz tér and, of course, to the wider right-wing camp, which had united by then in the absence of the MDF. The solution was the Civic Circles. In principle, a self-organizing, above-the-party, value-based mass movement, thanks to which like-minded, disappointed, but willing conservatives could find each other. In the next three months, create small groups of a few people, groups of friends, and civic circles. (…) It is necessary for hundreds of civic circles and societies to be formed (…) Our power is only real power if we are able to create and organize the public of bourgeois Hungary, Orbán pointed out. circular movement was a political product that was embedded in the long-term success of Fidesz. Orbán at the same time The first citizens' circle was created by Orbán himself under the name "Szövetség a Nemzetért Polgári Kör", which was joined by the Kossuth Prize-winning architect Imre Makovecz and the later president of Jobbik, Gábor Vona. "Readiness and action when the time comes", the former Prime Minister formulated the creed of civic circles, after these associations began to multiply like mushrooms: according to the news, seven thousand civic circles were born in one month, in 2002 a total of 11,300 were registered, a total of almost 160,000 people joined them. The election defeat hit us all hard. In the days before the election, we knew that Fidesz was leading by 6-7 percent. We felt a kind of paralysis when the Prime Minister announced the movement of civil circles. Encouraged by this, I immediately formed a civic circle of like-minded people. Then we waited to see what would happen - recalls Imre Pesti, a member of the Fidesz parliament. In 2002, the doctor and health politician, who is now in his fifth term as a representative, did not hold any political office. Previously, he was the founder of the MDF in Gödöllő, and from 1994 to 1998 he acted as the party's health policy advisor. The civil circle movement started his career as a front-line politician: he entered the parliament for the first time in 2006, after 2010 he was deputy mayor, and after 2014 he was the head of the capital's government office. Pesti told 24.hu that he found out about it after the establishment of his eight-person civil circle , that similar companies operating in Rákosmenté were called together for a private initiative. It turned out that the XVII. more than a hundred citizens' circles were formed in the district, seventy of them showed up. This meant approximately seven hundred active civil circles. At the event, a presidency was elected, and the board later unanimously nominated Pesti as its head. This is how the Rákosmente civic circles were created. After that, it occurred to me that if so many people had honored me with their trust, then something should be done. But what should we do? - Pesti recalled the initial uncertainty for our paper, adding that they did not even receive instructions from MDF's Csaba Hende, the coordinator of civic circles. Hende, who was already a politician in Fidesz, confirmed this in an interview in 2005, saying that the movement was not invented from above. We operated completely independently for a long time. I spoke to Csaba Hende for the first time when I went on television (at the beginning of 2004, after the demonstration in front of Tilos Rádió, the matter will be discussed later - ed.), and he told me to do it correctly and fairly. I asked him for some kind of guidance, to which he replied that it is not necessary, you are doing well. This was my first meeting with the leadership, Imre Pesti stated, adding that knowledge sharing only happened at meetings of civic circles; at that time the movement was not very organized and structured, it was more of a friendly nature. Rákosmenté met weekly at the presidency's apartment in Pest, and they discussed what the program for the next period should be. According to Pesti's recollections, they organized forums on a monthly or monthly basis, to which scientists, public figures, philosophers, churchmen, and artists were invited. Fidesz significantly increased its social embeddedness. Because at the beginning of the 2000s, the institutionalized right-wing subculture was not very present, and it was important for the voters who became the base of Fidesz to be able to mention their icons like Albert Wass without feeling bad and to openly support the church. All of this was a driving force in the initial period, to which the left-liberal side typically reacted by merging the bourgeois circles with the far-right initiatives that were also beginning to flourish at the time. In 2004, Imre Pesti and the Rákosmente bourgeois circles found themselves in the middle of one of the loudest scandals of the movement. they talked about how Christians should be exterminated, all perfectly timed, on Christmas Eve. We thought this was unsustainable, so we organized a demonstration. The demonstration against Tilos Radio surprised us too: we thought that two to three hundred people would come, but to our greatest astonishment, 10-15 thousand people were present, and even the press came from Sweden and Australia. A completely new world began, since until then we had only been active at the district level - recalls Pesti. After the speeches, the organizers of the demonstration failed to get the demonstrators to leave: the enraged crowd dragged the photojournalist of Magyar Narancs, broke the camera of the MTI photographer, and a smaller group burned an Israeli flag in front of a cordoned-off entrance. The civic organizers attributed the anti-Semitic incident to a narrow group of extremists, and distanced themselves from what happened. Pesti mentioned the provocation organized after the incident: he said that the flag, which was later set on fire, was taken from the building of Tilos Rádió to the demonstrators. But they wanted to tell Fidesz's newly formed base that he was anti-Semitic. The political goal was to push Fidesz and its sympathizers in the direction of the extreme right, the politician assessed, adding that after the flag burning, he had to go to TV studios all day because of the media attention, so the event was a kind of baptism of fire for him. At the time, Orbán spoke about "the election made it clear to the right-wing that it is not necessary to think in terms of parties", and "it is less important who is Fidesz, who is MDF, Christian Democrat or small farmer, this world is over" - however, in the end, all that happened was that Fidesz cannibalized the other right-wing parties with the bourgeois circles. This process already started when Orbán entrusted Csaba Hende, the second man of the MDF, with the coordination of the bourgeois circles. Dávid Ibolya, the president of the Democratic Forum, envisioned the role of the right-wing opposition in a completely different way, and already after the 2002 election defeat, he made it clear that "street, militant readiness" is not the MDF's world, they strive for more moderate politics. Then, according to Hende, he became the number one close enemy in the party: ethical and disciplinary proceedings were initiated against him, so the politician from Szombathely joined Fidesz in 2005. When new people and competitors appear on a political field, many do not look at it kindly. Let's be honest, everyone was afraid of themselves and their position, since the new people are perhaps more informed and in many ways more useful - analyzes Pesti, who, like Hende, from 2005 on the political community he found in Fidesz, the leadership entrusted him with party organization tasks. it was also received with distrust within Fidesz: the tension between the party and the movement came to the surface barely half a year after the change of government and the tearing down of the movement's flag. The right-wing went into the municipal elections in the fall burdened by internal conflicts, which resulted in another serious defeat. In many places, civil circles confronted the Fidesz organizations, demanded a change of elites and came up with their own candidates. In Szeged, for example, they lined up behind law professor Elemér Balogh, against Jenő Póda, nominated by the local organization of Fidesz. In the end, Fidesz also stood behind Balogh, who ran as an independent, but he was unable to defeat László Botka, who has led the city ever since. basic organizations can be purged and people with real public interests and ambitions can be included. According to Imre Pesti's view, Orbán primarily wanted to create a people's party, he wanted to involve new people in his political community, and for this he needed a social base. When the Prime Minister announced this, I think he also he was surprised that so many people would join him, that such a movement would emerge from it. Within the party leadership, this program was not an undivided success: many in Fidesz were not happy with the appearance of bourgeois circles. Many people thought that the transformation of Fidesz into a people's party was a blind alley, madness. This is the prime minister's genius, that he takes steps that at first glance are considered absurd, stupid, or suicidal, but the movement of civil circles was essential in terms of the transformation and strengthening of Fidesz into a people's party, he explained. they were given a position within the party. Pesti says that he was called to Fidesz because of the field work carried out in the district. The presidency of Rákosmente decided that seven hundred members of the seventy circles would set out and map the sympathizers from block to block. It became clear to the Fidesz general staff that the party could use the information obtained about political attitudes in future elections. indicated an activity similar to the field work carried out in the district as the main task of the civic circles: to "personally convince the electorate who to vote for", and "everything must be subordinated to this". Civil circles have found a place for themselves in political life. There were times when the local Fidesz simply swallowed it up and swept away the citizens, but there were also times when it integrated it in time, and from then on they worked together. There were perhaps two circles of citizens, those from Óbuda and us, who behaved differently. The opposite happened here: we integrated Fidesz. We were more numerous, we were consistent, we had definite ideas. When Fidesz appointed a constituency president, it was expected that the civil circles would also support him. The renewal of Fidesz started from the bourgeois circles, recalls Pesti. Orbán returned to the party chair in 2003 and announced the creation of a new organizational structure and the centralization of the party. Local politics was moved from the county to the constituency level, breaking the influence of the county presidents, while also opening up the organization to smaller settlements. In addition, eight departments were created. The name of the party was changed to the Fidesz-Hungarian Civil Alliance, and the party organization was entrusted to the leader of the Soroksár civic circle, Gábor Kubatov, who knew many people in South Pest through his car repair shop, and who told us several times: he was very satisfied with the first Orbán government, but not went to vote in the first round of the 2002 parliamentary election. The defeat hit him hard, and he started the civic circle work as a kind of penance. In 2003, Orbán explained at the general assembly of the civic circles that the goal of the movement is that "the whole country can move at the same time" when the time comes. A year later, the party president announced a five-point national petition to amend the budget, which he planned to strengthen with one million signatures. The document enshrined the rights to the possibility of creating a home, a safe livelihood and a healthy life, and condemned the privatization of hospitals and the rise in the price of food and gas. The initiative was signed by 1.2 million people, exceeding expectations. This served as a model for the subsequent national consultations. For a long time, Fidesz was the parliamentary force with the smallest membership, however, by strengthening local organization and facilitating the recruitment of members, they significantly increased the number of members. The elite of bourgeois circles also began to join the party, which created new tensions among the membership. Before the 2006 parliamentary election, the former dominant faces of the capital organization (Tamás Tirts, Róbert Juharos and Szilárd Sasvári) were replaced by citizens who had been in politics for a few years on the regional list in Budapest. In addition to Kubatov and Pesti, Tamás László, who from 2006 is the XV. became the mayor of the district, as well as Ildikó Bíró, the Budapest and later national coordinator of civic circles. Fidesz was received with terrible distrust. Just because of my well-bred nature, I won't mention the names of those who have stepped into the yellow soil. They thought we were unfit and didn't like how we got here so quickly. They didn't take kindly to the appearance of competitors, so in the beginning we received very harsh attacks, including me personally. But time resolved these contradictions - recalls Pesti, adding that two cycles had to pass for cooperation. In the 2006 local government election, the role of the civic circles became even more pronounced: about half of the Fidesz-KDNP representatives were elected through the civic circles. into the boards. Today, Rákosmenté is managed entirely by the former bourgeois circles. There is almost no one from the old Fidesz anymore, says Pesti. There were also citizens who did not like the fact that the largest opposition party saw them as its own base and used them to achieve its political goals. Károly Kovács, the former president of the 700-800-person association of Civic Circles in Pesthidegkút, spoke in an interview to Partizán: he gave up organizing civic circles after Fidesz appropriated the movement. The established activist network was suitable even after the civic circles flourished to ensure that the masses can be mobilized if party interests require it: during the 2006 autumn riots, civil circles organized several anti-government demonstrations, they took an active role in the campaign during the triple referendum in 2008, and they rely on their organizational network to organize the Peace Marches to this day , their experience, among other things, in the travel of the participants to Budapest. It is completely normal for a community to think about the present and the future in different ways. There were also those among us who thought that there was no need to build a close relationship with Fidesz. Some even crumbled. Many people here also thought that it was not important for us to do politics. It is an elegant position that we don't politicize, we don't join parties, we live the life of the cultural elite and we argue about the future locked in the ivory tower, that's the only way we have no impact on society. That's why in the Rákosmente Civic Circles we have remained bold in our politics - declared Pesti, mentioning that since Viktor Orbán called the movement into existence, it was obvious that they were aligned with his expectations. In 2006, a biweekly program on Echo Tv presented the most active members of the movement and its main events. After another election defeat in 2006, the political activity of the civil circles gradually began to wear off. According to Judge Ildikó Bíró, in the face of the defeat in 2002, it was not the will to act, but energy that dominated the membership. The organization's activities were mainly limited to local affairs and the organization of traditional and cultural programs. The omission of the circles was criticized by several people: in 2008, a member of the board of the civic circles in Budakesz announced that they were waiting for Fidesz to address them again, and Makovecz spoke at the Citizens' House designed by his students about how the second line of Fidesz "drilled" the world of civil circles. After the booth revolution of 2010, the importance of the movement continued to flatten. Judge Ildikó retired from public life in 2010, and since then there is no one responsible for organizing the circles. In 2019, László Csizmadia, the leader of the Civil Solidarity Forum that organizes the Peace Marches, already spoke about the fact that civil circles have ceased to exist, but his organization has successfully taken over the "civil front". On the other hand, civil circles continue to function sporadically: the circles in Eger, for example, are planning a national event for the twentieth anniversary of the movement's founding in mid-November. However, most of the civilians have apparently disappeared from the organization. The elite of the circles entered big politics, while the civilian majority, traditionally weakly connected to the parties, either faded out of public life or joined Fidesz at a lower level. The bourgeois circles were a successful initiative, and "there is no shame in learning a technique from the opponent", stated Attila Mesterházy the president of the MSZP in 2010, after the first democratic circle was established on the model of the civil circles. We haven't heard of left-wing public life clubs founded by socialists since their establishment, but until today several initiatives tried to follow Orbán's recipe to involve civilians. Such is the attempt of István Ujhelyi, who recently left the MSZP, to create Esély-körös, just as the Kossuth Körei of Péter Márki-Zay's movement can also be classified here, but a breakthrough awaits: no public figure has managed to create a civil mass movement of approximately the same importance, despite that even at first Orbán's idea only resulted in loosely connected local organizations. Imre Pesti sees that the success of civic circles lies in the right time and the will of the masses who had not been addressed until then. Many of us supported the Orbán government, and the public opinion polls also they indicated that half of the country. Yet the communists came back. A kind of bitterness and fear took over us, since we already had experience from the world of Lajos Bokros and Gyula Horn. There is no doubt that many people joined the Opposition Round Table, but it was not an all-social movement. It was the bargain of a narrow, future political elite, society as a whole did not participate in it. Maybe Viktor Orbán saw that there are still people who feel that they belong here and can be addressed. We had a desire: there were many of us who stayed out of politics, but we were happy to be involved in politics even outside of parties, and we would have liked to take on a role in public life.

The parliament will soon decide on the János Neumann Program, as part of which the name of the Eötvös Loránd Research Network (ELKH) may change to the Hungarian Research Network, reports Eduline, referring to the statement of the Ministry of Culture and Innovation. The aim of this measure is to ensure that the independent Hungarian research network can be easily and clearly identified by name among members of both the domestic and international research, development and innovation ecosystem. According to them, the new name (Hungarian Research Network in English) better supports the effective communication of research results, and "thereby contributes to increasing the recognition and recognition of the research network and, at the same time, Hungary on the international scene", as if the namesake, Loránd Eötvös, remained in the name of the institutional network. The research network previously belonged to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (MTA), but the government separated it from her four years ago, leading to tensions. Tamás Freud, the re-elected president of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, recently told Mandiner in an interview that although they had previously tried to negotiate with the government about the recovery of the research network, it has now given up. The new structure seems to have solidified. I would have tried to get the research network back while the situation was still flexible, but it is increasingly clear that the government's decision is final, said Tamás Freund in an interview published at the end of May.

For the time being, the level between 367.5-368 seems to be a strong support in the euro exchange rate, and the forint has not yet been able to break through it. The government announced in May 2022 that it would introduce extra profit taxes for several economic sectors from July 1. According to the communication at the time, these must be paid temporarily by the companies concerned, in 2022 and 2023, for example, in the law on extra profit tax, the air ticket tax called the contribution of the airlines was introduced, the excise tax was increased, and the public health tax was extended, as well as the payment of the transaction tax on securities transactions Since then, the original taxes have been raised several times and extended to the pharmaceutical industry. It was recently announced that, contrary to the original announcement, the extra profit taxes regulated in the state of emergency decree will be maintained until 2024, and in some cases even increased. It is already clear from the package of laws submitted by the government that several extra profit tax burdens, which were originally said to be temporary, will become permanent. According to Bank360.hu's summary, there will be a fixed deduction independent of emergency situations, for example, after the proposal is approved by the parliament, the air ticket tax, called the contribution of the airlines. According to the rationale, the tax levied indirectly on the airlines will be passed on as a kind of green tax, referring to the environmental burden. Similarly, the engraving of the transaction tax levied on securities transactions will affect a wide range of people. According to the burden, which was also originally introduced only for 2022 and 2023, a transaction fee must also be paid for securities transactions. This is based on the value (purchase price) credited to the customer account (securities account) of the investment. The transaction fee for securities transactions is 0.3 percent, but a maximum of HUF 10,000 per purchase. This is the same as the fee for transfers from bank accounts, the upper limit of which was also raised by the extra profit tax decree from HUF 6,000 to HUF 10,000. The government will also maintain this ceiling value according to the bill submitted to the parliament. The transaction fee charged on securities transactions will remain exempt if the investment service is provided by the Hungarian State Treasury or the institution operating the Posta Settlement Center. In practice, this means transfers related to purchases of government securities. The 2022 government decree extended the transaction fee to financial service providers that provide cross-border services in Hungary (such as Revolut or Wise). In the case of transfers from bank accounts, the transaction fee is the same as the rate otherwise applied, i.e. 0.3 percent per transfer, but no more than HUF 10,000 per payment transaction. The tax package also maintains this rule, so they also have to pay continuously. The draft law includes in the tax laws the increased rate of excise taxes from extra-profit taxes, as well as the extension of the public health tax, which affects, for example, energy drinks, soft drinks, salty snacks, flavored beers . The government will also raise some of the extra profit tax rules for energy suppliers to the level of law from 2024.

Pastor Jin Mingri had barely finished his dinner on Saturday evening, October 10, when twenty Chinese police officers stormed into his home in Beihai, Jiangxi Province. The officers immediately handcuffed the pastor after showing him an official arrest warrant, before conducting a thorough search of his home. They confiscated his phone, computer, books, and some personal belongings, and took him to a detention center in the city. The previous day, in a similar manner, Chinese police had detained a man named Wang Lin in Shanghai. Over the next two days, police, acting on a specific list of names, conducted coordinated raids in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Zhejiang, Shandong, and Sichuan, arresting approximately thirty pastors and other church staff members. All were taken to Beihai, a city on the Gulf of Tonkin in the northwest of the South China Sea. These actions were part of a broader Chinese security crackdown targeting pastors and church members. Zion, one of the largest unregistered Protestant congregations in the country, led by pastor Jin Mingri, also known as Ezra Jin, has been charged with "illegal use of information networks" under the People's Republic of China's Penal Code. These developments cannot be viewed in isolation from the state's strict policies regarding religious affairs. While the Chinese Constitution guarantees freedom of belief, it requires public practice to be registered with and subject to the oversight of government bodies. From this perspective, any activities outside this framework—whether house services or online preaching—are deemed "illegal," making those involved liable to prosecution. However, the case of Zion and similar institutions transcends these "regulatory" dimensions, reflecting a security perspective that views informal religious activity—especially that linked to external networks—as a "Trojan horse" that could be used to infiltrate the state's social fabric. China has carefully studied the West's long history of employing religious proselytizing to penetrate its social and political adversaries, and it fears a similar outcome. That this experience could be repeated on its soil, given the unprecedented ease afforded by the digital space. Therefore, for Beijing, the matter seems to transcend the usual explanations of "ideological control," veering towards genuine security concerns about a real breach of its social fabric. During the latter half of the 1980s, Jin Mingri, a young Chinese man of Korean descent, was still a probationary member of the Chinese Communist Party during his secondary school years, having not yet taken the oath of office due to his young age (under eighteen). At that time, student demonstrations were sweeping universities, and doubts about the legitimacy of the Communist Party were growing, with increasing calls for ideological liberation even from within the party itself. By 1987, in this relatively open atmosphere, Jin Mingri began frequenting the Chongwenmen Church, one of Beijing's oldest and most prominent churches, founded by American missionaries in the nineteenth century, which conducted services in Korean. Later, he began attending services and Bible study circles in Korean at the Gangwache Church, founded by British missionaries in the nineteenth century. Ten, according to a report by the China Change platform. Later, Mengri enrolled in theological studies at the Yanjing Theological Seminary, a replica of the Yicheng University School of Religious Studies, founded in 1919 by the American missionary John Layton Stewart. The seminary was closed following the Communist Party's rise to power in 1949, then reopened in 1986 as one of five seminaries in China run by the National Committee of the Three-Self Patriotic Movement, the official Protestant church recognized by the People's Republic of China, which was founded in the early 1950s with the aim of freeing Chinese Christianity from Western influence. After two years of theological study, Ezra Jin began his actual pastoral work, serving successively in the Zhongwenmen and Gangwache churches, two of Beijing's oldest Three-Self churches. By 1999, he had been ordained a minister under this system. However, the official religious system did not meet his aspirations. Mingri, who joined the Church of Zion in May 2007, was a member of a type of "independent" church known as a "house church," which is not directly controlled by the state. The Church of Zion was not the only such church that the state did not officially recognize, though it sometimes turned a blind eye to its activities. One of the most prominent of these was the Beijing Shuwang Church, founded by Jin Tianming, a close friend of Mingri. There was also the Ark Church, which gained many followers in Beijing. In Shanghai, the Wanbang Evangelical Church emerged, as did the Early Rain Covenant Church in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, in addition to many similar churches in various Chinese cities. These "believers" set out to preach Christianity in Chinese villages and towns, and many of them interacted with foreign missionary groups that had entered the country and worked with house churches in cities, taking advantage of the relatively open atmosphere in China during the first decade of the millennium. But by the end of Over the decades, the Chinese state has become increasingly concerned about the proselytizing activities of house churches, prompting it to take measures to suppress them. In 2009, when the Church of Zion was still in its infancy, authorities banned the Wanbang Evangelical Church in Shanghai. Later, in 2011, restrictions were imposed on the Shuwang Church in Beijing, preventing it from obtaining a headquarters, and its pastor, Jin Tianming, was placed under house arrest along with his family. By 2014, the Chinese government launched a campaign to remove crosses from the tops of churches. The following year, the Living Stone Church in Guiyang, the capital of Guizhou province, was banned, and its assets were confiscated. In 2018, it was the turn of the Church of Zion, which was officially shut down by the state after becoming one of the largest unofficial Christian religious entities. However, the closure of its headquarters did not end the church's existence; This prompted them to reposition themselves away from the rigid institutional structure, especially in the digital space during the COVID-19 pandemic. This allowed them to grow beyond the government's radar and enabled continued communication among members and the expansion of the network across multiple cities without a central headquarters or official status. This expansion of the "digital Quranic schools" phenomenon led Beijing to enact new legislation last September, restricting the right to online preaching to licensed platforms only and limiting unlicensed religious activity. Opponents see these measures as violating Article 36 of the Chinese Constitution, which clearly states that "citizens of the People's Republic of China enjoy freedom of religious belief." The government, however, considers them to be within the purview of the State Bureau of Religious Affairs, which is responsible for supervising and regulating religious affairs in the country. Nevertheless, the tension between the Communist Party and the Church of Zion (and unofficial house churches in general) goes beyond administrative violations. It stems from a view that considers informal religious activity—especially that linked to external networks—to be a "Trojan horse" that could be used to infiltrate the state's social fabric and undermine its stability. This perception is deeply rooted in the Chinese collective memory for reasons dating back to a well-known era. The "century of humiliation," spanning from the mid-19th to the mid-20th century, forms one of the foundational pillars of the modern nationalist narrative. This narrative reinforces the idea that the loss of Chinese sovereignty was not merely a result of military defeat, but rather the product of political and cultural incursions that accumulated over time. This contributed to the state's focus on the dangers of external penetration in its "non-military" forms, one of which, from the Chinese perspective, is religious proselytism. In the Chinese historical consciousness, Western missionaries were not spiritual guides, but rather an integral part of the Western imperial system. In their study, "Missionaries and Modernization in China," researchers Jiaoli Yan and Zhigang Wang point out that the timing of the missions' arrival, coinciding with the defeats of the Opium Wars, solidified the belief that the cross arrived on the backs of warships. This was not only a matter of timing, but also extended to the condescending discourse of the missionaries, who sought to bring about a comprehensive cultural transformation, disregarding China's value-based heritage. This stemmed from These practices stemmed from perceptions of Western civilizational superiority, leaving a profound mark on the Chinese psyche. The arrival of missionaries was directly linked to a moment of lost sovereignty, not to a moment of free choice or equitable cultural exchange. Hence, early suspicions arose regarding the intentions of these foreigners and the connection between missionary work and the political and economic interests of Western powers. This perception was reinforced by the system of "unequal treaties," which granted missionaries and their Chinese subjects "extraterritoriality," meaning they were subject to the laws of their Western countries rather than Chinese law. The American historian Kenneth Scott Latourette describes this situation as creating a "state within a state," where Chinese converts to Christianity sought refuge in foreign consulates, and countries like France intervened in the local judiciary under the pretext of protecting Catholics. Western powers did not merely protect the missionaries; they often used them as strategic tools to expand their political, cultural, and legal influence within China, with Western governments and commercial companies employing missionaries as... Translators and intermediaries, often the only foreigners fluent in Chinese. Some missionaries, such as Wells Williams and A.B. Martin, played a direct role in drafting the "religious tolerance" clauses in the 1858 treaties. These clauses later provided a legal basis for Western powers to interfere in China's internal affairs under the guise of protecting religious freedom. The treaty granted any missionary the right to purchase land and build churches, which many Chinese considered an intrusion into the country's geographical and cultural core and an expansion of foreign influence. This accumulated popular anger erupted in the Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901), a bloody uprising that targeted both the foreign and Christian presence, viewing them as two sides of the same coin. Approximately 100,000 people were killed, including 30,000 Christians. The rebellion ended with international military intervention by several Western powers and the occupation of Beijing for over a year, further wounding Chinese national pride. According to the study "The Boxer Rebellion and Missionary Activity" by American researcher Danielle Rossano-Simpkins, the "Fists of Justice and Harmony" movement emerged within a turbulent social and economic context before gradually transforming into what became known as the Boxer Rebellion. The study indicates that Christian missionary activity represented, in the popular Chinese consciousness at the time, one of the most prominent symbols of this influence, particularly given the legal and political privileges granted to missionaries and Chinese converts to Christianity under treaties imposed on China. American historian George Pruden notes that 1900 witnessed an escalation of violence against churches and the killing of Chinese missionaries and followers, leading to a response from Western powers through the direct military intervention of a coalition of nine nations. This resulted in China's defeat once again and the imposition of the "Boxer Protocol" in 1901, which included the execution of Chinese officials, the deployment of foreign troops in Beijing, and the imposition of massive financial reparations that lasted for decades. Consequently, communist China in 1949 inherited this legacy. The heavy legacy. Therefore, Mao Zedong hastened to expel the missionaries and establish the "National Three-Self Christian Movement," based on the principles of self-management, self-financing, and self-evident evangelism. The goal was clear: to sever the "umbilical cord" between Chinese Christians and the West, ensuring that the scenario of infiltration and the precursors to the century of humiliation would not be repeated. This understanding remains present in the Chinese consciousness even with the end of the era of traditional missions, especially with the shift of missionary activity to the digital sphere, where the tools of influence are more widespread and less restricted. According to a study by the American Barna Center, 58% of non-Christians have received religious content online. This figure reveals that the "Great Commission" (referring to the biblical commandment to spread the faith to all nations) has found its ideal medium in the internet. These figures acquire particular significance when placed in the context of evangelical Christianity, which is historically characterized by its universal missionary spirit and the centrality of the idea of spreading the faith beyond the confines of the community. Therefore, scholars of "digital theology" believe that technology has transformed evangelism from an elitist task For professional missionaries, this is a "decentralized" activity practiced by millions of believers via their phones. Researcher Heidi Campbell explains that we are witnessing the rise of "network religion," where religious practice is no longer confined to the church but has dissolved into the digital fluidity of daily life. According to this view, individuals do not live their faith in two separate spaces (one religious and one digital), but rather in a single hybrid reality where spiritual practice intersects with daily life patterns, communication, relationship building, and identity formation. From Campbell's perspective, the internet does not transport religion to a new space as much as it reflects deeper transformations that have occurred in religiosity itself, where faith has become more individualized, less subject to institutional control, and more connected to flexible social networks. The concept of religious authority, according to Campbell, is also undergoing a radical transformation in the digital environment. Instead of clergymen monopolizing the interpretation of texts and the direction of discourse, new forms are emerging, in which digital influencers and creators of religious content gain increasing power to influence religious perceptions. This opens the door to a more flexible and widespread proselytizing, but at the same time, one that is less controllable. And accountability. In this model, traditional hierarchical authority erodes in favor of "religious influencers." Personal testimonies and experiences—like a story in a short TikTok video—become a potent persuasive weapon, surpassing the impact of lengthy theological sermons, leveraging algorithms that know how to address audiences through emotional and personal content. Simon Dirks, a researcher in digital evangelism and the study of "faith communities," points to models of digital evangelistic groups presented as psychosocial support networks. He cites groups targeting women facing chronic illnesses or exhaustion from the pressures of daily life, where platforms like Facebook are used to build closed communities that allow them to share spiritual reflections and find respite from their daily struggles. This model relies on a cumulative personal discourse that addresses the audience's emotional needs before gradually leading them toward faith and belonging. Major missionary organizations are well aware of this opportunity, which consequently deepens Chinese concerns. For Beijing, digital evangelism is not merely religious content; it is a transnational activity capable of This involves reshaping citizens' loyalties away from the state. Heidi Campbell's approach illustrates this point, arguing that the digital space has not only changed the tools of proselytizing but also reshaped identity, shifting from a controlled institutional identity to a flexible, networked identity built through interaction, personal narratives, and emotional mobilization, potentially transcending traditional forms of national control and surveillance. This shift in the structure of identity and belonging explains why some countries have moved from treating proselytizing as a purely religious matter to considering it a sovereign and security issue. Modern history provides evidence of Western powers employing proselytizing as a tool for penetration and influence in other societies, going beyond declared spiritual aims. Adding to the complexity are historical precedents for the use of religion for intelligence purposes. In 1980, journalist Penny Lernow revealed in The Nation magazine the deep relationship between the CIA and missionaries, particularly in Latin America. Lernow documented how religious cover was used for espionage, recruiting informants, and even carrying out "black propaganda" operations. The report also details the smear campaigns against political opponents, as witnessed in Uruguay and Ecuador. It explains that cooperation between the CIA and missionaries and clergy was routine until 1975, with the latter being used as informants or on covert missions. The report documents 14 prominent cases, mostly in Latin America. It emphasizes that these practices were not marginal but rather part of the CIA's operational tools in highly sensitive political environments. The report presents the case of Adolfo Centeno Alancastro as a revealing example of this entanglement. Centeno, a Uruguayan official described in the report as "the CIA's old guard," had received training from the CIA in the 1960s and worked with a former CIA agent. Due to his expertise in church affairs, he was tasked with monitoring the Catholic Church in Uruguay. Between 1972 and 1976, his activities resulted in the arrest or expulsion of 15 clergy and the launch of a smear campaign against Archbishop Carlos Bartley. As a communist, he was targeted. The report indicates that these measures aimed to curtail the Church's role when it became critical of the authorities. American intelligence also employed these methods in Ecuador, Brazil, and Chile during the 1960s and early 1970s, with the goal of reshaping public opinion and discrediting opponents. This history is being studied with great care in Beijing. If Western powers previously used traditional missionaries to infiltrate societies, how will they deal with "digital missionaries" who do not require visas and are supported by algorithms designed by platforms owned by Western companies? Ultimately, China is not persecuting members of the Church of Zion simply because they pray in their homes or even preach their faith, but because—in the eyes of the state—they represent a "digital breach" in the wall of sovereignty, reviving the nightmares of the 19th century. With the world rapidly sliding toward a potentially open confrontation between superpowers, Beijing no longer views these networks merely with historical suspicion, but as a direct and imminent security threat. In the calculations of this new Cold War, and what might To develop into it, the state does not have the luxury of tolerating potential “ideological pockets” with transnational loyalties that are not subject to its central control. The Chinese authorities realize that these networks, with their encrypted communication channels and suitable social incubator, could turn into “zero hour” platforms for Western influence, and effective tools for destabilizing the home front when the battle heats up.

Following the Israeli Security Cabinet's approval of a series of decisions aimed at altering the legal and civil status of the occupied West Bank and consolidating Israeli control, numerous questions arise regarding these steps. These measures deepen the ongoing occupation and its escalating efforts to annex the West Bank, amidst daily attacks, settlement expansion, and violations of international law. The occupation's actions include lifting restrictions on land sales to Israelis by repealing the Jordanian law that prohibited the sale of Palestinian property to Jews, and declassifying land records. Israel has also transferred planning and building authority in areas of Hebron—specifically the area surrounding the Ibrahimi Mosque—from the Palestinian municipality to the Israeli Civil Administration. Furthermore, it has expanded its control and demolition powers to include Areas A and B, which are under Palestinian Authority control according to the Oslo Accords. Under the 1995 Oslo II Agreement, Area A is under Palestinian control, Area B is under Palestinian civil control and Israeli security control, while Area C, comprising approximately 60 percent of the West Bank, is under full Israeli control. Hassan Breijieh, head of the International Law Unit at the Commission Against the Wall and Settlements, believes that the decisions clearly violate international law, which restricts the occupying power's authority over occupied territories, particularly regarding the use of resources, property, and archaeological sites. He emphasizes that Palestinians remain "a people under occupation," and that the Geneva and Rome Conventions govern their relationship with Israel, while the Oslo Accords have been used internally in a way that has served Israel more than the Palestinians. Breijieh believes that the Israeli steps constitute "creeping annexation" aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians, taking advantage of American support, Arab weakness, and Palestinian division. This comes within a long history of Israeli violations of international law in the West Bank and Gaza, where it has committed a devastating war of annihilation. According to Breijieh, Israel lacks the legal authority to unilaterally abrogate a bilateral agreement like Oslo because it “created a new legal and administrative reality.” Nor can it repeal Jordanian law, which was in effect before the 1967 occupation of the West Bank, even though it effectively disregards it on the ground. He argues that many previous Israeli statements regarding annexation and the application of sovereignty have not translated into official, enforceable measures, but are used to gauge international and Palestinian reactions. Since the start of the genocidal war on Gaza on October 8, 2013, the occupation's attacks in the West Bank have escalated significantly, with increased killings, arrests, house demolitions, and settlement expansion. Palestinian data indicates that more than 1,112 Palestinians have been killed and approximately 11,500 injured, in addition to the arrest of more than 21,000 during the same period. There are fears that this Israeli escalation is a prelude to the formal annexation of the West Bank, which would definitively undermine the two-state solution stipulated in UN resolutions. Political expert Suleiman Bisharat believes that the essence of the Israeli decisions transcends the legal aspect and is connected to the logic of “imposing” “Facts by force.” He says that Tel Aviv acts on the conviction that whoever controls the ground sets the rules and defines the boundaries of the political future. He emphasizes that Israel pays no heed to Jordanian or Palestinian laws, and that its settlement project is based on the idea of a “Jewish presence on Palestinian land,” supported by the extreme right wing and American acquiescence. According to Bisharat, Israel is working to dismantle the legal and political structure upon which Palestinian identity is based, presenting itself as the “custodian of Palestinian land.” He believes that what remains of Palestinian land and presence faces a serious threat, and that the Palestinian and Jordanian legal frameworks are no longer capable of providing protection against confiscation and seizure. He considers that Israel is carrying out a comprehensive redefinition of the nature of the occupation, which undermines international agreements and treaties related to it. Marouf al-Rifai, media advisor to the Palestinian Jerusalem Governorate, says at the governorate headquarters in the al-Barid suburb of al-Ram, north of Jerusalem, that Israeli authorities began implementing what he called the “year of decision” in Jerusalem at the beginning of 2025 by accelerating settlement projects. He confirmed that Israel began implementing projects following the genocidal war in Gaza. A settlement project is already underway, spearheaded by the "Jerusalem 2050" plan, which aims to increase the number of Israeli settlers in Jerusalem, both East and West, to 5 million, thereby reducing the Palestinian population to less than 10 percent. This plan, considered one of the most dangerous projects of the Israeli right wing, began to be discussed in the Israeli media in 2017. It includes expanding the boundaries of the Jerusalem municipality, establishing an international airport near the Al-Buqai'a area, just a few kilometers from the city, connecting it to a railway network, and developing industrial and commercial zones and hotels. Expert Basharat believes that confronting this requires a clear Palestinian political will, a parallel Palestinian stance, and the implementation of Palestinian resolutions issued in recent years regarding the need to redefine relations with the Israeli occupation and how to deal with the Oslo Accords. "Come in!" she says into the silence, and a sigh and a step filled with faces from all corners of the world echoes. There are Egyptians, Chinese, Cameroonians, all the soldiers of Moscow. They signed up to fight under the Russian banners "for freedom," "for wages for work," and "under duress" before being captured at the front. Now they are in a secret prison in western Ukraine, waiting for an uncertain prisoner-of-war exchange, according to the AFP agency. In prison, she was allowed to spend a day talking, out of the sight of guards, to prisoners who had hoped for the promise of a new life before being overshadowed by the horrors of war. All names have been changed in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, which prohibit exposing prisoners of war to "public curiosity." The building, with its white walls and tiled floors, retains its austere Soviet style. From the window, new prisoners receive shirts, trousers and jackets, in indigo blue. They pack toothbrushes, soap and gloves. On the steps, Eric, a Togolese, talks to a Nigerian and a Chinese. In this modern Babylonian prison, a rigid routine reigns supreme. Eric did not speak either language, and he improved it in prison. Like his Nigerian fellow prisoner, he claims to have been seduced by Russian “ideology and history”; the Kremlin has made a glorified Soviet past a state policy. Both men took up arms “in the name of freedom” for the Russian-speaking population of Ukraine, a phrase used by Moscow-backed pro-Russian separatists to spark conflict in eastern Ukraine in 2014 as a prelude to the Russian invasion eight years later. "I don't know the history of either country," admits Eric, a doctor who left his neurosurgery studies in Lome a year before the war for personal reasons. Canada was "too expensive" for him and France rejected it. Then he discovered an "affordable" offer to study at Moscow State University and even the promise of Russian citizenship after military service. "I got the tip on the social services," he says. According to the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), Russian job offers are flooding the social services in French-speaking Africa. They promise about 2,300 euros (about 56,000 K) after signing a contract, monthly salaries of 2,300 and 2,500 euros and a Russian passport. But from November, all foreigners aged 18 to 65 must enlist in the army to obtain a residence permit or naturalization, the IFRI adds. The Africans in prison claimed that they were first lured with attractive offers of civilian jobs and then forcibly recruited into the army. Several countries, including Togo, have advised their citizens not to travel to Russia. “I knew what I was going into,” Eric says, declaring that it was his personal choice, which he did not inform his family about. His father learned in a phone call that he had been drafted into the army and had been captured. The prisoners stand closely together in the lunch line, their hands behind their backs and heads bowed, while the famous Ukrainians in the portraits on the walls look down on them. At the dining room, they sit in rows, eating and standing up at the same time. Only the horseshoe in Ukrainian during the meal breaks the solemn silence that slows down the passage of time. In front of a workshop where prisoners can make their own sparrows, Giuseppe tries to explain that he would like to call the woman he lived with in Russia for eight years. He followed her to Siberia from his native Campania in southern Italy because his salary from a pizzeria there could no longer be made when prices skyrocketed. A TV advertisement convinced the cook to go to the front. He claims that he was just "cooking" for the Russian army before an explosion at an infantry camp cost him four toes and his freedom. However, the Italian media claim that Giuseppe fled the country to avoid trial for raping a child. "If my country had offered me a decent job, I wouldn't have had to make this trip," says Wediwela from Sri Lanka. He claims that he wanted to find work abroad to escape the crisis on the island. In prison, he condemns the war frenzy and the destruction of children's futures, but he blames the West for starting the war out of "anger at Russian advances." During his walk, a crowd of people gathers on the sidewalk, young and old, thin and fat, but all with shaved heads. Some smoke, they chat. Many just stand there. And they cast curious glances at the newspapers; in prison, the arrival of someone new is an event. Aziz from Uzbekistan claims that he was forced to sign a contract with the army after the police accused him of drug trafficking. "They gave me a choice between 18 years in prison and being drafted into the army," he whispers, adding that he was promised that he would serve in the army like a Jew. He has not received any money, but he does not want any. To avoid a fight, he first tried to injure himself, but since the "mines didn't explode," he chose the second option: he raised his hands in front of the drone that led him to the Ukrainian soldiers. "I showed them our positions on the map," he whispered. According to a Council of Europe report, detainees are generally treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions in this facility. However, one of the prisoners objected to racist remarks by some guards. On the Russian side, the UN condemns the systematic torture and killing of Ukrainian prisoners. The Ukrainian Prisoners of War Center estimates that about seven percent of the soldiers in Ukrainian captivity are foreigners from dozens of countries that Russia is not interested in exchanging, and so they could remain in captivity for years. Aziz is one of the few prisoners who refuse to be exchanged for fear of reprisals. The others are pinning their hopes on the American plan to end the war, Giuseppe wants to return to Russia, and so does Eric. Wediwela hopes to return to Sri Lanka and reunite with his family, but that is the hope. "What is the meaning of a life that is so similar to death? Tell me, kill me! I am ready for it," he says in his diary. Add Hospodské noviny to your favorite titles on Google News.

The Kladno heating plant on Friday called on the Energy Regulatory Commission (ER) to select a new heat supplier for the city by April. It can, but does not have to use the technology of the heating plant. However, the heating plant cannot continue to produce and supply heat after the 31st due to economic unsustainability, said Eva Makov, the spokesperson for the Northern Czech Energy. The Kladno heating plant belongs to the Northern Czech Energy Pavel Tykač subgroup, and heat is produced by coal. However, there should not be any interruption in heat supply without compensation. Heat supplies are not at risk, reiterated the Kladno mayor Milan Volf (Volba pro Kladno). ER is investigating whether the situation of the Kladno heating plant meets the legal grounds for the established measures, i.e. the selection of a supplier. The situation is being intensively investigated, ER spokesperson Michal Kebort answered the TK question. Last November, the heating plant announced that it would cease operations in December 2026, at the latest in early 2027. "The price at which we will supply heat in the long term will not cover production costs, and we will spend tens of millions of crowns on heat production every year," said Michal Hons, director of the Kladno Heating Plant. According to him, the reason is the expensive emission allowances, the settings of the European energy market, and the contract with the local heat distributor Tepo concluded before the energy crisis, which is valid until 2030. According to the ER, the announcement of the Kladno Heating Plant is not a reason for the ER to impose measures outside the scope of the license. "The only legitimate reason can be objective facts that must be resolved at this time. We will of course deal with the situation intensively and announce the necessary steps as soon as we discuss the possibilities with all parties involved," explained Kebort. According to Volf, the Kladno management was willing to seek a compromise solution with the heating plant, but an agreement was not reached. "On the contrary, the whole situation confirms the correctness of our two strategic decisions to prepare the installation of our own heat source, which will ensure the city of Kladno long-term energy security and stability," said the mayor. According to Hons, the heating plant management presented a possible way to transform the heating plant from a coal-fired to a gas-fired cogeneration unit with additional gas boilers, but the Tepo company did not accept the proposal, including the price. The heating plant thus produces coal-fired electricity. In this case, it is scheduled to cease operation in December 2026, at the latest in early 2027. The transmission system operator EPS stated in January this year that the closure of the Kladno Heat and Power Plant does not threaten network operations. Prague - The government has decided to abolish the National Economic Council of the Government (NERV). Finance Minister Alena Schillerová (ANO) said this at a press conference after the cabinet meeting. NERV advised the previous cabinet of Petr Fiala (ODS) on structural economic measures, such as pension reform or public finance reform. Fiala criticized the abolition of NERV today. Schillerová emphasized that she is not preparing to abolish the National Budget Council (NRR). Schillerová stated that the previous government prepared the abolished NERV for its own needs. "We leave open what the development will be towards the possible creation of our government's NERV. We must consider what we would need the experts for, who they should be, so that it serves that purpose," she said. The minister also pointed out that the government is currently using its own experts for consultations instead of the council. According to her, they act as advisors to the prime minister or individual ministers. Former prime minister Fiala called the abolition of NERV a bad decision on the X network. "NERV experts came up with a number of ideas, proposed recommendations that helped us maintain healthy public finances or improve the competitiveness of the economy. The question arises whether the government abolished NERV so that experts would not talk it out of irresponsible cancellation of our reforms and dangerous indebtedness," he wrote. XTB Chief Economist Pavel Peterka told ČTK that the abolition of NERV was a shame. "The existence of NERV was supposed to further accelerate pro-growth reforms and other legislative changes that will kickstart economic growth. The problem is that the vast majority of these measures were not enforced by the Fiala government," he said. "The mere existence of NERV or another advisory body is not enough to move our country forward. It must be combined with the political will to take sometimes unpopular measures, or measures that have a positive impact beyond the horizon of the government's term. At the same time, NERV's recommendations and proposals are still publicly available and can therefore be used in the coming years," he added. NERV was originally introduced by the government of Mirek Topolánek (ODS) in January 2009 as an independent advisory body to the cabinet. Subsequently, in September, the council published its final report. The council's activities were then resumed by the government of Petr Nečas (ODS) in August 2010. After the fall of the government, NERV's activities were suspended in August 2013. The government of Bohuslav Sobotka (ČSSD) then incorporated the council's agenda into the renewed Council for Sustainable Development in 2014. Subsequently, NERV was renewed by the government of Andrej Babiš (ANO) in April 2020. Under Fial's cabinet, NERV has been operating since May 2022. In its last composition, it had 17 members. The opposition criticizes the decision of the coalition cabinet of ANO, SPD and Motorists to abolish the National Economic Council of the Government (NERV). The government abolishes what does not suit it, say politicians from the parties of the former government. Some of them rhetorically asked on the X network whether the National Budget Council or even the Supreme Audit Office would be abolished. The previous cabinet of Petr Fiala (ODS) was advised by NERV on structural economic measures, such as pension reform or public finance reform. Finance Minister Alena Schillerová (ANO) explained the decision by saying that the previous government had prepared the council for its own needs and that the new government was using its experts for consultations. "We are leaving open the question of what the development of the possible creation of NERV by our government will be. We have to consider what we would need the experts for, who they should be, so that it serves that purpose," she said. "I consider abolishing NERV not only stupidity on the part of this government, but above all harm to this country. Having experienced experts who are not afraid to state their opinions clearly and, above all, are supported by arguments and data is always important for every decision-making, and this is especially true at the state level," former Deputy Prime Minister Marian Jurečka (KDU-ČSL) said on social media. According to him, many important things were achieved under the former government thanks to the council's initiatives. He mentioned, for example, changes to the Labor Code, changes in the setting of unemployment benefits, or the setting of lifelong and digital education. The deputy chairman of the ODS parliamentary club, Štěpán Slovák, linked the decision to the recent statement by the National Budget Council, according to which the government violated the rules when preparing the budget. "The government is abolishing NERV so that it doesn't have time to state this too, just to be sure. What else do 'responsible budget officials' have to do? Abolish the National Budget Council or even the SAO," he asked X. Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies Jan Skopeček (ODS) said that the government does not dare to abolish the Budget Council, but at least it is scandalizing and ignoring it. "They decided to abolish NERV completely, just to be sure, what if its members dared to criticize Minister Schillerová's adventurous budget policy," he pointed out. According to the leader of the People's Party, Marek Výborný, the government of Andrej Babiš (ANO) will be more comfortable if no one talks her out of wasting money, canceling reforms and rapidly increasing the country's debt. Former Minister of Science and Research Marek Ženíšek (TOP 09) believes that the minister will not take advice from people who understand economics unlike her. "What next? Will they abolish the courts because they are losing them? They want to govern without control. No way," he continued Slovák's reasoning. "The abolition of NERV is a resignation from professional work with facts and data at a time when public finances are under the greatest pressure in recent years. This is not responsible state management, but preparation for the Hungarian path and Orbánization," said Pirates chairman Zdeněk Hřib. NERV was originally introduced by the government of Mirek Topolánek (ODS) in January 2009 as an independent advisory body to the cabinet. Subsequently, in September, the council published its final report. The council's activities were then resumed by the government of Petr Nečas (ODS) in August 2010. After the fall of the government, NERV's activities were suspended in August 2013. The government of Bohuslav Sobotka (ČSSD) then incorporated the council's agenda into the renewed Council for Sustainable Development in 2014. Subsequently, the NERV was renewed by the government of Andrej Babiš (ANO) in April 2020. Under Fial's cabinet, the NERV has been operating since May 2022. In its last composition, the council had 17 members. Minister Schillerová is not preparing to abolish the National Budget Council (NRR). At a press conference after the government meeting, she pointed out that the council was established by law. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš (ANO) described the NRR as unnecessary over the weekend, and Schillerová's deputy Petr Mach (SDP) spoke about its abolition. Schillerová admitted that she always disagrees with the council on everything. "I am not preparing to abolish the National Budget Council," she emphasized, however. The Ministry of Finance entered into a dispute with the NRR in connection with the draft state budget for this year. According to the NRR, the government submitted a budget with a deficit of 310 billion crowns in violation of the Budget Responsibility Act, because the deficit exceeded the spending limits. The ministry has repeatedly expressed its belief that the deficit limitation does not apply to the budget, because the government dealt with it after it was returned by the Chamber of Deputies, not in the regular term in September. Babiš said on Saturday's Nova TV program Za pět minut dnivaně that he disagreed with the NRR's position on the budget. He described the institution as unnecessary. A day later, Mach said on Václav Moravec's Questions on Czech Television that he would abolish the NRR, which would save the state tens of millions of crowns. The National Budget Council is an independent expert body whose main mission is to evaluate whether the state and other public institutions comply with the rules of budgetary responsibility set by law. The Council is three-member by law. The chairman is elected by the Chamber of Deputies on the proposal of the government. The current chairman is Mojmír Hampl. Pilsen - The Regional Court in Pilsen today sent 27-year-old Adam Chmura to a maximum security prison for 17 years for attempted murder. The defendant confessed to stabbing a randomly selected 60-year-old pedestrian in the center of Sušice last June after drinking alcohol. The man survived only thanks to timely and specialized medical assistance. According to the indictment, Chmura's motive for his actions was an attempt to get back to prison. The defendant, garbage collector Chmura, pleaded guilty, thereby agreeing with the description of the event and the qualification of the act according to the indictment, so the court did not have to conduct lengthy evidence and closed the case during the morning. Chmura faced up to 20 years in prison. The verdict is final, and Chmura and the public prosecutor have waived their right to appeal. "I had no motive for it, I heard voices. I went home, took a knife, wanted to stab myself, and at that moment the voices woke up and told me to kill someone else," he said in court. He said he wanted to seek treatment because of the voices he heard, but no one believed him. The attack took place on the evening of June 18 last year in Sušice. According to the court, Chmura, who had previously been convicted three times, took a kitchen knife with a 20-centimeter blade from home and went into town. He leaned against a shop window and made it clear that he wanted to go back to prison. In a voice message, he told his friend that he was going to prison today, to kill a person. Then he quickly got up and stabbed a random man passing by four times in the neck and chest. He then called the police himself, waited for them, did not run away and cooperated with the police, Chmura's defense attorney recalled in his closing argument. The defendant expressed remorse. "I would like to apologize once again, I am terribly sorry, I admit my mistake. I am glad that the gentleman survived," Chmura said in court. He admitted that he often drank beer, and on the fateful day he had also had hard alcohol. According to the court, Chmura had had behavioral problems since childhood; he was first sentenced as a juvenile to 110 hours of community service. He had already received a suspended sentence for other thefts, but when he failed to prove himself during the probationary period, he went to prison for six months. He received another sentence, two years and three months in prison, for continuing robbery, rape and extortion. He then spent several years in protective sexological institutional treatment, which was changed to outpatient treatment in 2023. Czech Republic court murder Pilsen Author: ČTK

Prague - According to the Supreme Audit Office (SAO), the Ministry of the Interior has not created a functional system for protecting schools, shopping or cultural centers or hospitals even after eight years, even though the concept of protecting soft targets for the years 2017 to 2020 assumed this. The SAO reported on the conclusions of the review in today's press release. According to the SAO, the Interior has also neglected its coordination role and fulfilled two of the four pillars on which the system was supposed to stand. Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar (ANO) announced that he would establish a working group that would help put the adopted measures into practice. Culture Minister Oto Klempíř (for the Motorists) said that in response to the review, he would revise his ministry's budget so that investments in security could begin as soon as possible. "The Ministry of the Interior has not even developed a follow-up concept for the next period and, on the contrary, in 2021 it reduced support for protecting soft targets," the SAO said. According to the SAO, the Interior Ministry and other institutions began to pay more attention to soft targets only after the shooting at the Faculty of Arts of Charles University in December 2023. The killer shot 14 people at that time, then injured himself and 25 other people. According to Metnar, the SAO's conclusions published today confirm that the previous government and the then leadership of the ministry failed to adequately set up and manage the system for protecting soft targets. "That is why, after taking office, I decided to establish a working group that will develop a follow-up concept and help put the adopted measures into practice," the minister wrote on the social network X. According to the SAO, the Interior Ministry did not fulfill its coordinating role, mainly in financing the protection of soft targets, even though their owners or operators requested a program for the purchase and modernization of security elements, such as camera systems. According to the audit office, there is also a lack of an up-to-date overview of the most endangered targets. "The educational activities of the Ministry of the Interior for security institution employees and the professional public did not take place in 2022 and 2023 and were only resumed in 2024, i.e. after the attack on the Faculty of Arts of Charles University," the SAO said. The SAO also criticized the Interior for not fulfilling the task of sending warnings to selected representatives of soft targets by the set deadline. In addition to the Interior, the Audit Office also inspected the Ministries of Culture, Education and Health. According to the SAO, the situation changed after the attack on the Faculty of Arts. For example, according to the SAO, the Ministry of Education increased the subsidy program to strengthen school security from 130 million to 200 million crowns, and the Ministry of Health updated the traumatology and crisis plans of hospitals. "However, the SAO audit showed that a number of measures are still in preparation and their implementation will only take place in the coming years," the office noted. According to Klempíř, the Ministry of Culture will provide money to systematically strengthen the protection of cultural institutions. "I have ordered the immediate revision of the ministry's budgets so that we can start investing in increasing security as soon as possible. The tourist season is approaching and I refuse for the ministry to continue this irresponsible behavior," Klempíř told ČTK. In cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior, his office will prepare specific recommendations. In culture, soft targets include museums, galleries, theaters, libraries, and monuments. The current inspection focused on the protection of soft targets covered the years 2021 to 2025. The motion for an inspection was decided by deputies from the control committee in December 2023, two weeks before the shooting at the Faculty of Arts. They were discussing the conclusion of a previous similar inspection from 2021. At that time, the SAO concluded that the Czech Republic still lacks a comprehensive system for protecting soft targets from terrorist attacks. The Ministry of the Interior responded by stating that the review aimed to support the increase in the resilience of soft targets, not the entire system. The decision to carry out the review, which has now been completed, was made by the broader management of the SAO two years ago in January.
