Prague - Actor, presenter, entertainer and singer Miroslav Donutil celebrated his 75th birthday today on the stage of the National Theatre (ND). He was congratulated by colleagues including Jiřina Bohdalová and the theatre management. The completely sold-out auditorium of the historic theatre building welcomed Donutil with a standing ovation. Donutil said today that he returned to the stage of the "golden chapel" after ten years. "I am moved. And I am not exaggerating. I never thought that I would return to a packed ND after ten years," said Donutil. The last time the long-time member of the ND drama troupe stood on its stage was at the finale of Carlo Goldoni's The Servant of Two Masters in December 2016. The National Theatre staged the play with Donutil in the role of Truffaldino from 1994 to 2016, reaching 600 reruns. The first of the congratulators, the director of the ND Jan Burian, dedicated a reminder to Donutil of another production in which he excelled. It was Chekhov's Uncle Vanya, which Donutil first played at the National Theatre in 1990. Burian gave him a framed poster of the production. "I even saw the performance twice," said Burian, who was accompanied by director Michal Dočekal. The audience also welcomed the 94-year-old congratulatory guest Bohdalová with a standing ovation. "They say about him that he is the second (Vladimír) Menšík, but that is not true. It cannot be true, because two gems are not comparable," said Bohdalová about Donutil. Actor, director and principal Bolek Polívka came with stories about Donutil that the actor did not want to listen to. He has been friends with Donutil since his student days. Polívka brought a shot glass and an offer for a role, which he will tell the birthday boy in person. Jiří Pavlica, Jitka Čvančarová, Slovak actress Zuzana Krönerová and Bára Basiková also sang for Donutil today. "You're like wine, the older you get, the better," said Basiková to the actor. His wife from the film Pelíšek Simona Stašová, the real-life son and daughter-in-law of Martin and Sára Donutil, and music producer and composer Karel Vágner also congratulated him. Czech Radio Director René Zavoral offered Donutil the opportunity to prepare his own show on the Dvojka program. The live broadcast of today's celebrations at the National Theatre was provided by the Czech Radio program Tobogan. The congratulations from former football striker Pavel Kuka were a surprise. Kuka compared the packed National Theatre to the football stadium in London's Wembley, where Czech football players played for the European Championship title against Germany in 1996. After the loss, when they were feeling miserable, Donutil came to cheer on the players. "European runners-up and I was there, what more could I have wished for," Donutil responded. Donutil, who was born on February 7, 1951 in Třebíč, is known for choosing his roles and preferring his own judgment over a fee. A graduate of the Janáček Academy of Performing Arts, he started out at the Brno Theatre on a String. He and his actors shone in 1978 in the film The Ballad of a Bandit. At the beginning of 1990, Donutil moved to the Prague National Theatre. In addition to his theatrical roles, he played a number of film and television characters. Donutil is also a singer (Songs from The Ballad of a Bandit, Songs I Love), a presenter and a sought-after voice actor. Czech Republic people theatre Donutil AUDIO PHOTO Author: ČTK

Tehran - Iranian security forces have begun mass arrests of reform movement leaders in the country, including a number of prominent figures, the AP reported today, citing local media. The government suspects the reformists of disrupting the political situation in the country during the nationwide anti-government protests that broke out in late December. According to the IRNA agency, citing a statement from Tehran prosecutors, four people have been arrested and others have been summoned for questioning. The charges relate to alleged activities related to "organizing and leading activities aimed at disrupting the political and social situation in the country" during the anti-government demonstrations. An Iranian court sentenced Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi to more than seven years in prison over the weekend. At least four members of the Iranian reform movement have also been detained, including its leader Azar Mansouri and former diplomat Mohsen Aminzadeh. Also arrested was Ebrahim Asgharzadeh, who led the 1979 student protests that saw students seize the U.S. embassy in Tehran. The arrests of the opposition figures, according to the AP, likely stem from their January reformist statement calling for Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei to step down and for a transitional governing council to oversee the country. "After brutally silencing the people in the streets, the regime has turned its attention inward and targeted the loyal opposition," said Ali Vaez, an Iran expert at the International Crisis Group think tank, according to the AP. However, it remains unclear how much political support the reformists have in Iran, the AP writes. Iran has been ruled by a theocratic regime since 1979. Recent large-scale anti-government protests have been violently suppressed by Iranian security forces. The Iranian human rights organization Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), based in the United States, said that 6,872 people, 6,443 of whom were protesters, were killed in the demonstrations that began in late December. Around 50,000 people were detained. Iran opposition government Author: ČTK

Kiev - "Entry!" is heard in the silence, and then there is a stampede and the staircase fills with faces from all corners of the world. There are Egyptians, Chinese, Cameroonians, all the soldiers of Moscow. They signed up to fight under the Russian banners "for freedom", "for wages for work" or "under duress" before being captured at the front. Now they are in a secret prison in western Ukraine and have nothing to do but wait for an uncertain exchange of prisoners of war, writes the AFP agency. She was allowed to spend a day in the prison and talk, out of sight of the guards, with prisoners who were attracted by the promise of a new life before it was overshadowed by the horrors of war. All the names have been changed in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, which prohibit exposing prisoners of war to "public curiosity". The building, with its white walls and beige floors, has retained its austere Soviet style. Through the window, the new prisoners are given a shirt, trousers and jacket, all in indigo blue. They also pack toothbrushes, soap and towels. On the staircase, Eric, a thirty-something from Togo, chats with a Nigerian and a Chinese. In this modern-day Tower of Babel, broken Russian reigns supreme. Eric had never spoken the language before, and only improved it in prison. Like his Nigerian cellmate, he claims that he was seduced by Russian "ideology and history"; the Kremlin has made glorifying the Soviet past a state policy. Both men took up arms "in the name of freedom" for the Russian-speaking population of Ukraine, a pretext that pro-Russian separatists backed by Moscow used to provoke conflict in eastern Ukraine in 2014 as a prelude to the Russian invasion eight years later. "I don't really know the history of either country," admits Eric, a medic who, for personal reasons, had to abandon his neurosurgery studies in Lomé a year before the war. Canada was "too expensive" for him and France rejected him. Then he discovered an "affordable" offer to study at Moscow State University and even the promise of Russian citizenship after military service. "I got the tip on social media," he says. Russian job offers are flooding social media in French-speaking Africa, according to the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI). They promise about 2,300 euros (about 56,000 CZK) after signing a contract, a monthly salary of 2,300 to 2,500 euros and a Russian passport. But since November, all foreigners aged 18 to 65 have had to enlist in the army to obtain a residence permit or naturalization, the IFRI adds. The Africans in prison claimed that they were first lured with misleading offers of civilian jobs and then forcibly recruited into the army. Several countries, including Togo, have advised their citizens not to travel to Russia. "I knew what I was getting into," Eric says, declaring that it was his personal choice, which he did not inform his family about. His father learned in a phone call that he had been drafted into the army and had been taken prisoner. The prisoners stand closely together in the lunch line, with their hands behind their backs and heads bowed, while the famous Ukrainians from the portraits on the walls look down on them. In the dining room, they sit in groups of four, eat, and get up at the same time. Only a thank you in Ukrainian for the meal breaks the monastic silence that slows down the passage of time. In front of the workshop, where prisoners can earn extra money by making chairs, Giuseppe tries to explain that he would like to call the woman with whom he lived in Russia for eight years. He followed her all the way to Siberia from his native Campania in southern Italy because he said he could no longer live on his salary from the pizzeria when prices rose sharply. A TV commercial convinced the chef to go to the front. He claims he was just "cooking" for the Russian army before an artillery shell took his four toes and his freedom. However, Italian media claim Giuseppe fled the country to avoid trial for child rape. "If my homeland had offered me a decent living, I wouldn't have had to make this journey," says Wediwela from Sri Lanka. He claims he wanted to find work abroad to escape the crisis on the island. In his diary, written in prison, he condemns the war's fury and the destruction of children's futures, but also accuses the West of starting the war out of "jealousy for Russia's successes." At the time of the walk, a crowd of people gathers in the courtyard, young and old, thin and fat, but all with shaved heads. Some smoke, chat. Many just stand quietly. And they cast curious glances at the journalists; in prison, the arrival of someone new is an event. Aziz from Uzbekistan claims he was forced to sign a contract with the army after Russian police accused him of drug trafficking. "They gave me a choice between 18 years in prison and being drafted into the army," he whispers, adding that he was promised a job as a driver in the army. He says he received no money, but he doesn't want any. To avoid fighting, he first tried to injure himself, but because "the mines didn't explode," he chose the second option: he raised his hands in front of a drone that led him to Ukrainian soldiers. "I showed them our positions on the map," he whispers. According to a Council of Europe report, detainees are generally treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions at the facility. However, one of the detainees complained about racist remarks by some guards. On the Russian side, the UN condemns the systematic torture and killing of captured Ukrainians. The Ukrainian Prisoners of War Center estimates that approximately seven percent of Ukrainian prisoners are foreigners from four dozen countries that Russia has no interest in exchanging, and so they could remain in captivity for years. Aziz is one of the few prisoners who refuse to be exchanged for fear of reprisals. The others are pinning their hopes on the American plan to end the war; Giuseppe wants to return to Russia, as does Eric. Wediwela hopes to return to Sri Lanka and reunite with his family, but hopes are fading. "What is the point of living a life that is so similar to death? Hang me, kill me! I am ready for it," he confides in the diary. World Ukraine Russia prisons battles MONITOR Author: ČTK

Hong Kong - A Hong Kong court today sentenced pro-democracy activist and former media mogul Jimmy Lai to 20 years in prison for violating a national security law. The AFP and AP agencies reported that the sentence is the highest imposed since the adoption of the China-imposed law that has virtually silenced critical voices in Hong Kong. Lai denies all charges and can appeal. The United States and Britain have previously described the case as political and called for Lai's immediate release. On the contrary, according to Hong Kong administrator John Lee, the verdict is proof of the rule of law and will bring great satisfaction to citizens. "The court believes that the total sentence imposed on Lai in this case should be 20 years in prison," according to the AFP verdict. The court, which found the 78-year-old activist guilty of conspiring with foreign forces and distributing seditious materials in December, justified the sentence by saying that Lai was the leader of the conspiracy. According to AFP, after including previous sentences, today's decision means that Lai, who was facing up to life in prison, should spend another 18 years in prison. The harsh critic of Beijing has been behind bars since the end of 2020. Other convicts in the same case received sentences ranging from six years and three months to ten years in prison. Lai's son Sebastien described the sentence as draconian. "It means the complete destruction of Hong Kong's legal system and the end of justice," he said. His sister Claire considers the sentence cruel and is convinced that if it is carried out, her father will die behind bars as a martyr. Amnesty International called today's court decision a cold-blooded attack on freedom of expression in Hong Kong. "A harsh 20-year sentence for Jimmy Lai, who is 78, effectively means a death sentence," said Elaine Pearson of Human Rights Watch. The founder of the now-defunct pro-democracy newspaper Apple Daily is currently serving a sentence of five years and nine months for fraud. According to agencies, his trial has become a symbol of the rapid erosion of press freedom in Hong Kong under pressure from the pro-Chinese government. The national security law, which was introduced in 2020 for the Hong Kong territory by the central government in Beijing and against which mass demonstrations broke out in Hong Kong in 2019, focuses on acts of separatism, subversion of state power, terrorist activities and cooperation with foreign or external forces to threaten national security. Violations of it can result in a sentence of up to life imprisonment. The European Union and Britain today called for Lai's release. Brussels described the prosecution of the 78-year-old man as politically motivated. On the other hand, Beijing, according to , expressed its belief that the Hong Kong authorities had fulfilled their duty and that Lai deserved a severe punishment. Kiev - This week, a Ukrainian soldier, Nazar Daletsky, who his family thought had fallen, also returned from Russian captivity. They even buried the remains that, according to DNA tests, were his. The BBC News station wrote this on its website, where it published a video showing his mother Nataliya talking to the soldier after his release. The whole story of Nazar's return from the grave is extraordinary, especially in a war-torn country where good news is rare, writes the BBC. According to it, how the remains could have been mixed up is now being investigated. Daletsky joined the fight after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022. According to the British station, the then 42-year-old man had experience, having fought in 2014, when an uprising by Moscow-backed separatists and an armed conflict broke out in eastern Ukraine. Daletsky disappeared in May 2022. His mother then received a call from a Russian-speaking man, saying that her son had been captured but that everything would be fine. The mysterious voice said nothing more, the BBC reported, adding that the family did not know whether to believe the man. There was no official news. A year later, Daletsky's mother received information that a body had been identified in a morgue in southeastern Ukraine based on DNA samples she had provided. "It was badly burned... When they started looking through the lists of missing soldiers, the dates matched. They identified the body as Nazar," his cousin Roksolana said. So the family buried the body and mourned, the BBC reported, adding that Daletsky's relatives experienced a shock last September. One of the Ukrainian soldiers released from Russian captivity called them and said that Nazar was alive, that he had seen him in prison. "It was hard to believe," Roksolana said. Without evidence, the family was unsure. This week, Daletsky called his family, exhausted and weak. But from Ukrainian territory. On Thursday, after five months, another prisoner exchange with Russia took place, and 157 prisoners returned to Ukraine, wrote the Ukrainska Pravda server, which also reported on Dalecki's return. "Nazarku, my dear son," Dalecki's visibly upset mother says into the phone in footage published by the BBC. "I've been waiting for you for so long... Do you have everything, arms, legs?" she asked afterwards. "That's good... God," she apparently reacted with tears to her son's answer. "You can't talk for a long time, can you?" Dalecki's mother continued, and before saying goodbye to her son, she told him that she loved him very much. "It was so strange, because my son died, I buried him, and now (I hear) his voice. Can you imagine the mother's emotions? Happiness. Huge happiness. I couldn't hold back my tears," Nataliya said later, according to the BBC. Officially, about 70,000 people are missing in Ukraine, which is suffering from Russian military aggression, most likely soldiers. Some died on the battlefield, but many were captured and for their families, the story of Nazar Dalecki will be a spark of hope, the BBC noted. Ukraine Russia society fighting PHOTO Author: ČTK

Prague - Small entrepreneurs will be able to choose whether to pay a flat tax or be subject to electronic sales records (EET). The coalition council agreed on this today, said the Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies Tomia Okamura (SPD) after its meeting. However, according to the Ministry of Finance, the alternative to EET will not be identical to the current form of the flat tax. Minister of Finance Alena Schillerová (ANO) is preparing a law that would renew EET. The records should start operating from next year. "There will be a choice for those who want EET or continue to want the flat tax," said Okamura. According to him, the goal is not to increase bureaucracy for small entrepreneurs. The turnover limit at which entrepreneurs will be able to choose will be set so that it applies not only to occasional businesses, but also to sole traders for whom this is their main activity. The Ministry of Finance specified in a press statement that EET will be a blanket measure with a minimum of exceptions. "The coalition council has agreed on a compromise solution for the smallest self-employed persons, who will receive the option of an alternative regime to the EET. However, this will not be identical to the current advantageous form of the flat-rate tax, which will remain a privilege for registered taxpayers," the ministry said. After the government meeting, Schillerová said that she would present details of the EET at a press conference on February 18. The flat-rate tax can be used by self-employed persons who are not value-added tax (VAT) payers and whose annual business income reaches a maximum of two million crowns. The tax is paid in three bands, graded mainly according to the amount of income. In January this year, approximately 125,000 people were registered for the flat-rate tax regime. The Ministry of Finance plans to prepare a draft law on the EET by mid-February, followed by an internal and external comment procedure. The government should approve it in the first half of this year and the first reading in the Chamber of Deputies should follow by the summer at the latest, Schillerová said earlier. The renewed obligation to record sales is to apply from January 2027 and will apply to traders, restaurateurs and craftsmen. According to the minister, the upcoming sales record will equalise conditions for entrepreneurs, reduce the grey economy and also strengthen state budget revenues. The intention to restore the EET was also welcomed this year by the International Monetary Fund mission, according to which the project will help reduce tax evasion. Sales record was introduced by the ČSSD and ANO government in 2016, but from spring 2020 it was suspended until the end of 2022 due to the Covid-19 pandemic and became de facto voluntary. From January 2023, the government of Petr Fiala (ODS) abolished it. Czech Republic taxes government EET coalition Author: ČTK

Prague - Excalibur Army, part of the CSG arms group of businessman Michal Strnad, has won a contract in Southeast Asia to produce over 100 Patriot armored vehicles for more than six billion crowns ($300 million). Deliveries of mortar vehicles or armored personnel carriers are to be completed within three years. CSG told ČTK today. The contract includes, among other things, wheeled infantry fighting vehicles or armored ambulances. Patriot vehicles use a Tatra wheeled chassis with a central support tube, which, according to Excalibur Army, ensures good mobility even in difficult terrain. This is not the company's first order in this region; in the past, it has already exported bridge systems or rocket launchers there, recalled Excalibur Army CEO Vladimír Stulančák. At the end of last year, the company concluded a multi-billion-crown contract for the supply of small-caliber ammunition for the Ministry of Defense of the state from Southeast Asia. CSG (Czechoslovak Group) is one of Europe's leading manufacturers of artillery ammunition. It expanded in this sector even before Russia's full invasion of Ukraine in 2022. CSG also produces smaller-caliber ammunition, ground systems at Excalibur Army, and vehicles at Tatra Trucks. In addition to the Czech Republic, the company operates production plants in the US, Britain, Spain, Italy, Germany, Slovakia, Serbia, and India, employing more than 14,000 people. CSG shares began trading on the stock exchanges in Amsterdam and Prague in January; CSG raised 3.8 billion euros (roughly 93 billion crowns) from the sale of shares, which represents 15.2 percent of its share capital, it said. Prague - Some councilors of Czech Television (ČT) and Czech Radio (ČRo) sent an open letter to members of the government and deputies calling for a dialogue with the professional public on the financing of public service media. Due to the government's intention to abolish fees for television and radio, they are concerned about the future of public service media. The letter, which is available to ČTK, was signed by 11 of the current 17 councilors of Czech Television and one of the current seven councilors of Czech Radio. The councilors also supported the call by the general directors of Czech Television Hynek Chudárek and Czech Radio René Zavoral to the Minister of Culture Oto Klempíř (for the Motorists) to create a working group that will discuss the financing of Czech Television and Czech Radio. The government of ANO, SPD and Motorists plans to abolish television and radio fees and is counting on transferring the financing of public service media to the state budget. The coalition has already agreed that the change will take effect from January 2027. The government justifies the planned change by trying to reduce the financial burden on people and companies. He also argues that funding in the form of fees only works in ten of the 27 EU countries. Klempíř said on Wednesday that the Ministry of Culture is preparing several models for financing Czech Radio and Czech Television. The coalition will discuss them, then offer them to the professional public for debate. "We are turning to you because we are concerned about the future of Czech Radio and Czech Television. Strong, independent and stably financed public service media represent one of the basic and necessary pillars of a democratic and healthy society. Any threat to them is therefore a risk for all citizens of this country, both now and in the future," the councilors said in the letter. According to them, Czech Radio and Czech Television have long been the media with the highest share of trust among citizens of the Czech Republic, and this trust must be protected and sensitively nurtured. According to them, public media are not just another player on the market, but are unique in that, without direct dependence on private and political interests or advertising budgets, they perform a service that, by its nature, no one else can provide. This concerns the preservation of spiritual, cultural and natural heritage, for example, minority topics, specialized broadcasting for children and youth or seniors. According to the councilors, the content given by law, and now also the memorandum on the method of fulfilling the public service, cannot be maintained without a stable, long-term predictable and independent financing system. They consider the current financing through fees to be this, which transparently and demonstrably separates the public service from any hidden economic influence. The appeal was signed by David Brabec, Jefim Fištejn, Ivana Chmel Denčevová, Vlastimil Ježek, Ladislav Mrklas, Karel Novák, Jiří Padevět, Bára Procházková, Ilja Racek, Milada Richterová and Tomáš Řehák from the Czech Television Council and Zbigniew Czendlik from the Czech Radio Council. Last year, after more than a year of negotiations, the television fee was increased by legislative amendment from 135 to 150 crowns per month, and the radio fee from 45 to 55 crowns. Czech Television has an estimated annual income from fees of around CZK 6.7 billion and radio CZK 2.5 billion. Czech Republic media government Czech radio Czech television Author: ČTK

Prague - According to the Big Mac index, the Czech crown was undervalued against the dollar by 10.2 percent in mid-January. In the US, one Big Mac hamburger cost $6.12, while in the Czech Republic it cost 115 crowns. The theoretical exchange rate should be around 18.79 crowns per dollar, but it currently stands at 20.93 CZK per dollar. Purple Trading analyst Petr Lajsek told ČTK. In the July index, the crown was undervalued against the dollar by more than 14.6 percent. The Big Mac index, named after the famous hamburger, compares the purchasing power of various world currencies. It compares how much a Big Mac costs in different countries and is intended to indicate overvaluation or undervaluation of the exchange rate. The index is compiled by The Economist twice a year, in January and July. According to Lajsek, the index also has shortcomings; it primarily compares purchasing power parity, so looking at theoretical exchange rates is more of an interest. The final price of sandwiches in each country is influenced by factors such as demand, energy costs and wages. The comparison from the inflation perspective is also interesting. In the Czech Republic, the Big Mac has become more expensive by CZK 6, in the US by USD 0.11, or CZK 2.30. However, December's year-on-year inflation in the Czech Republic was only 2.1 percent, in the US 2.7 percent. "The significant strengthening of the koruna against the dollar is mainly due to US President Donald Trump's constant attacks on the leadership of the Fed and also the trend of 'dedollarization', which is gaining momentum thanks to tariff wars. Despite this, according to the index, the koruna is still undervalued compared to the USD," said Lajsek. Despite the large weakening, the dollar maintains its position thanks to still relatively high interest rates and geopolitical threats. According to the index, the Polish zloty is overvalued by 2.2 percent against the dollar and the Hungarian forint is undervalued by 18.4 percent. Both currencies have strengthened significantly against the dollar, by more than five percent compared to the July measurement. The Japanese yen is still extremely undervalued, by 50.5 percent. This is related to the still relatively relaxed monetary conditions on the Japanese market. Although the Japanese central bank has already raised interest rates to 0.75 percent, the US dollar is still significantly more attractive in terms of the interest rate differential. Thanks to the large weakening of the dollar, the number of currencies that are overvalued against it has increased. In July, there were seven, now there are 11. The Swiss franc is the most overvalued, by 48.4 percent. The Uruguayan peso is second, by 43.1 percent. The Norwegian krone is third, with an overvalued value of 22.8 percent. Compared to the USD, the Swedish krona is also overvalued by 18.6 percent, followed by the Danish krone by 16.7 percent, the British pound by 15.7 percent, the euro by 15.3 percent, and newly also the Israeli shekel, the Polish zloty, the Colombian and Mexican pesos. The government has completed its proposal for a reform of the Procurement Act, which limits the ability of municipalities and welfare regions to purchase services from companies they own without competitive bidding. Minister of Labour Matias Marttinen says that the reform will increase competition in public procurement and will bring savings of hundreds of millions of euros in the longer term, although costs may increase in the initial phase. In future, municipalities and regions will have to own at least 10 percent of a company in order to be able to make purchases without competitive bidding. The government has finally completed its proposal for a reform of the Procurement Act. Minister of Labour Matias Marttinen (Kok) presented the bill on Thursday. No major changes have been made to the reform of the Procurement Act that is now being presented after the Chancellor of Justice stopped its progress earlier in January. The changes mainly concern more comprehensive justifications for issues that the Chancellor of Justice drew attention to. The Procurement Act simplifies the question of how municipalities and welfare regions can make purchases. The government wants to restrict how municipalities and welfare regions will use companies that they partly own themselves in the future. Such companies are called in-house companies. Municipalities and welfare regions have purchased information management and waste management services from municipalities, for example. The reason for the restriction is that it is believed that this will create more competition between different service providers. Currently, procurement can be made from in-house companies without competition. In principle, the tender should be renewed once, even when only one bidder participates in the tender. Currently, a maximum of two bidders participate in 40 percent of tenders. Market mapping carried out in advance will also be encouraged more than before. The changes are expected to increase competition and thus reduce the costs of public procurement. “It is clear that this is a very significant structural reform, the purpose of which is to increase competition and markets for tenders,” Marttinen said. However, many municipalities have estimated that genuine competition would not arise, as there is not a sufficiently large market for waste management in remote areas, for example. Minister Marttinen admits that in the initial phase, the costs of municipalities and regions may increase. In the longer term, the minister estimates that the costs will still decrease by “several hundred million euros”. The problems encountered by the legislative project have concerned the limitations described above. The first problem has been the question of how much the law would interfere with the constitutionally guaranteed self-government of municipalities. For example, the statement requested by the Association of Finnish Local and Regional Authorities pointed out that the effects of the law should be assessed from the perspective of the constitution on a municipality-by-municipality basis and that the law should be used through the Constitutional Law Committee. The proposal now being presented is acceptable from the perspective of the Chancellor of Justice, but according to Marttinen, it is possible for the Constitutional Law Committee to take the project up for consideration in Parliament. According to Minister Marttinen, however, the official assessment is that the reform of the Procurement Act would not interfere significantly with the self-government of municipalities. Another problem has concerned the question of how much of a company must be owned by municipalities or regions in the future in order to avoid competition. The government is aiming for a new rule of at least ten percent ownership, which it considers to mean a sufficiently large degree of control over the company. Currently, municipalities and regions may own very small shares in companies. According to Minister Marttinen, the ten percent ownership requirement is needed because in certain municipalities, ownership has been so small that it has been possible to circumvent the Procurement Act through in-house companies. In some places, the companies have also had an impact that hinders the functioning of the market, according to the minister. “Municipalities and cities will continue to be able to use in-house companies in the way they want, as long as the conditions are met,” Marttinen assures. Marttinen believes that the reform of the Procurement Act will lead to municipalities and regions making more joint procurements in the future. Earlier in January, the Chancellor of Justice asked the government to better justify why the limit is ten percent. Olli Hyvärinen, Commercial Counsellor at the Ministry of Employment and the Economy, said on Thursday that the ten percent limit has now been justified by the fact that scenarios with different ownership stakes have been made in the preparation. Of these, the ten percent ownership requirement has been assessed as having been implemented in the best way to improve competition and the functioning of the market.

The hearing of MP Päivi Räsänen (KD) on Wednesday before the US House of Representatives Judiciary Committee caused a stir in advance: has Räsänen been asked to appear only to promote the MAGA movement? Räsänen, who testified at the hearing titled "Europe's Threat to American Freedom of Speech and Innovation," feels differently.
