Aku Leijala, a separatist from Veikkola, stands in the snowdrift and peers into the dense forest. A small hill rises from the pine trees and snow-covered spruces. This is roughly where the Veikkola train station was supposed to be, which Leijala and many other Veikkola residents have been eagerly awaiting.

The proposed change in the funding model for welfare areas would mean cuts, especially for Helsinki residents. Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov considers the proposal unfair, because Helsinki would bear more than three times the share of the cuts than Pirkanmaa. Many other regions would also suffer from the harsher cuts. The Petteri Orpo (KOK) government's funding reform for welfare areas would target Helsinki and Western Uusimaa hard. The government announced its plans on Monday. Funding would decrease the most in Helsinki, which organizes its own social and health services: up to 102 million euros by 2029. Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov (KOK) considers the proposed model unfair to Helsinki and other well-performing regions. "It is completely incomprehensible that the government is proposing a cut for Helsinki that is twice as big as the national average," says Sazonov. HS reports on the proposals related to the funding model reform in more detail in this article. In practice, it is a change in the funding basis for welfare areas. The government is aiming for significant savings with the reform. The model may still change before the government makes its actual proposal on the matter. According to the draft law, the financing reform would save up to 390 million euros by 2029. Helsinki would now account for more than a third of the proposed savings. The city would lose out, especially because the population would weigh less in financing in the future. The greater impact is related to the proposed changes to diagnostic data and so-called transitional equalizations. Transitional equalizations are money used to equalize the differences caused by the social and health care reform. When social and health care funding was transferred from municipalities to welfare areas, some areas would have received much less money than before. Transitional equalizations have compensated for this difference so that the change would not be too sudden. Permanent transitional equalizations are now being cut from their current level. In addition to the savings, the government is aiming to reduce the economic differentiation of welfare areas. Helsinki and Western Uusimaa in particular have survived the social and health care crisis better than many other areas. Instead, for example, the regions of Central Finland and Central Ostrobothnia are struggling with large deficits. Sazonov considers it irresponsible that the regions that have managed their finances responsibly are being targeted by the largest cuts. "I understand that the government is making savings in the public finance situation. But they must be allocated in a balanced and fair manner. It is not that money is added to the health services of some Finns and taken away from others," he says. According to Sazonov, per capita costs in Helsinki are at a moderate level. "Is it right that a Helsinki resident bears more than three times the share of social and health care cuts than a resident of Pirkanmaa?" Sazonov asks the Ministry of Finance and Minister of Local Government and Regional Development Anna-Kaisa Ikonen (Kok) whether the government's message is that the better a region manages its affairs, the more it will be cut. "The government should re-evaluate this legislation," Sazonov says. Along with Helsinki, Western Uusimaa would lose out in the model. The region, whose largest city is Espoo, is planning savings of up to 54 million euros by 2029. The reason is largely the same as in Helsinki and other growing, populous welfare regions: the population would have less of an impact than it does now. Henrik Wickström, a member of parliament from Inkoo, a member of parliament for the ruling party RKP, like Sazonov, considers the cuts in their current form to be difficult. In Wickström's opinion, Western Uusimaa would suffer disproportionately. "This is a very difficult proposal for us [in Western Uusimaa]. However, the model could have been even worse," he estimates. In Wickström's opinion, reforming the Finance Act in this way would mean that regions that have adjusted in a front-loaded manner would have to pay for the looser finances of other regions. He hopes that the reform will be refined after the consultation round and that the population will be taken into account better. In Wickström's opinion, the entire financing model for social welfare should be reviewed urgently. “The social welfare financing system is broken. No one could have believed at the beginning of the government term that the situation would be this difficult. This is due, among other things, to differences in the starting level and in how diagnostics are performed in different regions,” he states. Differences in diagnostics, in the recording of different patient records, are one reason for the differentiation of social welfare costs between regions. Recording practices have been different in different regions. Diagnoses contribute to how much money is distributed to different regions. The government is now partially intervening in this as well. In the future, diagnoses made in private settings would not be taken into account in financing unless they are linked to public healthcare. The change would have the greatest impact on the financing received by the regions of Southern Finland, as these regions use private healthcare services more than the rest of the country.

The ruling parties, the National Coalition Party and the Finns Party, are dissatisfied with the proposal by Otto Andersson, the chairman of the RKP parliamentary group, to temporarily abolish the asset transfer tax. The government partners fear that a public proposal could cause home buyers to postpone their purchase decisions in the hope of a tax reduction, which would further paralyze the housing market. Andersson says the proposal is his personal view, not the official position of the RKP. The revenue from the asset transfer tax for this year is estimated at 670 million euros, so abolishing the tax would likely make a dent in the state finances. The major government parties are displeased with the opening of the parliamentary group chairman of the RKP parliamentary group, the chairman of the parliamentary group, to temporarily abolish the asset transfer tax. On Monday, Otto Andersson proposed at the parliamentary group's winter meeting to abolish the tax for, for example, a year. The aim would be to speed up the housing market and support the construction industry. Representatives of the National Coalition Party and the Finns Party do not want to take a position on the proposal by name, but commented to Helsingin Sanomat in a hushed tone in background discussions. The parties even consider the RKP's approach to buying a home to be dangerous. Those considering buying a home may anticipate that the proposal coming from the ruling party will also be implemented. They may therefore postpone their purchase decision in the hope of a future tax reduction, which would further paralyze the housing market. The government partners believe that negotiations regarding possible changes to the transfer tax should be held in secret from the public due to market effects. This is how the government acted in 2023, when it concealed for months its decision made in government negotiations to reduce the transfer tax and at the same time remove the tax benefit for first-time home buyers. Otto Andersson commented on the government partners' criticism of HS at the winter meeting of the parliamentary group. He says that the proposal to temporarily abolish the transfer tax is his personal thinking, not a position discussed in the RKP party bodies. “Different MPs from the ruling parties are constantly making dozens of proposals. That doesn’t mean that all of them will be implemented. I don’t see any drama here,” says Andersson. However, isn’t it a different matter when the chairman of the ruling party’s parliamentary group makes an opening statement at the group’s winter meeting? Such an opening statement is easy to interpret as the party’s position. “That’s my personal view. In this economic situation, we need a discussion about all the ways in which the situation can be improved,” Andersson replies. Anders Adlercreutz, chairman of the Finnish People’s Party, also says that Andersson’s proposal is not a party proposal. In his opinion, a more important issue for housing transactions than the transfer tax is the speed of economic growth and people’s faith in their own future. “If the government were to consider this, it would be a matter for consideration. This was Andersson’s idea of what could have an impact. The range of methods is of course substantially wider,” says Adlercreutz. Andersson’s proposal does not necessarily have good chances of success. In its spring budget debate, the government will again look for at least some new savings targets for next year. The estimated revenue from the transfer tax for this year is 670 million euros. The majority of the revenue comes from housing and real estate transactions. The temporary abolition of the tax would likely put a dent in state finances, even if the measure would stimulate housing transactions somewhat.

The government is cutting social and healthcare funding and reforming the model by which it distributes money to welfare areas. The change will reduce funding, especially in densely populated areas, by reducing the weight of the number of inhabitants and emphasizing the need for services. Helsinki will lose 102 million euros by 2029, or 143 euros per inhabitant, while Central Ostrobothnia's funding will increase by 21 euros per inhabitant. In total, the changes will reduce funding for welfare areas by 66 million euros next year and 390 million euros in 2029. The government wants to make big savings in social and healthcare funding and is reforming the model by which it distributes money to welfare areas in many ways. The reform of the funding model went out for comment on Monday. The change in the model will reduce funding, especially in areas that have previously received funding based on the number of inhabitants. The government is reducing the weight of the number of inhabitants in calculating funding and is emphasizing people's need for services more than before. The aim is to reduce regional segregation, meaning that some areas are already doing quite well, while others are struggling to cope. The proposed changes will hit densely populated areas, especially Helsinki, which is not exactly a welfare area, but organises social and health services itself. According to the proposal, Helsinki's social and health funding will decrease by 102 million euros by 2029, or 143 euros per inhabitant. The combined impact over three years would be around 2.9 percent compared to Helsinki's 2029 funding level, which is estimated to be 3.5 billion euros. The government estimates that the funding received by the City of Helsinki is "sufficient to secure the conditions for organising services" in the future. The change will also be significant in Western Uusimaa, which is centred on Espoo. Its funding would decrease by 54 million euros, or 103 euros per inhabitant. In some areas, funding would increase. The range is from -143 euros per inhabitant in Helsinki to +21 euros per inhabitant in Central Ostrobothnia. According to the bill, the largest cuts will be made to areas that are estimated to have financial capacity from the perspective of sufficient funding. In total, the proposed changes will reduce the level of funding for welfare areas by 66 million euros next year, 225 million euros in 2028 and 390 million euros in 2029. This is a saving that has already been agreed in the government programme. In addition to the savings agreed in the government programme, the funding model will be revised so that the impact of diagnoses received in private healthcare on funding is removed. When the funding for welfare areas is currently calculated, the model is largely based on how sick the people in the area are. This is determined using information from the area about diagnoses. These have not only been diagnoses made by the welfare area, but since 2024, private diagnoses have also been included, which has also favoured the areas of Southern Finland in funding and intensified the differentiation of the areas. In the future, only private diagnoses that are somehow connected to the public sector will be accepted, for example diagnoses made with a service voucher issued by a region. In addition, the government will change one of the obscure details of the financing model, namely the transitional equalization. The transitional equalizations were agreed upon when the former municipal-based social welfare system was switched to a regional model, and they were intended to prevent excessive fluctuations in the level of funding by region. Permanent transitional equalizations will be cut, but they will not be eliminated, although experts have recommended it. This cut will also increase the savings for Helsinki, as the city has received 120 million euros in transitional equalization annually despite its surplus social welfare result. Some regions are very dependent on transitional equalizations, and eliminating them completely in a short time frame could ruin their economy. The government will also update the diagnosis information in the financing model, but not as extensively as the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL) had proposed. There have been problems with the diagnostic information, and the government does not want to complicate the system any further. In addition, THL and the Ministry of Finance will be able to make corrections to diagnostic data in the future, which they did not have the right to do before. Archipelago areas will receive additional funding in the future, which will benefit, among others, Western and Eastern Uusimaa. This was particularly important for the Rkp.

The Economic Policy Review Council proposes that the funding of welfare areas be calculated based on demographics and unemployment instead of diagnosis data. Tanja Rantanen, Financial Advisor to the Ministry of Finance, considers the proposal problematic because it does not take into account the large differences in the morbidity of Finns between different regions. The current funding model has been criticized as being complex, and shortcomings have been identified in the diagnosis data, which have caused unforeseen annual fluctuations in funding. Anna-Kaisa Ikonen, Minister of Local Government and Regional Development, has appointed investigators to investigate the fluctuations in the diagnosis practices of welfare areas. Tanja Rantanen, Financial Advisor to the Ministry of Finance, considers the Economic Policy Review Council's criticism of the funding of the regions to be understandable but surprising. In its annual report, the Review Council criticizes the model by which welfare areas currently receive funding from the state. The model is largely based on how sick people in the region are, and it is determined using information on diagnoses from the region. The Evaluation Council believes that diagnostic data should be completely discarded in the distribution of funds between regions. In the opinion of the Evaluation Council, the need for regional services could be calculated more simply based on the demographic structure and certain socio-economic factors, such as the region's unemployment. Rantanen understands this view because the regions have criticized the current financing model as being complex and opaque. The criticism intensified last summer when several regions were able to demonstrate that there were shortcomings in the diagnostic data: for example, Northern Ostrobothnia had an unusually high number of respiratory failure diagnoses, which was estimated to bring in up to 10 million euros in additional money for the region. "There have been differences in the data base between the regions, and in some regions there have also been shortcomings. The regions have improved the data base at different rates, and this has affected the need factors of all regions, which has resulted in unpredictability and problematic annual fluctuations in funding," says Rantanen. "That is why the Evaluation Council's proposal is easy to understand." However, according to Rantanen, it is surprising that the Evaluation Council recommends switching to demographic and socio-economic indicators instead of diagnostic data, i.e. looking at the age structure and unemployment rate of the region, for example. According to Rantanen, calculations by the National Institute for Health and Welfare THL show that switching to a demographic model would not be very simple. “Our concern is whether such a model would be able to adequately capture the differences in morbidity between regions,” Rantanen says. “We know that the population in Western Finland is healthier than in Eastern Finland, where there are more certain endemic diseases. The financing model should meet the service needs of the residents of the region.” THL Senior Researcher Tuukka Holster says that THL’s results show that switching to demographic data would mean major financial impacts for the regions. In other words, some regions would benefit and some would suffer considerably if other need factors were emphasized instead of diagnostic data. Rantanen believes that in the next parliamentary term, one option in the development of the financing model would be to investigate a model in which, in addition to population data, morbidity would be taken into account in some way, but in a much simpler way than at present. In November, Minister of Local Government and Regional Affairs Anna-Kaisa Ikonen (Coalition Party) appointed Professor Ulla-Mari Kinnunen and Professor Tomi Voutilainen as investigators to investigate the reasons for the variation in diagnosis practices in welfare areas. The deadline for the work is now the end of February.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo announced that the government will establish a parliamentary group to prepare a reform of the welfare area model. The opposition parties SDP and the Centre Party are praising the decision, but the SDP in particular is criticizing that the group is focusing on preparing for the next parliamentary term and not on the acute financial problems of the welfare areas. The working group is intended to begin its work in early winter and will be based on Marina Erhola's report. Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's (Kok) announcement of the establishment of a parliamentary group on social and health services is receiving praise from the SDP and the Centre Party. Orpo told Yle's Ykkösaamu on Saturday that the government will establish a parliamentary group to prepare a reform of the welfare area model. According to Orpo, the group's work will begin in early winter, when he has given the Prime Minister's announcement on social and health services. "Even the boots have already dug into the ground so that there is a pretty deep hole, since we have been waiting for this," says Markus Lohi (Centre Party). In the autumn, the opposition parties jointly appealed to Orpo to establish a group, but the Prime Minister did not warm to the idea at the time. However, Orpo already hinted at the idea in his New Year's greetings. "It was very welcome news that the Prime Minister came to his senses on this matter," says Joona Räsänen (SD). The announcement does not gather only praise. Räsänen criticized the fact that the group's work would focus on preparing for the upcoming election period. According to him, this would ignore the acute and "most annoying" problem of welfare areas, namely the obligation to cover deficits. "The Prime Minister could have stated quite clearly that each welfare area would also be given additional time if necessary," says Räsänen. Under the current law, welfare areas must cover the deficits incurred during their operations by 2026. Last November, the government announced that around ten regions would receive additional time until 2027 or 2028. Lohi also criticizes the government for ignoring the acute problems of social and health services. He estimates that the group would not have time to address them during this election period. “Of course, the implementation will inevitably take place during the next election period,” Lohi says. In the autumn, the opposition parties appealed to Orpo to ask the government to give welfare regions additional time to put their finances in order. This week, it emerged that many welfare regions have managed to improve their finances more than expected over the past year. Nine regions still ran a deficit last year. According to Orpo, the group is preparing a reform of the welfare region model as the basis for the next government programme. In his opinion, the work should be based on Marina Erhola’s report. The report contains several recommendations on which the parliamentary parties disagree. For example, the report states that 6–11 welfare regions would be sufficient to implement social and health care and rescue services. There are currently 21 areas. In addition, the expert group recommended, among other things, assessing the consolidation of the hospital and emergency department network. According to Räsänen, the working group should not spend its time on, for example, reducing the number of welfare areas, as this would increase costs in the short term. He also briefly acknowledges the consolidation of the hospital and emergency department network. “It has always been a doomed idea that the great hall of Parliament should decide where on-call services are allowed and where not.” According to Lohi, the Erhola report dealt with solutions to the problems of welfare areas in a partly superficial way. According to him, the working group should first and foremost deepen its knowledge of the benefits, disadvantages and costs before drawing conclusions about the structures. “Yes, we are also ready to rethink the division of labor in hospitals, because the focus needs to be on the basic (healthcare) level and productivity needs to be improved,” Lohi says, adding that he does not mean abolishing hospitals. Räsänen, for his part, estimates that at least a large part of the parliamentary parties could reach an agreement on, among other things, strengthening the decision-making power of welfare regions and increasing cooperation between regions in the procurement of ICT support systems. “It would be important to start work as soon as possible so that preparations can be made in such a way that any changes can be quickly carried forward in the coming parliamentary term,” says Räsänen.

Antti Kaikkonen will seek a second term as the leader of the Centre Party at the Tampere party conference in June. Kaikkonen announced the matter in a speech and a press release at the Centre Party conference. “Finland must be lifted out of this quagmire, where we unfortunately find ourselves. I am ready to give my full contribution to this work. The country needs a safe change,” Kaikkonen said. Kaikkonen has been the leader of the Centre Party since June 2024. Kaikkonen also said that the Centre Party is considering leaving the issue of mass unemployment as a matter of urgency. According to him, the government has failed to reverse the trend of Finland’s rising unemployment. “More and more Finns are out of work and the situation is getting worse all the time. Finland has sunk to the bottom of the European unemployment statistics. We now have more unemployment than any other EU country. This is downright unbelievable, but unfortunately true,” Kaikkonen said in a press release. The Centre Party left the issue of mass unemployment as an issue of urgency last autumn.

According to Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (Kok), inappropriate behavior and harassment are very bad things from the perspective of Parliament. Orpo commented on the matter on Yle's Ykkösaamu on Saturday. The harassment scandal has been raging around the SDP for the third week now. Orpo did not want to comment on internal issues within the SDP, but stated that the issue of those who were harassed must not be forgotten. "Those issues must be investigated. If people have been harassed or treated inappropriately, those victims must also be remembered," Orpo said. According to Orpo, strong language can be used in politics, but getting personal is not part of politics. Orpo said that he himself has not encountered any cases of harassment in Parliament. He added that as Prime Minister, he does not spend that much time in Parliament. According to Orpo, Parliament has changed for the better during his political career. “In the big picture, things are going well in Parliament. The staff is satisfied. But of course, there is also inappropriate behavior in every work community. Parliament has tried to fix these issues, but we must ensure that such incidents do not occur,” Orpo said. The harassment scandal took new turns on Wednesday when the news agency STT published a story in which the chair of the SDP parliamentary group, Tytti Tuppurainen, is alleged to have behaved inappropriately towards the SDP parliamentary group’s assistants and MPs. Tuppurainen has denied the allegations. On Thursday, Iltalehti reported that Miapetra Kumpula-Natri’s (SD) former subordinates are accusing her of inappropriate treatment. Kumpula-Natri apologized to them on Friday. Orpo admitted that no party is free from sin when it comes to inappropriate behavior. He said that the National Coalition Party is a large party and parliamentary group with many employees. “There can certainly be something.” Orpo also said in Ykkösaamu that the government will establish a parliamentary working group that will start preparing a reform of the welfare area model in early winter. The reform will be prepared on the basis of the next government program. “I think the basis should be the report of the expert working group of Undersecretary of State [Marina] Erhola, which raises two key issues that need to be reviewed and reformed. They are the financing model in a larger sense and also the structures.” According to Orpo, he will explain the matter in more detail when he gives the Prime Minister’s announcement on the state and future of social and health services. Orpo returned from a visit to China on Wednesday, where he met, among others, the country’s President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Li Qiang. In Ykkösaamu, Orpo said that he had sent a message to China that the country should not cooperate with Russia or trade with Russia that would enable Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine. According to Orpo, he appealed to the president to use his own authority over Russia to end the war. Jani Mäkelä, the chairman of the Finns Party parliamentary group, commented during Orpo's trip that meetings with the Chinese leadership are "problematic". According to him, one must be able to talk to everyone, but at the same time it must be remembered that China is an "authoritarian and imperialist country that does not respect human rights". In the first morning Orpo acknowledged Mäkelä's criticism by saying that all the governing parties were aware of the trip. According to Orpo, Mäkelä should direct his criticism at his own party, the Finns Party. According to Orpo, more and more of his own time is spent on foreign and security policy. According to him, Finland's decision to join NATO was absolutely right and there was no alternative. "We cannot manage alone in this world. We can raise the bar with our own strong defense." However, according to Orpo, a longer-term conflict requires an alliance. He admits that NATO is currently facing challenges related to the changed behavior of the United States. However, Orpo does not believe that the United States would ultimately jeopardize NATO or transatlantic cooperation with Europe. According to him, NATO and its fifth article can be trusted. Orpo did not answer the question of whether he intends to seek a second term as chairman of the National Coalition Party. He said that he is motivated to work for Finland. Orpo said that he will announce his intentions when the time comes.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov says there is still a long way to go to find a peace solution in Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has proposed new trilateral talks with the United States this week, but no date has been confirmed. The previous US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia ended in Abu Dhabi last week without a breakthrough. There is still a long way to find a peace solution in Ukraine, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in an interview with the Russian NTV channel. US President Donald Trump has said that peace should be achieved in Ukraine by the summer. If this does not happen, the Trump administration would start putting pressure on both Russia and Ukraine. Lavrov commented, according to the Russian news agency Tass, that Russia should not be happy about Trump's pressure on Europe and Ukraine, because the talks will take some time. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that he had proposed trilateral talks to be held in the United States, most likely in Miami, Florida. The date of the talks has not been confirmed, but Zelensky has hoped they will be held this week. Ukraine has already said it will participate. The previous US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia ended without a breakthrough last week in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Various drafts have been drawn up during different rounds of talks, but no agreement has been signed. This winter has been very difficult in Ukraine, perhaps even the most difficult of the entire four-year war. For example, it has been colder than usual in Kiev, while Russia has been fiercely attacking Ukrainian energy facilities. Electricity has had to be rationed and ordinary Ukrainians are dependent on the help provided by emergency tents.

British Prime Minister Keir Starmer's position has been further weakened as more information comes to light about his former ambassador to Washington, Peter Mandelson,'s connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Among other things, Mandelson has been accused of leaking confidential documents to Epstein during his time as a minister. Mandelson's actions are now under police investigation. Starmer and the Labour Party's popularity has plummeted during a government that has lasted just over a year and a half, as Britain suffers from economic problems and worsening unemployment. A possible defeat for the Labour Party in the by-election at the end of February would further weaken Starmer's position. Britain's Labour Party was supposed to save Britain, but Britain itself does not seem to want a Labour government as its savior. Prime Minister Keir Starmer has only been at the helm of the country for just over a year and a half. Time is short in months, but there is time to set records: Starmer's popularity has plummeted. Starmer's center-left Labour party has sunk to the bottom with him. Speculation has been rife in Britain for some time about Starmer's possible resignation. According to the odds of the water companies, many believe that he will leave this year. In February, Starmer's position has become even more precarious. The reason is the new Jeffrey Epstein revelations at the end of January. Documents have revealed that a former confidant of Starmer's government in the United States had been even closer friends with Epstein than previously known. In December 2024, the British government appointed a new ambassador to Washington. The choice fell on Labour's old ringleader, the multiple former minister and EU Trade Commissioner Peter Mandelson, known as the "Prince of Darkness". The government perhaps thought that Mandelson, who has been through a lot and has a questionable reputation, is exactly the right person to handle relations with President Donald Trump. Peter Mandelson only had time to serve as Britain's ambassador to Washington for seven months in 2025. In the photo, Mandelson and President Donald Trump are shaking hands to celebrate the UK-US trade agreement last May. Photo: Leah Millis / In hindsight, one should have thought twice. As early as September 2025, Mandelson was fired when more Epstein information began to leak out. However, that was just the beginning. The latest information has revealed much more: Mandelson had leaked confidential government documents to Epstein during his time as a minister. Mandelson and his wife are also alleged to have taken money from Epstein. Now Mandelson's actions are already under police investigation. Mandelson has also become another nail in the coffin for Starmer and his government. The ambassadorial appointment, which turned out to be a bombshell, calls Starmer's judgment into question. At the same time, the Prime Minister's reputation is deteriorating. Over the weekend, the Prime Minister's Chief of Staff Morgan McSweeney, from Starmer's inner circle, was sacrificed. McSweeney resigned, thus taking primary responsibility for Mandelson's appointment. The prime minister's situation is made worse by the fact that his position is already weak. There are many reasons for this. The British government has been forced to backtrack on many of its reforms, which has created an image of weak governance. Voters might not care if Britain's weak economic situation did not fuel public discontent. Both the state and consumers are suffering from a cash crunch. Taxes are rising. Unemployment threatens to rise to its highest level in about a decade this year. Police remove evidence from Peter Mandelson's London home on Friday, February 6. Photo: Isabel Infantes / Starmer's sharp decline in popularity may seem unfair when you look at the British leader's background. Starmer, who has been criticized as boring, is a policy director, lawyer and former director of the Public Prosecution Service. He is a pragmatist who has emphasized the importance of economic growth and working relations with the EU. Starmer is also a staunch supporter of Ukraine and an advocate of European defense. Illegal routes to future immigration Starmer's government has taken a hard line. At the same time, returns have begun to be stepped up. In personality and style, Starmer is completely different from the Conservative prime ministers who preceded him: David Cameron, who lost his Brexit gamble, Theresa May, exhausted by Brexit negotiations, the popular but chaotic Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, who almost collapsed the British economy, and Rishi Sunak, who cleaned up the messes of his predecessors. Read more: A dull and ennobled expert who betrayed old left-wing promises - This is almost certain to be the next British prime minister Starmer's goal as prime minister has been to reform Britain's outdated structures. However, the British political system does not reward the government for focusing on work whose fruits will only be seen after many years. Voters want a better life now and immediately. When that does not happen, alternatives are sought from the opposition. The Labour Party is losing supporters to both the right and the left. On the right, the right-wing populist Reform Party of Nigel Farage, known as the Brexit man, is benefiting from Starmer's downfall. Liberal and progressive voters, on the other hand, are turning to the Liberal Democrats and the Greens. And the weaker Starmer is, the more he will be challenged from within his own party. At the end of January, Labour's decision-making body prevented Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham from seeking the Labour Party's candidacy in the parliamentary by-election. In practice, this meant that at the same time the path for Starmer's challenger to carry out a possible coup was blocked. The internal strife and possible rebellion within Labour have not been suppressed by the rescue movement. According to a recent poll, more than half of Labour Party members believe that Burnham should have been allowed to try to become a Labour MP. The by-election for the Gorton and Denton constituency will be held on the last Thursday of February. If the Labor Party loses, the Prime Minister will have even more explaining to do.

The latest material on Jeffrey Epstein has been wading through the days of the week. On Friday last week, the US Department of Justice released more than three million pages of documents, 180,000 photos and 2,000 videos. Epstein, a wealthy businessman, died in custody in 2019 on suspicion of sexual abuse of minors and human trafficking. According to the Department of Justice, Epstein had more than a thousand victims over a twenty-year period.

Spain and Portugal have been battered by the powerful storm Leonardo this week, and now a new storm called Marta is on its way, according to . The Spanish Meteorological Agency warns that Marta will hit the Iberian Peninsula on Saturday, bringing more heavy rain. The situation is particularly difficult in the provinces of Jaen and Córdoba in Andalusia, where the Guadalquivir river has flooded heavily. 30 millimeters of rain is expected on Saturday. According to , the regional governor of Andalusia, Juan Manuel Moreno, said that the rainfall is very worrying because the soil is no longer absorbing water as usual due to previous rains. There is also a risk of landslides due to the waterlogged soil. According to , more than 11,000 people have been forced to leave their homes in southern Andalusia in recent weeks due to a “storm train,” or successive heavy rain fronts, that has swept through the region. More homes may have to be evacuated due to the storm arriving on Saturday. A body was found in the province of Malaga near where a woman was swept away by a flooded river while trying to save her dog. Authorities said the body's identity had yet to be confirmed. In southern Portugal, the Sado River has flooded heavily, leaving many streets in the town of Alcacer do Sal, which is located on its banks, submerged for several days. A local resident interviewed by was forced to leave his home with only the clothes he was wearing. Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro announced that a state of emergency has been declared in 69 municipalities and will be extended until mid-February. At least six rivers are at risk of flooding. At least 1,100 people have already been evacuated due to flooding and a new storm, according to Portuguese television channel RTP. On Friday, the Portuguese army rescued 83 people and 15 animals from the weather. The army has also built flood defences.

The first deputy head of Russia's military intelligence service, Lieutenant General Vladimir Alekseev, was shot dead outside his apartment in Moscow on Friday morning. Alekseev is in critical condition in hospital. He is suspected of being responsible for the torture and ill-treatment of Ukrainian prisoners of war after they surrendered at the Azovstal steel plant. Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Ukraine of the assassination attempt, but Russian police have not released the suspect's identity. The first deputy head of Russia's military intelligence service, Lieutenant General Vladimir Alekseev, was shot dead in Moscow on Friday morning. He is in critical condition in hospital. According to several Russian Telegram channels, Alekseev was shot by a person who entered his house posing as a food delivery man. Some sources claim the perpetrator was a woman. The assassination attempt took place at around 7 a.m. Moscow time, as Alekseev was leaving his apartment. According to the independent website Ruscriminal, the general lived on the 24th floor of a 28-story building in northwestern Moscow. HS has confirmed the exact location of the incident from photographs taken at the scene. “According to neighbors, many did not know that their neighbor was a high-ranking military leader,” Ruscriminal writes. A car with a personal driver was waiting for Alekseev downstairs. The general had no other bodyguards. According to the Telegram channel Mash, which specializes in accidents, the attacker shot Alekseev three times in the back. After this, the general lost a lot of blood and was close to death. During the day, he underwent a complex operation in a Moscow hospital, after which he has been in a coma. According to the popular Telegram channel Baza, an apartment was located on the same 24th floor, which was rented out for a short term at a low price. The registration of tenants took place remotely, without any personal meetings with the owner of the apartment. There has been speculation that this apartment could have been used to prepare for an assassination attempt. Ruscriminal, citing residents of the building, claims that the surveillance cameras on the floors were not working. So far, the Russian police have not said anything about the suspect's characteristics. This may indicate that the authorities are having difficulties investigating the case. Lieutenant General Vladimir Alekseev in 2023. Photo: Russian Ministry of Defense Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Ukraine of the assassination attempt on Alekseev. "This terrorist act once again confirmed the desire of the [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy administration to engage in continuous provocations aimed at sabotaging the negotiation process," Lavrov said at a press conference in Moscow, according to the RBC news agency. Denys Prokopenko, commander of the 1st Army Corps of the Azov Brigade of the Ukrainian National Guard, published a message on the X service in which he said that Alekseev was Russia's chief negotiator in May 2022 during the surrender of Ukrainian soldiers at the Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol. According to Prokopenko, Alekseev promised that Russia would treat prisoners of war in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and signed a document guaranteeing this. “The word of an officer, the word of a man from the Vinnytsia region and a traitor to his homeland, turned out to be worthless,” Prokopenko wrote. The systematic torture, denial of medical care and starvation of the captured Azov soldiers are evidence of this, according to Prokopenko. He did not take direct responsibility for the shooting of Alekseev, but concluded his message with the phrase: “Revenge will find everyone.” Alekseev is one of the highest-ranking Russian military leaders to be the target of an assassination attempt since Russia launched a large-scale invasion of Ukraine. He was born in a village in the Vinnytsia region of the Ukrainian Soviet Republic. In 1984, he graduated from the Ryazan Landing Officer School. Since 2011, Alekseev has served as the first deputy head of the GRU. He is responsible for the activities of all GRU units in the area of the Ukrainian offensive war, the so-called special military operation. The exact number of intelligence personnel participating in the war in Ukraine is unknown, but they constitute a significant force there. They also carry out punitive operations in the occupied territories against residents who oppose Russian policy.

The United States and Iran held eight hours of talks in Oman on Friday on Iran's nuclear program. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the talks had progressed constructively. However, President Trump immediately announced new sanctions on Iranian oil exports, targeting 14 ships. The talks between the United States and Iran in Oman on Friday lasted eight hours, Axios reported, citing its own sources. The talks are aimed at resolving Iran's long-running dispute with Western powers over its nuclear facilities. Failure could bring the Middle East closer to war. "It was a good start for the talks. And there is an understanding to continue the talks," said Iranian Foreign Minister and head of the Iranian delegation Abbas Araghchi, according to . "If this process continues, I believe we will reach a good agreement." Araghchi said that the talks dealt exclusively with Iran's nuclear program. The United States has sought to expand the talks to include Iran’s ballistic missiles, support for armed groups in the region and “its treatment of its own people,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday. US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said on Friday night that President Trump was “committed to driving down the Iranian regime’s illicit oil and petrochemical exports through a maximum pressure campaign.” The sanctions target 14 ships. Last June, the United States struck Iranian nuclear facilities. Iran has since said it has halted uranium enrichment. The United States, its European allies and Israel accuse Iran of using its nuclear energy program as a cover for efforts to develop nuclear weapons. Iran says its nuclear program is for peaceful purposes only.

US President Donald Trump posted a video on Truth Social, in which former first lady Barack and Michelle Obama were depicted as monkeys. The video was later removed, and according to the White House, it was posted by an employee, not Trump himself. The post has caused outrage, with California Governor Gavin Newsom calling on all Republicans to condemn the post. US President Donald Trump has shared a video on his social media account, in which former first lady Barack Obama and Michelle Obama were depicted as monkeys. Democrat Obama was the first black president of the United States from 2009 to 2017. Late Thursday Finnish time, Trump posted a 62-second video on Truth Social, towards the end of which the Obamas are seen. Their faces have possibly been embedded into the bodies of swaying monkeys using artificial intelligence, and a snippet of the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight plays in the background. The video has since been removed, reports US media outlet CNN. The video focuses on conspiracy theories that something suspicious happened in the 2020 presidential election. Republican Trump lost the election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he has never admitted his defeat and has claimed that the Democrats stole the election. According to The New York Times, it is unclear whether Trump realized that the Obama-related part was part of the video he shared. Trump's post about the Obamas has caused outrage on social media, among other things. "Welcome to America, where the president gets away with racism like a dog!" Lebanese diplomat Mohamad Safa said in a message on the X service. California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, demanded "all Republicans condemn this. Now." White House spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt said in a text message to The Washington Post that the excerpt from the video about the Obamas was taken from a previous meme video featuring Trump as the king of the jungle and Democrats. “Stop this fake outrage and report today on something that really matters to the American people,” Leavitt said. The White House later commented on Friday that the video was mistakenly posted by a White House staffer, not Trump himself. Trump has built his political career, among other things, on his racist statements. For years in the 2010s, he promoted a conspiracy theory that Obama was not born in the United States and was therefore an illegitimate president. Obama was born in Hawaii. Trump has made racist statements about many people and ethnic groups. In January, he spoke in a mocking tone about Somalis at the World Economic Forum in Davos, suggesting that Somalis have low IQs.

Two Finnish freeskiers died in an avalanche in the Solda ski resort in northern Italy on Thursday, one Finn was rescued. There was a high avalanche risk in the area. About 40 rescuers and three helicopters participated in the rescue operation. Two Finnish tourists died in an avalanche in northern Italy on Thursday. One Finnish man was rescued from the avalanche. The deceased were Finnish freeskiers. The freeskiers were skiing outside the ski slope when they were hit by an avalanche. The avalanche occurred in the Solda ski resort area in South Tyrol. The ski resort is also known by its German name Sulden. On Friday, HS unsuccessfully contacted the area's alpine rescue team, Soccorso Alpino Solda, and the South Tyrol police to report on how the rescue operation was progressing. According to information from the Italian Alto Adige magazine, the Finns were hit by two different avalanches. The man who survived was a victim of a smaller avalanche and escaped with minor injuries. However, two other skiers were caught in a much larger avalanche. The newspaper describes the second avalanche as “huge”. According to rescue director Olaf Reinstadler, who spoke to HS on Thursday, the skiers caught in the second avalanche were found dead. The accident occurred at around 1:30 p.m., or 2:30 p.m. Finnish time. According to Italian public broadcaster RAI, the accident site was spotted from a helicopter when rescuers were flying to check for signs of another avalanche nearby. It is unclear whether the third skier also received an alert for help. From the helicopter, rescuers saw a man digging snow with his hands on the slope. When rescuers arrived, the man told them that two other skiers had been caught in the avalanche. One of the skiers was 60 centimeters deep, but he had hit his head in the accident. The other was significantly deeper, under up to 1.5 meters of snow. Reinstadler, who spoke to HS on Thursday, said that there was a high avalanche risk in the area at the time of the incident. According to RAI, the accident occurred near the Madriccio ski hut on the slopes of Punta Beltovo. About 40 people from volunteer rescue organizations and the Italian Ministry of Finance's paramilitary police participated in the rescue operation. In addition, three helicopters were involved in the operation. There have been several other fatal avalanches in the area this winter. According to the Austrian newspaper Krone, a 33-year-old snowboarder was hit by an avalanche in the Tarvisio area in Italy on Wednesday and later died of his injuries in hospital. On Saturday, two skiers were hit by an avalanche in Tyrol, Austria, but managed to escape on their own. Five German mountaineers died in Solda in early November after being caught in an avalanche. At the end of December, one person died in Riesernock in South Tyrol. In mid-January, eight skiers died in three different avalanches in Austria in one day. According to the Finnish skiing website Lumipallo.fi, the Solda ski resort is aimed particularly at more experienced and more skilled skiers and those interested in skiing off-piste. The centre's main ski area is the Madriccio glacier. According to the Lawinen.report website, which also monitors avalanches in the Alps, conditions in the Solda area are currently dangerous for skiing off-piste and for mountaineering.

Two Finnish tourists have died in an avalanche in northern Italy on Thursday. One man was rescued from the avalanche. Rescue director Olaf Reinstadler confirmed to HS by phone on Thursday evening that those who died in the avalanche were Finnish freeskiers. The Italian public broadcaster Rai reports on the matter, for example. The Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs told HS on Friday morning that the ministry is aware of the incident. The Ministry for Foreign Affairs confirmed that according to their information, two Finns have died in the avalanche and a third person involved was injured. Due to privacy concerns, the Ministry for Foreign Affairs is not commenting on the details of the incident. The freeskiers were skiing outside the ski slope when the avalanche hit. Everyone was wearing appropriate equipment. The avalanche occurred in the Solda ski resort area in South Tyrol at around 2:30 p.m. Finnish time. According to Reinstadler, there was a high avalanche risk in the area at the time of the incident. The avalanche occurred on the Punta Beltovo slope, which is accessible by ski lift. According to Rai, rescuers spotted the avalanche from a helicopter while on their way to investigate another avalanche in the area. While flying over the area, they saw a person digging through the snow. Those trapped under the snow were found using an avalanche beacon, but they were already dead. “One of them was really deep, 1.5 meters deep. The other was maybe 60 centimeters deep, but he had been hit in the head,” Reinstadler says. The local rescue service estimated on Thursday that there may have been other people in the avalanche area, but this has not been officially confirmed. According to the local newspaper Alto Adige, all three are Finnish men aged 50 to 60. According to Reinstadler, the identities of the three are still being established. They are believed to have been a group of friends. The surviving Finn is being treated at a local hospital. The case is known to the Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs.

Microsoft founder and billionaire Bill Gates says he regrets his association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. “I was a fool to hang out with him. I was one of many people who regret ever knowing him,” Gates told Australian television station 9News on Wednesday. Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice released the final batch of documents related to the Epstein sex crimes investigation, according to a statement. Two draft emails were revealed. One draft is a resignation letter from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. The message laments how Bill Gates allegedly had to get medication “as a result of having sex with Russian girls.” The second draft, which begins with the words “dear Bill,” laments the end of their friendship with Gates. The email claims Gates wished he had antibiotics to treat an STD so he could give them to his wife, Melinda French Gates, without her knowing. The draft emails were apparently never sent. Gates's spokesperson recently denied the claims in the documents, but now the 9News interview is the first in which the billionaire himself has commented on the allegations. "Apparently Jeffrey wrote the email to himself. It was never sent. The email is fake," Gates says, claiming Epstein may have tried to frame him. "I don't know what he was thinking. Was he trying to attack me in some way? I regret every minute I spent with him. I apologize for what I did," Gates continues. Melinda Gates commented on the published allegations in a podcast on US radio NPR on Tuesday. "For me personally, it's hard every time these details come up. Because they bring back memories of very, very difficult times in my marriage." The Gateses divorced in 2021. US media have previously reported that Melinda was upset about her husband's connections with Epstein even before their separation. In the podcast, Melinda Gates said that people who appeared in the documents, including her ex-husband, should answer questions that remain unanswered. Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, the son of former Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi, has been killed. Prosecutors say the 53-year-old Gaddafi died of gunshot wounds in the western Libyan town of Zintan, according to AFP and the British newspaper The Guardian. His death was reported on Tuesday. An investigation has been launched into the killing. Gaddafi's representatives say four masked men broke into his home on Tuesday and executed him. They described the incident as a "cowardly and treacherous assassination." Saif al-Islam Gaddafi's father, Muammar Gaddafi, was ousted from power and killed in 2011. The son announced in 2021 that he would run in Libya's presidential election, but the election was postponed until further notice. Gaddafi has been indicted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity. In 2015, a Libyan court sentenced him to death for crimes committed during the 2011 uprising. Gaddafi's exact whereabouts had long been a mystery, and the events leading up to his death are also unclear. Claudia Gazzini, a Libya expert with the International Crisis Group, who was interviewed by AFP, described the timing of his death as strange. "He had lived a relatively quiet life out of the public eye for several years." Gaddafi's lawyer, Marcel Ceccaldi, said Gaddafi moved frequently but had been living in Zintan for some time. Ceccaldi said there had been concerns about his safety in recent days, AFP reports. The lawyer said Gaddafi's tribal leader had even called him and said he would send people to ensure his safety, but he refused.

Russian reconnaissance satellites have come close to European communications satellites and may have intercepted their communications, reports the British newspaper Financial Times. Two Russian satellites have made repeated passes over European satellites over the past three years and stayed close to them for weeks at a time. Major General Michael Traut, head of Germany's space command, says the satellites are suspected of being engaged in signals intelligence. The vulnerability of European satellites is due to their age, as some of the communications may be unencrypted. Russian reconnaissance satellites have come alarmingly close to European communications satellites, reports the British newspaper Financial Times (FT). According to security officials who spoke to the newspaper, the activity may even have enabled the interception of communications transmitted via the satellites. According to the Financial Times, two Russian satellites, Luch-1 and Luch-2, have repeatedly passed close to European satellites over the past three years, staying close to them for weeks at a time. According to the FT, Luch-2, launched in 2023, has approached 17 European satellites. According to Major General Michael Traut, head of the German Space Command, the satellites are suspected of signals intelligence. According to another senior intelligence official who spoke to the FT, the satellites are likely to aim to get between the satellites and the ground stations that transmit data to them. Of particular concern is the satellites' control and command link, which can be used to adjust the satellites' orbits. The satellite technology is old, so communications can be unencrypted in many places. Using the recorded control traffic, Russia could later try to send false control commands to the satellites and, for example, move them out of place. Even if Russia were unable to decrypt the content of the messages passing through the satellites, simply monitoring the communication traffic could still reveal who is using the satellite, when, and from where. The information could later be used to support cyber operations, for example.

The Utah Jazz, playing away from home, defeated the Miami Heat 115–111 in the NBA. Lauri Markkanen, 28, represented the Jazz, which had lost its previous two games. Markkanen scored 17 points and grabbed eight rebounds against the Heat, even though he did not play in the final quarter of the game. The Jazz's top scorer was new signing Jaren Jackson Jr. with 22 points. The Jazz led the game by three points before the final quarter. After that, Jazz head coach Will Hardy kept Markkanen and Jackson Jr. on the bench until the end of the game. Experts have stated that the Jazz are implementing what is known as tanking, in which they prepare well in advance for the reserve opportunity of players. This means that the team is trying to train losses so that it has a better chance of a good reserve turn. Hardy was asked at a press conference how close he was to putting Markkanen and Jackson Jr. in the final quarter of the game. “I wasn’t [close],” was the head coach’s response. Utah is 13th in the Western Conference.

Furniture retailer Ikea is recalling Nymåne wall lamps due to a risk of electric shock. The company urges customers to stop using the lamps in question immediately and contact customer service. The recall is due to a manufacturing defect. The insulation of the power cord is not sufficient, which can cause a risk of electric shock if the power cord is damaged, the company says in a statement. The recall affects three Nymåne product models: a wall and reading lamp in white and anthracite, and a two-piece wall lamp in white. The recalled products can be identified by the date stamp and supplier ID. The recall applies to products with a date stamp between 2217 and 2550 and the supplier ID is 23241. The date stamp and supplier ID can be found on a sticker inside the lampshade or on the back of the lamp. Two-piece Nymåne wall lamp and Nymåne wall/reading lamp, anthracite and white. Photo: Ikea

From a distance, nothing has changed much. Jukka Jalonen stands in the interview area of the main stage of the qualification tournament in his familiar blue tracksuit and gives comments after the training. Now the blue tracksuit is adorned with the colors of Italy instead of the Lions logo. There is also no longer the media frenzy that surrounded him during his years as the Lions' head coach. As the Lions' head coach, Jalonen was the head coach of Finland's hockey team. The interest and pressure were like from another planet compared to his current job, as the head coach of the Italian men's ice hockey team. "The situation is of course completely different compared to my previous Olympics. Finland always plays for gold in qualification tournaments. Italy's goals are a bit different," Jalonen smiles. "We can go quite relaxed. We have to be open-minded." During Jalonen's, 63, era, the Lions won two medals at the Olympic tournaments, bronze in 2010 and gold in 2022. Jukka Jalonen guided the Lions to Olympic gold in Beijing 2022. The tournament was played without NHL players. Photo: JUSSI HELTTUNEN In Jalonen's opinion, Italy has a clear role in the top tournament, which is decorated with NHL stars. "We want to be a nuisance. It's not worth coming against us with a smile on your face. It's possible that that smile will freeze - at least in some sense," Jalonen says. From the beginning, Jalonen has been brutally honest about Italy's chances of success at home. Italy is the tournament's lilliput, from whom nothing worse is expected. "The players are not stupid. They know and I know that we are facing great players and teams. There are teams with more skill, but we are ready for this challenge." “We have to play strong as a five-man team and trust each other. On top of that, if there is a little luck, the goalie plays well and the opponent is a little bit crazy, then who knows what will happen,” Jalonen says. Above all, Jalonen wants to see his team throw themselves into the game with courage. “Even if an NHL defenseman goes for the puck from the end, we will be 95 kilos behind. It doesn’t matter which country a player from. It will definitely hurt. We have players who are willing to tackle.” According to Jalonen, there has been no pressure from the Italian Federation that the team must achieve a certain position. “The fourth match is the most important for us. It is a one-off and all teams will qualify for that match. We have to be at our best in the fourth match.” Jalonen has a clear opinion about the main stage of the Olympic tournament, the Santa Giulia arena, which attracted a lot of people. “The ice was already good a month ago. Otherwise, the arena is not in top condition. The booths and other facilities are what they are, but the rink is ok, and otherwise there is nothing to complain about.” The Santa Giulia arena was hastily renovated to match condition. Photo: Jukka Ritola / Aamulehti The playing conditions are in order, but otherwise the arena conditions are in a state of flux. “Little things, but you can’t focus too much on them. It doesn’t help, no matter how much you screw up,” Jalonen laughs. “We had a good few days of preparation and a warm-up match in Bolzano, and everything has gone well here. We are in a pretty good situation.” According to Jalonen, the Italian players still have a lot to get used to the size of the Olympic rink. The Santa Giulia rink is tailored to close to NHL size. “The guys have played in a larger rink for years. It’s certain that it will still be a bit noticeable and there will be a rush with the puck.” A smaller rink could also be beneficial for underdog teams like Italy. “If we played in an airport rink, we wouldn’t have any chance against well-skating opponents. When there’s less space and time, it’s easier to break and defend,” Jalonen sees. “When we set up a tight defensive game, whether it’s trap, aggressive scrimmage or defending our own zone, it’s not easy to play against that. There aren’t as many top chances.” In a small rink, scoring opportunities also arise more quickly. Defensive readiness and puck confidence are emphasized. “The best players are damn skilled and their speed skills are incredibly high. We’re forced to make puck mistakes and turnovers. In these situations, top players can create a plot in two seconds. We can’t give that to our opponents,” Jalonen emphasizes. Italy opens the Olympic tournament on Wednesday, February 11, against Sweden. The Lions will face Jalonen’s Italy on February 14.

HJK's men's football team has signed 23-year-old Danish striker Mads Borchers. He will join HJK from Ingolstadt, Germany. HJK announces that the 188-centimeter Borchers will join the Helsinki club on a loan deal until the end of July, which includes an option to buy. Borchers previously played for Vaasa Palloseura. He finished the 2024 season with ten goals in 16 Veikkausliiga matches for Vaasa Palloseura. Borchers' strong form continued in Vaasa at the beginning of last season, when he scored five goals in six Veikkausliiga games. "Mads knows the Veikkausliiga and we know him. The wooden sauna at the Yrjönkatu swimming pool in Helsinki has been closed for the time being, just a couple of days after the opening ceremony. On Sunday, a smell of smoke was detected in the swimming pool, which is why the rescue service was called to the scene and the building was evacuated. The wooden sauna will be closed until the city has ensured its safe use. The other facilities and saunas at the swimming pool are in normal use. There were several rescuers in front of the hall. Photo: Petteri Tuohinen / HS The wooden sauna on the second floor of the Yrjönkatu swimming pool has been closed for the time being, the City of Helsinki reports. The city will announce separately when the sauna is available for customers again. The smell of smoke is suspected to have come from the chimney of the wooden sauna on the second floor of the hall, the City of Helsinki press release says. The decision is based on a smoke observation on Sunday, which is why the rescue service was called to the scene and the swimming pool was evacuated. The fire chief on duty told HS on Sunday that there was no actual smoke or fire in the swimming pool, but rather the smell of smoke. At the time, a soot fire was suspected in the swimming pool chimney. The wooden sauna is now closed until the city has confirmed that it is safe to use. The other facilities and services of the swimming pool are in normal use. In addition to the wooden sauna, the hall has two electric saunas, a steam sauna, an infrared sauna and a sauna on request. The swimming pool was opened to the public at the beginning of February. Finland's oldest public swimming pool underwent a major renovation that lasted more than two years, during which, among other things, the technology was renewed and the pool structures were repaired.

There have been worrying changes in the reading and writing skills of upper secondary school students, says Irene Bonsdorff, who has worked as a mother tongue and literature teacher in upper secondary schools for 30 years. The Milan-Cortina Games will see a new Olympic sport on Monday, the alpine skiing team event. Previously, this competition format was known as the alpine combined, where the same athlete has run both the downhill and the slalom. Now there are different men in both. The change suits the Finnish team perfectly, whose sharpest teeth in alpine skiing are downhill cannon Elian Lehto and slalom sensation Eduard Hallberg. Although Lehto's Olympic downhill and 20th place on Saturday were disappointing, he has finished in the top ten twice this season in the World Cup. Hallberg, on the other hand, has already climbed to the podium twice. Is even an Olympic medal a realistic goal for the team event? "That's the goal. That's it," Hallberg underlines. "But Elian will only go for his own good run and then I'll follow suit. Then we'll see," the Sipoolian continues. The team downhill starts on Monday at 11:30, the slalom at 15:00. Elias Lehto placed 20th in Saturday's Olympic downhill. Photo: Harald Steiner / MVPhotos Each country can enter a maximum of four teams in the team competition. Finland is not one of the medal favourites in the competition, but talking about it as such is not entirely a stretch. This has been shown by previous results this season. On a really "bad day", the Finnish men have proven that they have the capacity to even make it to the top of the team competition. "Last year we were able to try it out a bit at the World Championships. It's a really nice concept, when you get to race with a good friend. And it's nice that you can experience this kind of team competition in alpine skiing too," says Hallberg. The duo, who train together in the summer, finished last winter's World Championships with Hallberg's elimination in the slalom section. Eduard Hallberg will arrive at the Olympics in 8th place in the slalom cup. Photo: Lisi Niesner / Before this season, Hallberg was not a hot name when it came to Finnish Olympic winners. Now the situation is completely different. Hallberg has rushed to the forefront of the slalom world this season and has repeatedly shown his incredible potential. The men's slalom will be contested on the Bormio Olympic slope in a week's time, on Monday, February 16. "At least at the moment I don't feel a lot of pressure. It's nice to go to the games when you've done a good job, the skis are running and there's a good chance of getting a good result," Hallberg says casually. "Anyone from the hot group can take home a medal in slalom." The nine slalom races of the World Cup season have seen no fewer than seven different winners and 11 different podium finishers. Finland has never won an Olympic medal in men's alpine skiing. On the women's side, Tanja Poutiainen brought home the giant slalom silver medal from Turin in 2006. At the same games, Kalle Palander's slalom silver medal was also a hair's breadth away. At that time, Palander's time would have been enough for a medal, but his second-round run was bitterly rejected because his ski had bitten off one of the poles on the wrong side. Just over a month ago, Hallberg came in second in the Madonna Di Campiglio slalom. The Finnish team was elated. Photo: Luciano Maria Bisi / ZUMA Hallberg prepared for the Olympics in Reiteralm, Austria, together with Jesper Pohjolainen, the other male slalom skier on the Finnish Olympic team. The duo arrived at the Bormio Olympic Village on the opening day, Friday. For downhill skier Lehdo, Bormio is a familiar place from the annual World Cup race, but this location is not part of the annual slalom calendar. "I've never been on this slope before. Before the Olympics, I already received videos and pictures of the slope," Hallberg says. In the Olympic alpine skiing, the men compete in Bormio, the women in Cortina d'Ampezzo. Photo: /Angelika Warmuth Bormio's slalom slope is described as quite easy for top skiers. The slope is quite gentle compared to many World Cup courses. "It's quite 'inviting' at the beginning. There's a bit of shape, but the end is really gentle. It's not a demanding and steep slope, but it's also difficult to be fast on gentle slopes. In that respect, it's always challenging to say what's easy and what's difficult." But does this version suit the strengths of Finland's number one hope Hallberg? "It suits quite well. I've been able to get the speed from steep to flat sections quite well. If you put a good tactic into it and execute it, you can be quite good." Hallberg is scheduled to compete in three different sports at the Olympics. Between this Monday's team race and the slalom next Monday, she will also compete in Saturday's giant slalom. The article is the opinion of a Helsingin Sanomat reader. Finland talks about internationalization, but one of the world's most stable and prosperous markets is still almost ignored by us: Australia. We have worked in Sydney for years with Finnish companies and stakeholders and have seen up close how Finnish expertise is received here, and on the other hand, how often this market is not utilized due to outdated images. Finnish companies often look for growth in the United States, Central Europe or Asia. Fewer people look systematically at Australia, even though for many companies this market would be a natural and realistic next step. Australia is still easily perceived as distant or small. In reality, it is one of the largest economies in the world, with a GDP that has almost tripled since the late 1990s. Remote meetings in Europe are commonplace, purchasing power is high, investments are strong and the operating environment is predictable. Finnair's new route connection to Melbourne lowers the threshold even further and makes the market more concretely closer to Finnish companies. Australia's importance is also emphasized due to its geographical position. The country acts as a natural bridgehead to Asia, a region whose economic importance is growing rapidly. At the same time, Australia offers a more stable operating environment than many Asian markets: the rule of law, clear rules of the game and a predictable business culture. The competitive situation is also an often underestimated factor. Although Australia is a developed market, competition in many industries is more moderate than in the United States or major European markets. There is room for high-quality and specialized expertise, and new players are met with interest rather than suspicion. Finnish companies have a lot to offer here. Reliability, long-termism and a straightforward approach fit well with the Australian business culture. The perceptions of Finland and Finnish expertise are strong, and the value base between the countries is similar: an open economy, a rules-based system and a desire to build long-term partnerships. Interest in the Australian market has been growing significantly, but fully exploiting the potential requires new openings from Finland. In addition to traditional industrial expertise, Australia is looking for partners in high-tech sectors. In particular, the quantum technology and defense ecosystems offer significant growth opportunities for Finnish companies. We want to encourage Finnish companies to look at Australia from a new perspective: not as a distant side market, but as a stable, prosperous and strategically important partner. When they boldly turn their gaze south, many Finnish companies will find the growth they have been looking for elsewhere. Olli Mustonen Honorary Consul Sydney, Australia Senior Advisor, Sydney Trade Office Embassy of Finland in Australia The editorial team of HS selects and publishes opinion pieces. The article is the opinion of a Helsingin Sanomat reader. The aim of the social welfare reform has been to secure services and curb the growth of costs. However, the discussion has become bogged down in cuts, although the real solution lies in improving efficiency and management. Social and healthcare expenditure makes up a large part of Finland's public expenditure. The ageing population, labour shortages and the growing need for services explain part of the increase in costs, but not everything can be blamed on demographics. Structural inefficiencies, complex information systems and decentralised management increase costs without a corresponding improvement in service quality. In the business world, the profitability and efficiency of operations are monitored systematically. A similar comparison is still lacking in the social welfare sector. Costs should be examined using uniform measures, such as the cost per customer visit or working hour. Without comparable information, decision-making is easily based on assumptions, not facts. It would be particularly important to examine the total costs of welfare areas nationwide and openly. The comparison should cover not only nursing work but also support functions: real estate, maintenance, administration and information systems. Only the overall picture will tell where money is really being spent and where productivity can be improved. At the same time, we must dare to reform the division of labor. The expertise of doctors and nurses is still too often used for administrative tasks that could be transferred to other professionals or automated. This is not a personnel issue, but a rational use of resources. Instead of pitting the public and private sectors against each other, an open comparison is needed. Private service providers are showing that processes can be managed cost-effectively without compromising quality. This does not mean privatization, but learning. Efficiency and humanity are not opposites of each other. Sustainable social services are created by knowledge-based management, open comparison and the courage to examine operations as a whole – before the next list of cuts is written.
