Greece and Malta are concerned about the European Union's (EU) proposal to completely ban Russian oil transportation services, Bloomberg reports, citing sources. According to sources, the countries fear the restrictions could impact the European shipping industry and energy prices. Photo: Artem Dergunov, Kommersant Photo: Artem Dergunov, Kommersant The two countries raised this issue at yesterday's meeting of EU ambassadors, where the draft of the 20th sanctions package against Russia was presented. Greece and Malta also asked for clarification on proposals to impose sanctions on foreign ports for transshipping Russian oil and to tighten controls on ship sales, the sources claim. The list of tankers subject to EU sanctions will be expanded by 43 vessels, reaching 640 vessels. If all EU countries approve the ban on Russian oil transportation services, the G7 may be forced to find alternative tankers for 30-40% of crude shipments from Russia. Greek shippers will be the first to lose a significant portion of their revenues. For more details, see Kommersant’s article “Brussels is targeting tankers.”

On February 10, Roskomnadzor plans to begin partially restricting the Telegram messenger. Kommersant reports on what the watchdog has previously blocked and how. Photo: Anatoly Zhdanov, Kommersant Photo: Anatoly Zhdanov, Kommersant On November 17, 2016, Roskomnadzor (RKN) began blocking the social network LinkedIn. This marked the first time a major international resource had suspended operations in the country for violating the law "On Personal Data," which requires storing the personal data of Russian citizens within the Russian Federation. On April 16, 2018, the Tagansky District Court of Moscow upheld RKN's claim to block Telegram. The reason was the messenger's refusal to provide encryption keys to the FSB (a year earlier, the FSB had reported that Telegram was being used to plot a terrorist attack on the St. Petersburg metro). In 2020, Roskomnadzor (RKN) lifted the block, praising the "expressed readiness of the Telegram founder to counter terrorism and extremism." On March 10, 2021, Roskomnadzor first used a technical feature to slow down traffic, reducing the speed of Twitter (now X). A year later, Roskomnadzor first slowed down and then blocked the social network, claiming that it was disseminating "inaccurate socially significant information" about the SVO. Since March 4, 2022, Roskomnadzor has been blocking access to Facebook (owned by Meta, which is recognized as extremist in Russia and banned) due to "discrimination against Russian media and information resources." Since March 14, it has been blocking Instagram (owned by Meta, which is recognized as extremist in Russia and banned), which "disseminates messages encouraging and provoking violent acts against Russians." That same month, Meta Platforms Inc., the owner of Facebook and Instagram, was banned. was recognized as extremist and banned in the Russian Federation. In 2023, Roskomnadzor began blocking websites for LGBT content (the "international LGBT movement" is recognized as extremist and banned in the Russian Federation). Specifically, on August 21, access to Hornet, an LGBT dating app (the "international LGBT movement" is recognized as extremist and banned in the Russian Federation), was restricted. On August 9, 2024, Roskomnadzor restricted access to the Signal messenger. The reason was a violation of requirements "the fulfillment of which is necessary to prevent the use of the messenger for terrorist and extremist purposes." Since October 8, 2024, Discord, a popular gaming platform, has been blocked. Roskomnadzor justified its decision by citing the need to prevent the use of the messenger "for terrorist and extremist purposes, the recruitment of citizens for such purposes, and the sale of drugs." Viber was blocked for similar reasons in December of the same year. On August 13, 2025, Roskomnadzor (the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology, and Mass Media) announced restrictions on calls to Telegram and WhatsApp, explaining that these messaging apps had become "the primary voice services used for deception and extortion, and for involving Russian citizens in subversive and terrorist activities." In December, Roskomnadzor slowed down WhatsApp and threatened to completely block the messenger if it continued to fail to comply with Russian law. Follow us on:

Major retailers of household appliances and electronics are asking the Supreme Court to clarify the application of consumer protection laws, arguing that due to the lack of uniformity in practice, fraudsters are deliberately damaging equipment and then seeking compensation through the courts. There are currently "thousands" of such lawsuits, totaling billions of rubles. Lawyers believe the problem is partly due to fraudsters choosing "favorable" jurisdictions in certain regions. Illustration: Viktor Chumachev, Kommersant. Illustration: Viktor Chumachev, Kommersant. Kommersant has reviewed the appeal from M.Video, Restore, MegaFon, and MTS, sent on December 25 of last year to Supreme Court Chairman Igor Krasnov, requesting clarification from the Supreme Court Plenum on the application of the Consumer Protection Law. Retailers write that the lack of uniformity in judicial practice leads to significant abuses in certain regions: the Samara and Saratov regions, and the republics of Bashkortostan and Tatarstan, as well as to an increase in cases of individuals intentionally damaging appliances to obtain compensation. In these cases, the courts effectively side with the fraudsters. Retailers need the Supreme Court's clarifications to prevent abuses and "bad-faith behavior by the parties." Kommersant sent a request to the Supreme Court's press service. The retailers' letter is not listed in the extra-procedural appeals section of the Supreme Court's website. The annual damages caused by fraudulent groups amount to several billion rubles per year for the household appliance and electronics market as a whole, explains a Kommersant source in the market. Moreover, according to the source, there are "thousands" of lawsuits nationwide, and the Volga region, particularly the Samara region, accounts for up to 80% of all complaints in Russia regarding broken appliances. "The problem of so-called consumer extremism has been persistent for several years. Current law enforcement creates loopholes for fraudsters and creates opportunities for abuse," MTS's press service said. M.Video and Restore declined to comment. "The problem of consumer abuse of rights is indeed relevant for businesses. The purpose of this appeal is to bring uniformity to judicial practice," MegaFon's press service told Kommersant. "Consumer extremism" in Russia has been around for over 25 years (see Kommersant's March 15, 2000 report). Retailers regularly appeal to law enforcement agencies and relevant ministries to address the problem, but it has not yet been fully resolved (see Kommersant's May 22, 2013 report). Unscrupulous individuals regularly attempt to obtain compensation from retailers (see Kommersant, April 19, 2024), car dealers (see Kommersant, November 18, 2015), or developers (see Kommersant, November 23, 2023). The problem described by retailers is characteristic only of a small number of regions where organized groups, including expert organizations, operate, whose activities bear all the hallmarks of criminality, says Oleg Pavlov, head of the Public Consumer Initiative. "This problem cannot be resolved by clarifying civil law. We must use existing criminal procedural tools to deal with criminals without creating obstacles for ordinary consumers," he asserts. Lawyers interviewed by Kommersant acknowledge the problem, namely the lack of uniform judicial practice on a number of issues regarding the application of the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights (ZoZPP). The Consumer Protection Law was originally created as a tool to protect the "weaker" party (the consumer) against the "stronger" party (the company), "but sometimes it can become a tool for abuse of rights and unfair enrichment," notes Vasily Khokhlov, head of the consumer dispute resolution group at the law firm Kosenkov & Suvorov. Aleksey Stankevich, a partner at the law firm Orchards, believes the root cause of the problem lies in the imperfections of the law's mechanism, which allows for a wide range of judicial discretion. "Courts' views on similar situations can differ dramatically across regions. This creates opportunities for both unscrupulous consumers and unscrupulous lawyers who choose to file lawsuits in regions where the courts' approach is most favorable," explains Mr. Khokhlov. He notes that in some regions, an "entire industry" and "business model" has developed where consumer representatives file lawsuits with inflated demands. Alexey Stankevich adds that the number of lawsuits against one retailer in the Samara region is comparable to the number against the same organization in all other regions of the Russian Federation, which appears to be a classic sign of forum shopping (choosing a "favorable" jurisdiction). However, Mr. Stankevich notes that all the arguments and examples presented in the petition favor the seller, while the buyer's position is presented as unfair. He also cites no cases where the courts unreasonably rejected a bona fide consumer's claim: "This creates a one-sided, biased picture, which, of course, must be taken into account when evaluating the arguments." The lawyer clarifies that, for example, the issue of the seller's right to send the goods for inspection to any region, and the consumer's obligation to deliver them there, also requires clarification: "Forcing the consumer to transport the goods at their own expense." Furthermore, Mr. Stankevich points out, amendments to the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights came into force on February 1. These amendments introduce a penalty limit (no more than 100% of the product's price), grounds for exempting the seller from penalties if the consumer refuses to deliver the goods, and a ban on the assignment of the right to demand a penalty before a court decision takes effect. These amendments partially address the issues raised in the retailers' appeal. Secondly, the Supreme Court likely plans to provide clarification on the new regulations through a plenary resolution. The letter may serve to reiterate the current issues, the lawyer concludes. Alexey Zhabin, Anna Zanina Follow the authors:

The great "nuclear triangle" of the USA, Russia, and China is not the only one. There are also China, India, and Pakistan in Asia, and Russia, England, and France in Europe. This strategic conundrum seems to have no solution. Photo: Gleb Shchelkunov, Kommersant The great "nuclear triangle" of the USA, Russia, and China is not the only one. There are also China, India, and Pakistan in Asia, and Russia, England, and France in Europe. This strategic conundrum seems to have no solution. Photo: Gleb Shchelkunov, Kommersant February 5, 2026, the expiration date of the Russian-American Strategic Arms Treaty (START), is only a symbolic end to the 50-year era of arms control. In fact, the era of Russian-American negotiations and agreements in this area ended long ago. The main reasons are obvious and objective. Tectonic shifts have occurred in global geopolitics; Nuclear multipolarity has become a fact; modern technologies have transformed a number of non-nuclear weapons into strategic ones; new spheres of conflict have emerged—cyberspace, outer space, and biotechnology; quantitative limitations have become insufficient, and so on. The most important subjective reason was the reluctance of the American leadership to commit to the commitments made during the confrontation with the USSR. Arms control is often equated with strategic stability. This is not entirely accurate. Indeed, a system of verifiable limitations on nuclear warheads and their delivery systems increases the predictability of military arsenal development and thereby promotes the stability of relations between nuclear powers, but it does not guarantee peace among them. In the spring of 2022, when the US leadership publicly announced the goal of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia in the proxy war in Ukraine, the New START Treaty was still in effect, and Washington proposed consultations with Moscow on strategic stability. In other words, the Americans, seeking to defeat the nuclear superpower on the battlefield, were simultaneously attempting to use arms control to protect themselves from the possible use of nuclear weapons by Russia. Now that the Russian-American arms control system is a thing of the past, many fear a new nuclear arms race and even nuclear war. The hand of the famous Doomsday Clock has moved ever closer to midnight. It should be kept in mind, however, that arms control, from its first day to its last, limited the nuclear potential of only two countries—the USSR/Russia and the United States. The nuclear arsenals of the other "official" nuclear powers—Britain, France, and China—have never been limited. The same applies to the nuclear weapons of the "unofficial" nuclear powers—Israel, India, Pakistan, and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Meanwhile, the US-China standoff is deepening and escalating; relations between India and Pakistan were tested again by military conflict last year; Israel, along with the US, are striving to eliminate Iran's nuclear and missile programs; and the governments of Britain and France are recklessly provoking a direct military confrontation with Russia. Strategic stability in the 21st century does not mean approximate strategic parity and the existence of arms control treaties, but the absence of incentives for military conflicts between major powers, primarily nuclear ones. It will not be possible to scale up the experience of Russian-American agreements in a world with nine nuclear powers. In recent years, American strategists have been struggling with the “three-body” problem: how to reconcile limitations on the arsenals of the United States, Russia, and China (which is expected to reach the level of the two leading powers in a few years). But the large “nuclear triangle” is not the only one: there is also China-India-Pakistan in Asia and Russia-England-France in Europe. This strategic conundrum seems to have no solution. This does not mean that strategic stability is impossible. To maintain it, bilateral and multilateral strategic dialogues are necessary, as well as information exchanges; predictability measures, which are loosely called confidence-building measures, are needed; constantly open channels of communication are essential; Mechanisms are needed to prevent unintended collisions, and so on. Agreements on specific issues and unilateral parallel commitments may exist. However, this is not the main point. Stability today, as it was half a century ago, is based primarily on the reliability of nuclear deterrence—that is, on the availability of a sufficient arsenal of means and the willingness to use it. Dmitry Trenin, Director of the Institute of World Military Economy and Strategy at the National Research University Higher School of Economics, and Leading Researcher at the IMEMO RAS. Expectations of rapid economic impact from investments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure may be overstated, according to a study by researchers at the Higher School of Economics (HSE). They estimate that the global AI solutions market is developing according to a catch-up model—software revenues do not yet compensate for the enormous investments in the necessary hardware. The study's authors (albeit rather cautiously) therefore note the risk of an AI "bubble." HSE Academic Supervisor Yaroslav Kuzminov Photo: Irina Buzhor, Kommersant HSE Academic Supervisor Yaroslav Kuzminov and Associate Professor Ekaterina Kruchinskaya of the University's Faculty of Social Sciences attempted to assess the relative effectiveness of investments in generative AI in their study. The revenues of two groups of market participants were analyzed: manufacturers (AMD, Intel, Nvidia, and others) of AI hardware (chips, servers, semiconductors, and data center infrastructure) and companies developing and monetizing AI solutions (Sony, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Amazon, Apple, and others). The analysis covered the period 2016–2024. According to the authors' calculations, the relative annual return on investment in AI components was 0.9 in 2021, 0.88 in 2022, 1 in 2023, and 0.89 in 2024. To clarify, the closer the value is to one, the more effective the conversion of investments in components into commercial benefits from AI models. The authors' main hypothesis is that the software market is playing catch-up and does not yet recoup companies' investments in AI components. They also note that "effective monetization of these investments is critical to supporting the development of the field and preventing speculative bubbles." The study also notes the nonlinear nature of the generative AI market's development. While indicators were increasing until 2021 due to the development and commercialization of such models, they declined to a local minimum in 2022. In 2023, there was an intense but short-lived surge in market activity, and in 2024, investment efficiency fell to 2022 levels. "Increased demand for chips and computing power is driven by the development of large language models, but their commercial returns remain limited and do not offset the cost of hard technologies and further investment in them," notes Ekaterina Kruchinskaya. The model used for the analysis raises the question of the risk of a "bubble" forming in the AI market. According to Yaroslav Kuzminov, it can be cautiously concluded that such a risk exists. "AI is truly changing not only the economy and business models of companies, but also social life... At the same time, its influence is being realized and spreading, but not as quickly as it seems, and not as productively as we would like," he says. Another related study—by Stanford Business School professor Charles Jones, "Artificial Intelligence and Our Economic Future" (published in the Proceedings of the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)—suggests that general-purpose technologies, whose proliferation is global and contributes to productivity growth everywhere, will require several decades to fully realize their potential. In this work, the author identifies two scenarios for the impact of AI on the global economy. The first assumes a rapid acceleration of economic growth, the second - a limited impact of AI. To justify the possibility of the second scenario, Charles Jones cites the fact that many previous major innovations (for example, electricity, the internet) are also considered important general-purpose technologies, but have not significantly impacted long-term growth rates of real GDP per capita in the United States. It is noted that automation has been ongoing for over 200 years, while economic growth in the country remains stable at 2% per year. However, the author believes that AI's impact on the macroeconomy of countries will in any case be more widespread and profound than that of electricity and the internet. The World Defense Show 2026 international arms exhibition opened in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, on February 8. This year, the Russian exhibit, whose highlights included unmanned aerial vehicles and long-range systems, focused on showcasing developments based on recent combat experience and the needs of potential customers. Experts believe the exhibits are aimed at securing real export contracts, particularly in the highly promising Saudi Arabian market. One of the Russian highlights of the Riyadh exhibition was the new Sarma multiple launch rocket system. Photo: Rostec State Corporation Press Service. The World Defense Show will be held every two years starting in 2022. Organizers estimate that approximately 925 exhibitors from nearly 80 countries are participating in this year's exhibition, with the total number of visitors exceeding 130,000. In 2024, the event was attended by over 106,000 specialists, and the volume of agreements concluded exceeded 26 billion Saudi riyals (approximately $6.9 billion). Compared to previous exhibitions, this year's edition was more practical and focused on practical interactions with buyers. Organizers strengthened the sections dedicated to unmanned systems, high-precision weapons, and maritime topics, allowing participants to structure their displays around specific application scenarios rather than individual models. Russia has been present at the Saudi exhibition since its inception, presenting products through the state corporation Rosoboronexport (part of Rostec). As Rosoboronexport told Kommersant, this year the corporation organized a unified Russian exhibit with the participation of major defense holdings, including the Kalashnikov Concern and ZALA. The emphasis is on models that have already been field-tested. The main world premiere was the display of the Sarma 300mm multiple launch rocket system with a firing range of up to 120 km. According to Rosoboronexport, the system features high mobility, reduced deployment time, and the ability to use next-generation guided munitions. The Sarma is being demonstrated as part of a reconnaissance and strike system, along with the Supercam S350 unmanned aerial vehicle and the Planshet-A fire control system. Another notable new product was the BTR-22 armored personnel carrier. The vehicle boasts enhanced protection and can be equipped with a Ballista remote-controlled module with a 30mm cannon and anti-tank missiles. Rosoboronexport notes that this configuration increases the platform's versatility for foreign customers. In the unmanned and loitering munitions segment, Russian companies are focusing on expanding their export portfolio. For the first time abroad, the RUS-PE containerized munition with a homing head and artificial intelligence elements is being presented in its full form. Also on display is the KUB-2E combined with the Skat-350M UAV and the Lancet-E system, which includes a reconnaissance aircraft and two munitions. Furthermore, the Russian Federation's stand features the modernized RPG-29M grenade launcher, AK-15 and AK-19 assault rifles and their shortened versions, the RPL-20 light machine gun, and the GP-46 underbarrel grenade launcher. Foreign manufacturers are also well represented at the exhibition. Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and Northrop Grumman have confirmed their participation. India and China are also participating through major national defense corporations and industry consortiums, which have formed large national pavilions. Rosoboronexport hopes that the current exhibition will not only showcase new products but also intensify negotiations with partners from the Middle East, Asia, and Africa. The company cites the proven characteristics and adaptability to customer requirements as the main advantages of Russian products. The developments presented in Riyadh are primarily aimed at securing export contracts, rather than boosting image, according to Ruslan Pukhov, Director of the Center for Analysis of Strategies and Technologies. This primarily concerns Saudi Arabia, which the expert calls the most promising market in the region, given its large-scale modernization programs and focus on localizing defense production, which is now largely the focus of the entire exhibition. Riyadh could be interested in both air defense systems that complement existing systems, as well as unmanned and robotic solutions based on Russian combat experience, Pukhov explains. According to him, the development of "new generation warfare" places a premium on integrated reconnaissance, strike, and autonomous systems. The development of industrial cooperation is also of particular importance, the expert adds. He estimates that the willingness of Russian manufacturers to work through partial localization and joint production remains an important argument for the Saudi side. This approach has already been used in a number of export projects and could increase the chances of gaining a foothold in the market in a competitive environment with Western and Asian suppliers, Ruslan Pukhov concludes. The need for identification documents arose the moment humanity transitioned from primitive society to civilization. Ancient Egypt already had a strict passport regime, and in Rus', traveler's and passerby's documents had long been in use. Over time, the format changed and became more complex: simple notes gave way to documents with photographs, forms with various anti-counterfeiting features, and, in the 21st century, to chips storing biometric data. Photo: Courtesy of GOZNAK JSC Photo: Courtesy of GOZNAK JSC The essence, however, always remains the same: states invent increasingly reliable methods of identifying individuals, while criminals seek ever more sophisticated ways to circumvent them. Thanks to the development of modern digital technologies, biometrics have become routinely used in many areas of activity, providing solutions for such tasks as authentication, identification, identity verification, payment, and the search for criminals and missing persons—to name just a few of the wide range of applications biometric methods are designed to address. Biometric technologies are used in public administration and information security, immigration control, tourism, and many other industries. As a pioneer in the development of biometric products, Goznak has long since expanded beyond its original competencies, namely, the production of banknotes, documents, and other physical products. Today, it is a technology company with its own data centers and ready-made commercial IT solutions, particularly in the field of biometrics. While voice recognition still poses challenges, verification using other parameters—facial images, fingerprints, and irises—is now not only reliable but also secure from attempts to circumvent them. For example, using depth cameras allows us to determine that the person being identified is a living person, not a photograph or recorded video. A thermal scanner can distinguish a real face from a mask, as their thermal signatures are completely different. Active vitality detection methods are effective: even if a person is randomly asked to smile, blink, or tilt their head, attackers with a prepared image will be unable to replicate this algorithm. Photo: Courtesy of GOZNAK. Photo: Courtesy of GOZNAK. Finally, another pressing problem—neural network deepfakes—is being combated by the same technologies that gave rise to them. These are convolutional neural networks, which can distinguish between real and fake graphics, meaning artificial intelligence can identify similar individuals better than humans. All these methods are actively used in Goznak solutions, alongside biometric data protection technologies that meet the highest standards of the Russian FSB and the Federal Service for Technical and Export Control. These include encryption methods that prevent hacking, as well as their storage in the Unified Biometric System (UBS), which, by law, can store the biometric parameters of Russian citizens. All this allowed Goznak to become the first fully state-owned company to receive accreditation from the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications, and Mass Media of the Russian Federation in the field of biometric personal data authentication—in other words, the right to process and use biometrics. While this right was previously held primarily by representatives of the banking sector, Goznak's inclusion on the Ministry of Digital Development's list allows it to address the needs of many organizations: how to implement biometric technologies without undergoing accreditation themselves. The potential for application is vast. Essentially, biometrics can replace any physical medium that allows for human identification. For example, access control systems can eliminate the need for cards—turnstiles will literally recognize employees by face and screen out those who are not permitted to enter the facility. Autogates at airports and train stations, storage lockers, public transport fare collection systems, and immigration checkpoints can be similarly organized, all in a fully automated fashion: first, an initial biometric scan is performed, followed by a control scan at the next counter, after which the data is stored in a common database. This eliminates the need for human intervention and, therefore, eliminates the risk of human error. Moreover, Goznak's biometric capabilities are not limited to humans: a separate division, Goznak.Pet, focuses on animal recognition. Whiskers, paws, and tail are still not considered identification documents, but facial recognition accuracy is 98%. This means that a single image can be used to create veterinary passports for pets, search for missing animals, and keep track of strays—all without microchips or other interventions. Photo: Courtesy of GOZNAK JSC. Photo: Courtesy of GOZNAK JSC. The technology is currently in pilot status, so Goznak offers flexible trial periods—one or more months of free testing—to help customers decide whether to move it into commercial use. Overall, the company is focused on working with large clients, from the private corporate sector to regional and federal government clients. It's important to note that all hardware and software products used are the proprietary development of Goznak's Biometric Solutions Center, meaning they are entirely Russian-made and hosted within the Russian Federation, ensuring 100% technological sovereignty. Combined with accreditation from the Ministry of Digital Development, this allows customers to be completely confident in the system's security and its independence from external factors. Goznak's transformation into a provider of digital biometric solutions is not as unexpected as it might seem at first glance. Essentially, the company continues to focus on what it has developed impressive expertise in over the past 207 years—ensuring maximum authentication protection. First money, then documents, and now human identity itself. Thus, history may soon come full circle: if all this time we've had to carry some object proving our identity, modern biometric systems recognize it at a glance. Moreover, unlike humans, they cannot be deceived, bribed, or swayed, and identification accuracy is near absolute. From a technical standpoint, there are no longer any fundamental obstacles to completely abandoning physical identification documents—at least within the borders of a single country. This doesn't mean that digital passports will quickly and completely replace paper ones—just as cash didn't disappear from circulation with the advent of bank cards. But human life will definitely become simpler and more convenient. JSC "GOZNAK" Advertising

By the end of 2025, coal transshipment rates had fallen by more than 40%, to $10 per ton, and the current year has yet to revive the market, despite increased exports. Stevedores are seeking to maintain cargo volumes at ports through forced price reductions. Photo: Vasily Shitov, Kommersant Photo: Vasily Shitov, Kommersant The average weighted coal transshipment rate at Russian ports fell from $17.7 to $10 per ton during 2025, according to calculations by the Price Index Center (PIC). In December, an increase in coal export prices slightly supported transshipment costs, analysts note. However, they note that even the increase in exports at the end of the year was unable to reverse the situation. By the end of 2025, coal transshipment at Russian ports increased by 8% year-on-year, to 201 million tonnes. Roman Sokolov, Director of the Centralized Cost Center (CCC), says that January coal transshipment rates are maintaining December levels, with a slight negative adjustment of 1-2% month-on-month. In the Far East, the CCC estimates rates at an average of $9.7 per ton, in the Baltic region $8.5 per ton, and in the south $13.2 per ton. According to Mr. Sokolov, the lack of visible short-term drivers for export profitability growth and the continued surplus of port capacity are putting pressure on tariffs and restraining growth. According to NEFT Research, coal transshipment rates at Far Eastern ports are at $9-11 per ton, in Taman $12-15 per ton, and in Ust-Luga $8 per ton. Year-on-year, tariffs have decreased by 40-50%, 20-30%, and 41%, respectively, according to Alexander Kotov, consulting partner at NEFT Research. According to Mr. Kotov, stevedores are striving to retain customers and maintain shipping volumes. Results for the beginning of 2026 are mixed. The Osterra coal terminal (formerly Daltransugol), for example, increased transhipment by 25% in January, to 1.186 million tons. The "Small Port" in Nakhodka handled 310,600 tons, down 6.4% from last year, according to Mr. Kotov. The CCI report notes that some shipping companies are leaving the Azov-Black Sea basin (ABB), which may be due to a decrease in vessel turnover due to increased transit times under the Crimean Bridge. According to tanker tracking systems, of the 37 bulk carriers transporting coal from the ABB in the fall of 2025, almost two-thirds had transferred to other Russian or foreign ports by the beginning of 2026. This, the Central Information Center notes, could lead to a reduction in transshipment volumes in the ACB and prompt a tariff adjustment. Rates for the provision of railcars for coal transportation by the end of 2025 also showed a localized increase. However, according to a Kommersant source in the market, tariffs have risen from "very unprofitable" to simply "unprofitable." A significant portion of the rolling stock has been laid up, he explains, which led to a slight increase in rates. The positive trend that may have appeared in December could be interpreted more as the first signs of stabilization amid a protracted decline than as a definitive reversal of the trend, says another Kommersant source among operators. According to him, fundamental constraints remain. These include the unfavorable pricing environment, in which export shipments remain low-margin, as well as the high share of logistics and tariffs in the cost of coal. "According to industry estimates, the transport component of the export price reaches 60-70%," a Kommersant source says. A restoration of freight rates is possible, concludes one of Kommersant's sources in the operating market, but its pace and sustainability will depend on a combination of factors: global price levels and demand, the recovery of industrial activity in Russia's metallurgical sector, and tariffs, which were already indexed in December and are scheduled to change again in March. The determining factor will be balancing the gondola car fleet on the Russian Railways network by retiring excess freight from the transportation process, adds Kommersant's source. Freight traffic along the Northern Sea Route decreased by 2.3% in 2025 due to declines in bulk cargo, LNG, and oil, according to Gekon. Growth was seen in the transportation of petroleum products, ore concentrate, gas condensate, and containerized cargo by weight. Analysts do not foresee any compelling growth potential for freight traffic along the route in 2026. Photo: Dmitry Lebedev, Kommersant Photo: Dmitry Lebedev, Kommersant. Freight traffic along the Northern Sea Route (NSR) decreased by 0.87 million tons, or 2.3% year-on-year, to 37.02 million tons in 2025, according to an analysis of port cargo turnover and freight traffic along the Arctic segment of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor (TTC) in 2025 by Mikhail Grigoriev, head of the Gekon consulting center. The decline is primarily due to a drop in bulk cargo, LNG, and oil shipments. Export cargo accounted for the bulk of NSR cargo traffic (60%, or 22.2 million tonnes), while Arctic oil and gas projects accounted for the bulk of cargo traffic by type and origin. Hydrocarbons—LNG (58%), oil (21%), and condensate (4%)—account for up to 83% of NSR cargo traffic. The growth in shipments is driven by cargo from NOVATEK's Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG 2 (on the SND List, with 60% held by NOVATEK), and Gazprom Neft's Novoportovskoye field, all shipped from the port of Sabetta. The decline in LNG shipments (by 0.59 million tonnes, or 2.7%), despite increased shipments from the Arctic LNG 2 project, is explained by scheduled maintenance at Yamal LNG. The gradual decline in oil shipments from the Novoportovskoye field is due to the natural depletion of the field. Development of the Arctic zone depends on Rosneft's Vostok Oil project and the development of gas fields in Yamal and Gydan by NOVATEK and Gazprom, which are also focused on the external market, notes Mikhail Grigoriev. The volume of petroleum product shipments along the NSR increased by 43%, to 1.27 million tons, while gas condensate shipments increased by 17%, to 1.55 million tons. General cargo shipments, which include Norilsk Nickel products, remained virtually flat with last year's level, down 2.2%, to 3.91 million tons. At the end of 2024, Norilsk Nickel announced an increase in its own cargo shipments from 1.6 million to 3 million tons per year by 2028–2030. Bulk cargo shipments decreased by more than 2.5 times, to 0.41 million tons. In particular, coal shipments decreased by 30.9%, to 413,000 tons. The main coal flows go through Murmansk, with a small amount going through Anadyr. According to Mortsentr-TEK statistics, coal turnover at the port of Murmansk in 2025 decreased by 29.1%, to 8.7 million tons. The bulk of this volume was accounted for by the Murmansk Commercial Sea Port (MCSP), where transshipment decreased by 37.8%, to 7.6 million tons, and the Lavna Commercial Sea Port, which handled 1 million tons (no statistics for comparison). The port of Anadyr increased coal shipments by 20%, to 1.34 million tons. Ore concentrate cargo traffic increased by 13.5 times, to 365,000 tons. As Vladislav Yakovchuk, Commercial Director of the Murmansk Commercial Seaport, explained to Kommersant, in 2025, the port shipped two Capesize vessels carrying iron ore concentrate mined in the Murmansk Region to China via the NSR. The total volume was 330,000 tons. "We hope for higher figures in 2026, but it's too early to discuss specific plans," Mr. Yakovchuk noted. He added that the Murmansk Commercial Seaport is currently focusing on Capesize vessels—the most optimal for the NSR: they provide maximum load capacity (up to 180,000 tons), minimize logistics costs, and accelerate delivery to Asia by 10-14 days compared to the Suez Canal. According to Vladislav Yakovchuk, the Murmansk Commercial Seaport established a specialized container terminal in 2025, for which the port area is being equipped. Mikhail Grigoryev notes that during the 2025 summer-fall navigation season (August 1 – October 20), 17 containerized cargo voyages were made, transporting 321,000 tons. Compared to 2024, the volume of shipments increased by 135,000 tons, although the number of voyages remained the same. Moreover, Mr. Grigoryev notes that while foreign trade flows were virtually symmetrical in 2024 (83,000 tons exported and 94,000 tons imported), in 2025, 216,000 tons were exported, 2.5 times more than imported (85,000 tons). Rosatom's Special Representative for the Arctic, Vladimir Panov, spoke at the Eastern Economic Forum 2025 about a 20% increase in containerized cargo shipments on the NSR for the first eight months of 2025. In the Arctic segment of the Third Transport Ring, total cargo turnover at sea terminals amounted to 91.7 million tons, according to a Gekona study, of which 83%, or 73 million tons, was handled by Murmansk and Sabetta. In addition to the cargo turnover of seaports in the Arctic Basin (87.1 million tons, according to Mortsentr-TEK, a 6.3% decrease from the previous year), these statistics include the ports of Mezen and Dikson, as well as oil shipments from the Prirazlomnaya offshore ice-resistant fixed platform. According to Mortsentr-TEK, the largest contributors to the decline in cargo turnover in the Arctic Basin were the port of Murmansk, due to a 4.3 million-ton decline in coal and mineral fertilizer shipments and a 0.7 million-ton decline in liquid bulk cargo, and the port of Varandey, where liquid bulk cargo transshipment fell by 0.5 million tons. The NSR ports' cargo turnover amounted to 32.5 million tons, of which 29.1 million tons, or more than 90%, was accounted for by the port of Sabetta, according to a Gekona study. Mikhail Grigoryev believes that NSR traffic volumes will not exceed 2025 levels in 2026, as there are still no sources of growth. "The export-oriented nature of the TTR's cargo flow requires cooperation in Arctic shipbuilding and the development of new sustainable sales markets, access to which the TTR opens—both in the western Atlantic and eastern Pacific directions," the expert says. MTS (MOEX: MTSS) may liquidate its ecosystem under the new Erion brand. The company claims this is a "transformation of the management structure," with strategic decisions being made at the MTS level. Kommersant's sources attribute the abandonment of the existing management structure to the need to reduce unprofitable assets, as well as the existing ineffective management structure. Thus, the combined ecosystem, which was separated from MTS's telecommunications business, lasted just over a year. The holding structure of MTS assets, implemented about a year ago, appears to be falling apart. Photo: Evgeny Razumny, Kommersant. MTS is abandoning its holding structure under the Erion brand, into which its non-telecommunications assets were merged in 2025, several sources in the telecommunications market told Kommersant, and two media sources confirmed the news. "PJSC MTS continues to transform the management structure of its subsidiary, Erion LLC, which encompasses non-telecommunications assets. The functions of the management company, Erion LLC, will be changed, and the boards of directors of the assets and their management will be strengthened, granting greater independence and authority," the company's press service told Kommersant, adding that MTS Fintech, On Media (MTS Media), MTS Adtech, Yurent, and the IT vertical MTS Web Services (MWS) will continue to operate as before and develop according to strategy. The company's press service explained that the abandonment of Erion and its reorganization "will simplify and improve the corporate governance of the subsidiaries." Individual companies in the ecosystem have been spun off into "independent businesses with established management bodies." Strategic decisions will be made at the level of PJSC MTS. At the end of 2024, MTS announced that all verticals outside of telecom (IT, fintech, media, advertising, and kicksharing service Yurent) would be spun off into separate legal entities and consolidated under the management of the MTS Ecosystem. In October 2025, the company's CEO, Rovshan Aliyev, told Kommersant in an interview that the MTS Ecosystem would be renamed Erion, and each vertical would receive its own brand. IT products and cloud solutions are part of MTS Web Services (MWS). The MTS AdTech brand was created for the advertising division. ON Media (formerly MTS Media) includes the Kion online cinema, Kion Music, Kion Stroki, ON Studio (formerly KionFilm), and ON Label. Event production has been transferred to ON Show, the production center for MTS Live, while ticketing is handled by the Ticketland and Ticketscloud platforms. The kicksharing service has been renamed Yurent. Several segments, including Smart Home, Auto, Nuum, and the B2C storefront Travel, have been liquidated. The MTS Bank brand will remain separate from Erion/MTS Ecosystems. In an interview with Kommersant, Mr. Aliyev spoke about all companies preparing for an IPO, but added that "whether they go public depends on the market." Erion employees were also sent a letter today regarding the company's restructuring, according to two sources familiar with the letter. According to them, the functions and processes linking Erion and MTS PJSC will be transferred to PJSC MTS in the near future, and employees will be offered available positions within the group. A Kommersant source claims that Rovshan Aliyev will step down. A media source also notes that some of Erion's non-telecom assets may be transferred to AFK Sistema, a co-owner of MTS. MTS's press service told Kommersant that it had not disclosed any material details about such transactions and that they "would require prior approval from PJSC MTS." "Such decisions have not been made at PJSC MTS," the press service told Kommersant. "During the initial transformation at the end of 2024, management declared that there would be more opportunities for ecosystem companies. On the one hand, this was indeed the case, but on the other, some of them proved ineffective," says a Kommersant source familiar with the company's plans. He explains that the primary objective of the initial restructuring was to reduce unprofitable assets and improve financial and reporting transparency for ecosystem businesses, while the current changes are a consequence of the existing ineffective management structure: "The experiment failed, and taking individual companies public in the current economic climate is unprofitable. When the situation is right, AFK Sistema will be able to either list them or sell them." In the first nine months of 2025, Erion's revenue increased by 25.3% to 240.9 billion rubles, accounting for 41% of the group's total revenue, according to MTS Group's financial and operating results for the period. In an interview with Kommersant, Rovshan Aliyev stated that the company is targeting a 50% share by 2026. The number of ecosystem clients reached 18 million (an increase of 1.2 million year-on-year). Reorganizing the holding structure seems a logical step given the group's high debt burden (MTS's net debt amounted to 426.3 billion rubles in the third quarter), according to Oleg Zyryanov, director of Aspring Capital. "Once the legal separation and basic processes are completed, the next logical step is to remove the unnecessary management company layer, strengthen the boards of directors and management of the verticals, and give them more autonomy. This reduces management costs, speeds up decision-making, and increases transparency within each vertical," explains Anton Vinogradov, executive director of the business consulting practice at TeDo. However, he also sees risks: if the autonomy of businesses begins to lead to a loss of synergies between them or an increase in costs due to duplication of functions in each vertical. This transformation reflects a general evolution of telecom companies' strategies, rather than a rejection of ecosystems, according to Svetlana Arkhipkina, Director of the Digital Transformation Practice at Strategy Partners: "The industry is moving toward balance: the focus on core businesses—as the primary source of stable cash flow—is maintained, while mature digital assets are gaining greater autonomy for growth and monetization." Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin announced that the project to speed up commuter train service between the capital and neighboring regions will be completed in two stages. Authorities promise to launch new trains to Vladimir, Ivanovo, Smolensk, and Yaroslavl by 2030, and to Kostroma, Tver, and Ryazan by 2035. Commuter trains are planned to run every 20–30 minutes without a specific schedule, similar to the metro or the Moscow Central Diameters (MCD). The renovation of trains, platforms, and the construction of new tracks should improve the quality of passenger rail transport. Photo: Oleg Kharseev, Kommersant. The renovation of trains, platforms, and the construction of new tracks should improve the quality of passenger rail transport. Photo: Oleg Kharseev, Kommersant. In materials for the February 9 meeting between Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin and President Vladimir Putin, the Moscow government released new details of the Central Transport Hub (CTH) development project, which the authorities announced back in 2023. The idea is to have commuter trains from cities located 200–300 km from Moscow run to the capital every 20–30 minutes, rather than every 2–3 hours, as is currently the case. The design work has already been completed, Sergei Sobyanin said: reconstruction of tracks, platforms, and other structures will begin in 2026. "A clock-based schedule (where trains run at regular intervals, like in the metro—Kommersant) will be gradually introduced on CTU routes, making trip planning more convenient," the Moscow government explained. "Implementing this large-scale program will require a major upgrade of the rolling stock. The domestic mechanical engineering industry will be awarded an order for the production and delivery of 100 modern trains in 2026–2035." The Moscow government emphasized that the upgrade of the commuter train fleet has already begun on the Yaroslavl line. "As the tracks are reconstructed, we will also purchase trains for other routes," Sergei Sobyanin said. It is still unclear how the new trains will transport passengers. Previously, a scenario was discussed in which residents of regional centers would travel on new commuter trains to Moscow Central Diameters (MCD) hubs in the Moscow region and then transfer to larger diameter trains. However, in a late 2024 interview with Kommersant, Moscow Deputy Mayor Maxim Liksutov stated that "no final decisions" had yet been made. He also stated that "Russian Railways is working on options." The company is also not yet disclosing details. "At present, decisions have been made on the phased implementation of measures to improve transport accessibility for regions of the Central Federal District including the Moscow metropolitan area," the Russian Railways press service told Kommersant. "The Kaluga, Vladimir, Ivanovo, and Tula regions have been identified as priority areas. The project will provide a powerful impetus to the development of all of Central Russia, expand domestic tourism opportunities, and allow residents of neighboring regions to conveniently and quickly commute to the capital for work or study." In January 2026, in preparation for the launch of the Central Suburban Passenger Company (CPPC), the Central Suburban Passenger Company (CPPC) conducted a test run—without passengers—of the Ivolga electric train on the Moscow-Kaluga route. The trip included testing the actual travel time between stations, its passage through bridges, tunnels, and overpasses, and the operation of the traction and power equipment. The Ivolga traveled 300 km in two and a half hours, reaching a maximum speed of 160 km/h in places. "The main goal of the trip was to study the feasibility of operating the train on public infrastructure where commuter, long-distance, and freight trains operate simultaneously," explained CPPC. The CTU project should be implemented primarily on routes that already have four tracks (for example, the Kyivsky Railway), according to Kirill Yankov, a member of the Ministry of Transport's public council. In some areas, the expert adds, small "localized measures" are needed. In Odintsovo, for example, a four-track transit train service needs to be established (currently, two tracks are dead-end). Kirill Yankov points out that regular Lastochka and Express trains already operate on some routes; they could be converted to a synchronous schedule. "Purchasing new rolling stock will be cheaper than building additional tracks," Mr. Yankov believes. "The goal is to maximize the use of existing track infrastructure, with the primary investment in upgrading rolling stock and passenger infrastructure," Maxim Liksutov previously stated. According to the Moscow government, approximately 31 million people live in the CTU regions and account for almost 75% of all commuter transportation in Russia. The Smolninsky District Court of St. Petersburg has arrested rapper Oxxxymiron (Miron Fyodorov, listed as a foreign agent by the Russian Ministry of Justice) in absentia. The artist is accused of repeated violations of foreign agent legislation (Part 2, Article 330.1 of the Russian Criminal Code). According to the prosecution, the émigré musician fails to report his activities to the Ministry of Justice and fails to label the materials he produces and distributes. The court remanded the artist in absentia to pretrial detention for two months from the date of his extradition to Russia or from the date of his arrest in the country. According to lawyers handling the case against Miron Fyodorov, a foreign agent, in the UK, he likely resides in the UK. Russian rapper Oxxxymiron (Miron Fyodorov has been added to the Russian Ministry of Justice's register of foreign agents) Photo: David Frenkel, Kommersant Russian rapper Oxxxymiron (Miron Fyodorov has been added to the Russian Ministry of Justice's register of foreign agents) Photo: David Frenkel, Kommersant A criminal case for repeated violation of foreign agent regulations was opened against the artist after he was fined twice for lack of markings in 2023. According to Daria Lebedeva, head of the city courts' unified press service, the case began on February 26, 2024. Two months later, he was charged and a warrant was issued to place him on the wanted list. Since May of that year, Miron Fyodorov (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice) has been on the federal wanted list. "To date, Fedorov's whereabouts (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice) have not been established; he is deliberately hiding from investigative authorities," the court press service noted. Oxxxymiron (Miron Fedorov), designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice, is a Russian rapper who rose to fame after releasing the albums "Eternal Jew" and "Gorgorod." In 2021, after a long hiatus, the artist released the album "Beauty and Ugliness." Since 2000, he lived in the UK and studied at Oxford University. In 2013, he returned to St. Petersburg. At the beginning of the special military operation on February 24, Oxxxymiron (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice) spoke out against Russia's actions in Ukraine, posting a video explaining his position. The artist then canceled planned concerts in Moscow and St. Petersburg and left the country. At the court hearing, the rapper's defense attorney requested that the motion to remand his client to pretrial detention be denied. He justified his position by citing the fact that Miron Fyodorov (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice) was not present at the hearing and was possibly unaware of the criminal case against him. The Ministry of Justice declared Oxxxymiron a foreign agent on October 7, 2022. Later that month, on October 25, the Moscow prosecutor's office deemed his song "Last Bell" extremist and banned from distribution. On December 12, 2022, a St. Petersburg court fined the rapper for discrediting the army for publishing a video on social media on the day the military operations began, in which the artist condemned Russia's actions. A month later, on January 11, Oxxxymiron (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice) was fined for the track "Oyda," which contained slogans promoting the secession of Ingria (Ingria, also known as Ingermanlandia (the Ingermanlandia movement is designated as terrorist and banned), is a historical region in what is now Russia, including St. Petersburg and the Leningrad Region) from Russia. According to the prosecutor's office, the musician "points to the need to rebuild the home, that is, the country," which constitutes a "call for separatism." The track was removed from streaming services after the court's decision, and it was banned in June 2023. As a rule, neither the artist nor his representative attended the hearings. According to lawyers handling a separate case against Miron Fyodorov (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice), the rapper is likely currently living in the UK. In March 2025, two women, Victoria Kuchak and Vera Markovich, accused a foreign agent of sexualized violence and child molestation. In a podcast with journalist Anastasia Krasilnikova, they revealed that, using his position as an artist, he had sexual relations with each of them when they were under 18. The women insisted that he built trusting relationships with the teenagers in order to later engage in sexual relations with them. Similar accusations against him were later made online by anonymous users. However, the online community questioned the victims' status, claiming that the women had consented to contact the famous artist. Oxxxymiron (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice) himself did not respond to these allegations and later abruptly canceled a major tour of Europe and the United States, citing health reasons. Amid online discussions, the interregional public movement "Call of the People" appealed to the head of the Investigative Committee of Russia, Alexander Bastrykin, asking for an investigation into the artist on suspicion of violence against minors. The movement also requests that a criminal case be opened against the alleged foreign agent under articles of the Criminal Code that provide for punishment for violation of the sexual integrity of minors. One of the women who accused the rapper of molesting her also asked the Investigative Committee and the Prosecutor's Office to investigate the actions of Miron Fyodorov (designated a foreign agent by the Ministry of Justice). According to lawyer Konstantin Erokhin, they are asking law enforcement to question the musician and other female victims. Several lawyers have also initiated proceedings in the UK, as the rapper is a UK citizen and one of the women accuses the artist of rape in the UK. Polina Puchkova Follow the author:

The US team won the Olympic team event for the second consecutive time. Photo: Natacha Pisarenko / AP. The US team won the Olympic team event for the second consecutive time. Photo: Natacha Pisarenko / AP. In the US, where figure skating has always been held in high esteem, the Olympic team event has always been treated with reverence. After all, it is the event that formally defines the country that sets the tone for the event. And, of course, all the American media outlets proudly emphasized that their team had won its second gold in a row. However, not everyone paid attention to the details. Well, yes, it was a second. But the previous one, in Beijing 2022, didn't become gold right away. First, it was silver. And the Russian figure skaters savored their victory in the stadium, unaware that a couple of days later, everyone would learn of Kamila Valieva's doping scandal and the top prize—albeit after lengthy investigations and proceedings—would be redistributed to those who finished behind. And with that gold, too, not everything was sweet and smooth. This time, the Russian team, whose roster had seemingly lost not so much in depth or quality during four years of isolation, didn't even have to contend: their most formidable competitor was simply barred from the Olympics. But even without him, the Americans were unable to achieve a convincing victory, with true championship brilliance. The gold medal was won through adventures and somersaults, experienced primarily by those least expected. Of all the athletes who earned the right to represent American figure skating at this competition, only ice dancers Madison Chock and Evan Bates were truly outstanding. Pairs skaters Ellie Kam and Daniel O'Shea were, with some reservations. Their level was simply such that they couldn't expect great things. The pair representing Japan, Riku Miura and Ryuichi Kihara, Team USA's only rivals, were like something out of a galaxy far, far away. So, fifth place in the short program and fourth in the free skate are certainly an achievement. Team USA skaters Alysa Liu (left), Amber Glenn, and Ilya Malinin Photo: Ashley Landis / AP Kaori Sakamoto (center) Photo: Ashley Landis / AP Anastasia Gubanova Photo: Andrew Boyers / Team USA skaters Alysa Liu (left), Amber Glenn, and Ilya Malinin Photo: Ashley Landis / AP Kaori Sakamoto (center) Photo: Ashley Landis / AP Anastasia Gubanova Photo: Andrew Boyers / But something nasty happened with singles skating, that most reliable American trump card. The women's short program was given to Alysa Liu, the current world champion, by the way. She skated well, but, strictly speaking, was lost next to Japan's Kaori Sakamoto. A substitution was made for the free skate: Liu was replaced by Amber Glenn, who won gold at the Grand Prix Final in December 2024. In other words, the replacement was more like a reinforcement. Glenn, having botched her signature triple axel and combination, and only warmed up in the second half of her program, managed to lose not only to Sakamoto but also to Georgia's Anastasia Gubanova. Even though Glenn was widely considered a real gold medal contender before the Olympics, while Gubanova was only included in the extremely long list of medal hunters—behind the Americans, the Japanese, and Russia's Adelia Petrosyan. Anyone hoping to see the American prima dominate the singles gold medal, in addition to her performance, should have been wary of her comments about "monstrous fatigue" and "heavy legs" after pre-Olympic training. If they're heavy now, what will happen next?! However, the American singles skater was even more alarming. To hell with them, Liu and Glenn; after all, they didn't have a colossal reserve of strength. But Ilya Malinin seemed to have it, such a reserve that he could win blindfolded. Ilya Malinin Photo: Ashley Landis / AP Japanese figure skaters Shun Sato (left) and Yuma Kagiyama Photo: Claudia Greco / Yuma Kagiyama (center) Photo: Amanda Perobelli / Ilya Malinin Photo: Ashley Landis / AP Japanese figure skaters Shun Sato (left) and Yuma Kagiyama Photo: Claudia Greco / Yuma Kagiyama (center) Photo: Amanda Perobelli / And in the short program, Malinin, the invulnerable Malinin, holder of a ton of records and trophies, made a step-out on his triple Axel, underrotated his quadruple jump, and fell behind Yuma Kagiyama. The judges are usually so generous to Kagiyama and his components, as if the entire judging panel consisted exclusively of the Japanese leader's relatives. But in this case, no one even thought to quibble over the Japanese's ten-point advantage: it was clear that, no matter how you look at it, he knocked out the undefeated. Thanks to all this pandemonium, the competition culminated in a perfect ending. Going into the final act of the three-day marathon—the men's free skate—the US and Japanese teams are tied on 59 points each. And everyone who cares for the Americans silently thanks the Japanese for somehow not having seriously considered developing their dances: if they hadn't been so completely disastrous, they would already be popping champagne in celebration of such a pleasant success. And so they fill with optimism, surprised to see that Kagiyama wasn't included in the final routine. In his place, the second skater, Shun Sato, was selected. This gift, however, didn't loosen Ilya Malinin at all, nor did it relieve his jitters, a desire to minimize risk so uncharacteristic of truly great skaters. Filled with seven quadruple jumps in the most aggressive version, the free program shrank to something like that of, say, Russian singles skater Petr Gumennik, who is preparing to compete at the Olympics, with five quads. But even there, many things went awry: a fall on a lutz, a couple of landings saved by the skin of his teeth, barely. His score—two hundred points—was respectable, but by Malinin's standards, a complete pittance. Kagiyama, with his arsenal, could certainly have achieved that feat. But instead of Kagiyama, Sato skated, who only had three quads in his free program, and, naturally, even with a clean finish, he couldn't match the somewhat grimy Ilya Malinin. The Americans, oblivious to the nuances of their rise, staged a carnival. The Japanese cried heartily, digesting what had happened, along with the Georgians. The Georgian team, one of whose coaches is Eteri Tutberidze, who is much more closely associated with Russian figure skating, was close to bronze, though they never dreamed of winning. But the Italians snatched the bronze. It wasn't circumstances that helped, but their home team. Berry and berry production in Russia is gradually growing. Fresh strawberries and blueberries are available on store shelves even in winter, and there's an even wider selection of frozen berries. However, a steady increase in yield is still elusive, despite last year being a relatively successful one for the berry industry. Photo: Alexander Podgorchuk, Kommersant Photo: Alexander Podgorchuk, Kommersant According to analysts at Rosselkhozbank, farms of all categories harvested a record 29,100 tons of berries last year, 39% more than the previous year (21,000 tons). In 2025, as in the previous year, early frosts in the southern regions negatively impacted the harvest, but the overall situation was nevertheless improved. "There are no precise statistics from Rosstat yet, but preliminary results for 2025 will likely be better than in 2024. "In the 2024 season, frosts in central Russia's regions caused a 10.5% harvest decline. We can expect the situation to improve by about the same amount or even slightly more in 2025," comments Irina Koziy, head of the Berry Academy project and CEO of the FruitNews information agency. Moreover, the situation varies greatly by region. The southern regions, which literally eked out the 2024 harvest, faced early spring frosts in 2025, followed by a summer drought. Therefore, a similar 10% decline in berry production is possible in southern Russia. However, the central regions showed a better picture, although not for all crops. Strawberries (or garden strawberries) remain the favorite, accounting for about half of Russia's berry production in 2025, according to analysts at Rosselkhozbank. Last year, the harvest amounted to 12,700 tons. It is produced primarily in the Krasnodar Krai, Kabardino-Balkaria, Moscow, and Lipetsk regions. However, the berry selection is expanding—the production of currants, blueberries (demand currently exceeds supply), raspberries (interest in freeze-dried products is growing), gooseberries, and so on is on the rise. According to analysts at Rosselkhozbank, this is due both to the expansion of acreage and the introduction of new, intensive technologies. "The yield of everbearing raspberries, particularly those grown in tunnels, is growing. As a result, more and more Russian raspberries are appearing on shelves," says Irina Koziy. Overall, however, industrial raspberry production in Russia is relatively small—3,000-4,000 tons per year, while total fresh berry consumption is 5,000-6,000 tons. "However, this berry has good prospects for growth in both production and consumption," explains Ms. Koziy. AB-Center analysts previously noted increased investment activity in the raspberry market. According to experts, over 100 raspberry cultivation projects are being implemented in 26 regions of the Russian Federation. Most of these will reach their design capacity by 2027. To meet these targets, projects are being implemented to grow a total of 1.5 million seedlings. "Blueberry production is also expanding. Projects that were started in previous years are now entering the commercial fruiting stage. These are fairly large acreages, established in 2020–2022. As a result, the market is seeing more blueberries. But their volumes are increasing not only in our country but also in neighboring countries. Competition for Russian blueberry producers is becoming fiercer," says Irina Koziy. Among berry crops intended for processing, interest in blackcurrants is growing. Many farms are increasing their production, banking on rising prices. "However, this situation could be short-lived," believes the head of the Berry Academy. "For three years in a row, frosts occurred during the currant blossoming period, the flowers died, and there was almost no harvest. Demand and prices increased. But this is the market's reaction to the weather anomaly. It's unlikely that such berry prices will persist for long." According to Babken Ispiryan, chairman of the Association of Peasant Farms and Agricultural Cooperatives of the Kaluga Region, last year, due to a poor currant harvest, the price of 1 kg of berries directly from the producer reached 300 rubles. "In recent years, large areas have been planted for this berry, but most currant plantations have not yet begun bearing fruit. So, the shortage will not be filled by domestic berries in the next three to four years. Moreover, we must take into account the high demand from processors for them, since previously, 90% of the berries for industrial processing came from abroad. Now this is difficult. "So the price will remain stable, as will berry growers' interest in this crop," comments Mr. Ispiryan. Overall, the area under berry cultivation in Russia is gradually increasing—primarily due to small producers, experts note, but large projects are also emerging. For example, the Argoplant farm in the Vladimir region has planted over 120 hectares of blueberries, using the latest technology. Berry cultivation areas are generally expanding in regions close to primary markets. For example, in the Moscow region, berry fields are rapidly expanding in area and producing higher yields. Berry plantations are also expanding in regions that have specifically supported berry production—Kabardino-Balkaria, Tatarstan, and Chuvashia. According to joint forecasts by analysts at Rosselkhozbank and specialists from the NGO "Union of Berry Producers," by 2030 the Vladimir region will hold first place in terms of production rates, with harvests planned to increase from 200 to 5,600 tons. Analysts at Rosselkhozbank also predict a significant increase in future harvests in the Kaliningrad Region (from 500 to 3,000 tons), Crimea (from 600 to 3,100 tons), Tatarstan (from 500 to 2,400 tons), and Penza Region (from 400 to 1,900 tons). The top 10 regions will account for 45% of the total Russian harvest in the organized sector. In total, by 2030, according to experts at Rosselkhozbank's Center for Industry Expertise, the Russian berry harvest is expected to reach 52,000 tons. Wild berries also contribute a significant share to the Russian berry harvest. While official statistics are not kept, according to Alexander Deev, leader of the Wild Plants Association and CEO of Wild Siberia, the average annual harvest volumes in the country's forests remain unchanged. One of the most sought-after wild berries in Russia is lingonberry, which is primarily used for processing (jams, fruit drinks, and preserves). We currently lack domestic lingonberries, so we also import them extensively from China. "Lingonberries are harvested in China in the highlands of the northern provinces. Their quality best meets industrial processing requirements, and their environmental credentials are also valued. We harvest a lot of cranberries, but we still receive imported berries. Some cranberries for our processing are also imported from China and Canada—so-called lake cranberries. They are larger than our own, almost like grapes, and white inside. But our cranberries are much richer in composition than those grown on foreign plantations," says Alexander Deev. Wild sea buckthorn, however, is predominantly domestic. It actively grows along rivers in Siberia and on river islands. There is no pressing need for imported sea buckthorn, although its cultivated plantations in Russia are declining. Meanwhile, Russian wild berries are also actively exported. Last year, Russia increased its frozen blueberry export revenue sixfold, reaching $12.5 million, Interfax reported, citing data from the federal center Agroexport. In physical terms, shipments increased 2.4-fold, reaching almost 6,000 tons. The main buyers of the berries were China (29% of export revenue), Estonia (28%), and Serbia (20%). Moreover, exports to China increased 27-fold, reaching more than $3.6 million from $130,000 in 2024. The highest export revenue over the past ten years was recorded in 2020—around $19 million. Currently, domestic berry harvests, even for actively growing crops, are insufficient for industrial processing. And the issue isn't even the volume of produce grown, but its cost. In terms of production costs, Russian berries are much more expensive than imported ones—buying them is simply unprofitable for processors. "Processing is developing here both at the industrial level and on farms, which periodically come up with interesting new product ideas. Small farm projects processing berries, focused on working directly with consumers, are becoming more common. But industrial processing is still developing slowly," explains Irina Koziy. "To obtain ingredients ready for use in the food industry, a fairly long and expensive chain is required, consisting of many processes—freezing, cleaning, raw material preparation, and so on. We currently lack the berries and financial resources to create a network of such lines or factories." As a result, industrial producers of, for example, nectars, fruit drinks, and jams, find it easier and cheaper to purchase foreign raw materials. Berry farmers themselves are also more interested in selling fresh berries than handing them over to processors, according to Alla Andreeva, General Director of the Union of Juice, Water, and Beverage Producers. "In the beverage industry, berry raw materials are primarily used to produce fruit drinks. The most popular fruit drink in Russia is cranberry, and most cranberries are of Russian origin. However, raw materials from other berries are mostly imported. The specific nature of this market is such that Russian berry producers often find it more profitable to sell fresh berries than to hand them over to the beverage industry for processing," the expert believes. As a result, the deep processing market is currently seeing more farm-based solutions, but in very small quantities. These include all kinds of pastilles, berry snacks with extracts, antioxidants, vitamins, and even berry cosmetics. However, the industrial processing market has great potential. Given the growing trend toward a healthy lifestyle, players in the juice industry, for example, are counting on increased interest in juices, fruit drinks, and nectars. This means we can expect new projects in this area. "Juice products contain many beneficial micronutrients that play an important role in a healthy diet. Given the lack of fruit and vegetable consumption in Russia, they could play a significant role in strengthening healthy eating patterns," says Alla Andreeva. As for interest in "berry delights," consumer demand remains high due to the overall trend toward a healthy lifestyle, but another trend—thrifty living and mindful consumption—is already making its own adjustments. According to the ICMR (GfK-Rus) consumer panel for November 2025 (versus November 2024) in Russia, the fresh fruit and berry category is growing in terms of turnover, primarily due to an increase in the average price (+11%; bill increase of 5.9%). However, there has been a significant decline in purchase volume (-4.6%, with a 0.6% decrease in purchase frequency). The fresh berry category in the fruit and berry basket is significantly smaller than the fresh fruit category. Experts explained that this is a general trend of shifting products from the consumer basket to a cheaper and more essential segment, which is currently being observed. Consumers are reducing their purchases of more expensive products in favor of basic ones, increasingly strengthening the trend toward mindful consumption. Nevertheless, retail chains currently offer a wide selection of berry products throughout the year. "Depending on the store format, shelves are stocked with 11 to 48 types of frozen berries, including strawberries, cherries, currants, lingonberries, blackberries, raspberries, blueberries, sea buckthorn, and chokeberries. The selection of fresh berries is also wide: at the end of January, chains offered up to 42 varieties," says Stanislav Bogdanov, Chairman of the AKORT Presidium. During the winter, the most popular fresh berries are blueberries, blackberries, strawberries, raspberries, and cherries. Blueberries are perceived as a premium product with high nutritional value. Other berries, such as currants, are traditionally a summer harvest, so during the cold season they are most in demand in frozen form for home cooking and baking. "The fresh berry market is distinctly seasonal: the bulk of the Russian harvest occurs in the summer months, and by the end of January, the shelf space is largely formed by shipments from countries with milder climates. In the fresh berry category, approximately 75% of the volume during this period is imported. The main suppliers of fresh berries are Belarus, Armenia, Morocco, Peru, Azerbaijan, Egypt, Mexico, Chile, Turkey, and Moldova. In the frozen berry segment, the situation is different: the share of Russian berries reaches approximately 95%, and imports are supplemented by supplies from Belarus, Serbia, Egypt, Vietnam, and China," noted Stanislav Bogdanov. Imports cover the existing deficit in the Russian berry market. Farmers note that interest in domestic berries is growing. Buyers consider them more environmentally friendly, tasty, and of higher quality. "Retailers, in turn, are responding to this demand by more actively engaging with domestic berry farms and even offering farmers very favorable conditions," noted Babken Ispiryan. For example, X5 launched a partnership with a berry aggregator to steadily increase the share of local produce on store shelves and attract farmers to collaborate, explained Mr. Bogdanov. "In turn, the growth of domestic production is contributing to an expanded product range, and the sustained consumer interest in berries as a natural source of vitamins is supporting demand for this category," said Yulia Zhitnikova, chair of the AKORT presidium.
