According to the National Rating Agency, the average rating for adherence to best environmental practices increased by 13% over the year, reaching 59%. Companies in the oil and gas and metallurgy sectors are the most active in this area. Kommersant-Review investigated whether this means companies are striving to reduce their environmental impact at all costs to meet national project targets, or whether investments in the green agenda are finally starting to yield results. Photo: Dmitry Lebedev, Kommersant. Photo: Dmitry Lebedev, Kommersant. As part of their environmental protection efforts, metallurgy companies are investing in projects to use more environmentally friendly raw materials and fuels, reclamation and reforestation, and the development, modernization, and integration of water recycling systems and air purification systems for waste products. The positive impact of green investments is already noticeable: the anthropogenic load on ecosystems is decreasing and new low-carbon products are emerging, notes Antonina Pavlova, a sustainability ratings analyst at Expert RA. Moreover, this is happening against a backdrop of an unfavorable economic backdrop: real interest rates are among the highest in the world, and companies' own investment resources are limited amid declining profitability for some players. International investment in the energy transition grew by 8%, reaching a record $2.3 trillion last year, according to BloombergNEF data. This occurred despite concerns that a changing political landscape and economic uncertainty would slow progress in clean energy. Approximately $1.2 trillion was invested in renewable energy and power grids, while electrified transport attracted $893 billion last year. Andrey Makarov, Deputy Director of the Operational Risk and Sustainability Group at Kept, attributes the increase in investment to two factors. First, there are the costs of maintaining current green technologies. Secondly, it is a response to tightening environmental legislation. The Russian metallurgical sector is a leader in this trend—the implementation and development of environmentally friendly production technologies and the modernization of production in accordance with new requirements. According to the federal "Clean Air" project, Russian metallurgical enterprises are required to reduce air pollutant emissions by 20% by the end of 2026. Companies are taking active measures to meet these targets, modernizing equipment and improving production processes. However, achieving these goals is generating considerable controversy and doubt. The main concerns relate to the potential economic damage caused by the rapid pace of change. Boris Kopeikin, Chief Economist at the P.A. Stolypin Institute for Growth Economics, emphasizes that "the goals of the 'Clean Air' project fail to take into account both the progress achieved and often the economic reality—the deteriorating domestic and export market conditions and the refusal of Western suppliers to sell the necessary equipment, including under existing contracts." These circumstances force companies to choose: either suspend operations of individual divisions or limit investment in developing their production base. Environmental protection is thus becoming an obstacle to economic growth. Another danger is excessively strict regulatory oversight. "Economically, excessively stringent regulatory requirements have shut down entire systemically important industries, including chemicals, metallurgy, and even automotive manufacturing," asserts Mr. Kopeikin. This state of affairs leads to job losses and budget revenue losses, which is unacceptable for the national economy. To avoid negative impacts, further adjustments to environmental standards and the development of clear criteria for assessing progress are necessary. Only a reasonable combination of strict environmental standards and consideration of economic realities can maintain a balance between the interests of the state and business. Metallurgical plants have a significant impact on water resources, consuming large volumes of water for cooling and cleaning raw materials. Water pollution problems are acute for the ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy industries, forcing them to seek ways to conserve water resources and use it rationally. Rusal demonstrated significant success in conserving water resources, significantly reducing freshwater intake. Completely closed water supply systems allowed for water reuse, eliminating the need for additional pumping. Severstal similarly strives to become a leader in efficient water management, maximizing the efficiency of reused water. Industry experts point out that effective water conservation requires proactive management that understands the importance of resource conservation. A case in point is the dam built by Magnitogorsk Iron and Steel Works, isolating its own production pool from surrounding bodies of water. This project prevented pollution of the local waters and minimized production waste. The next step should be to eliminate the discharge of waste liquids into natural waterways. For example, Evraz plans to ban the discharge of liquid waste into the Malaya Kushva River, thereby simultaneously addressing two important objectives: environmental protection and ensuring the safety of water resources. Energy plays a vital role in reducing the environmental impact of ferrous and non-ferrous metal production. The implementation of environmentally friendly technologies helps companies reduce their carbon footprint and improve their competitiveness in the international market. One of the key aspects of the global environmental agenda is the active promotion of low-carbon metal products. International markets are increasingly demanding environmental performance standards, increasing competition among manufacturers. In particular, in China, a crucial export market for several industries, requirements for both domestic producers and international suppliers are steadily becoming more stringent, explains Boris Kopeikin. These requirements are evolving in a manner similar to EU regulations: the goal is to achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. Therefore, continued active work in this direction is clearly becoming a key condition for operating in international markets. This is why domestic companies are striving to comply with international standards and seeking product certification. For example, Rusal products have received the Green Power Aluminum certificate, confirming their low carbon footprint. Among the key areas of this work is research and testing of inert anodes, which can significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Severstal is also working on developing products with a minimal environmental impact. Direct reduction iron technology promises to revolutionize carbon emissions, making iron a carbon-neutral product. A wide range of innovations is aimed at accelerating the adaptation of Russian enterprises to the new environmental rules of the game. "Absolutely harmless industrial production does not exist, but the concept of zero impact is something we must strive for. The main barrier is not technological, but economic. Implementing such solutions requires colossal investments, which will only pay off with government support and a market willingness to pay a premium for green metal," says gold mining company Seligdar. It's unrealistic to expect the metallurgical industry to go completely green in the foreseeable future. "Breakthrough decarbonization technologies are very expensive and knowledge-intensive. The key technologies for metallurgy are hydrogen and CCS." One measure that could be considered is the development of effective instruments for concessional lending for decarbonization projects (greenfield and brownfield) through budgetary and extra-budgetary financing. "Today, Russia has adopted a taxonomy of green projects, but there are virtually no financial instruments to support them," Severstal says. Rusal is preparing for a breakthrough in low-carbon aluminum production. It is already a world leader in the development of inert anode technology made from non-consumable materials (ceramics or alloys). This technology completely eliminates greenhouse gas and other hazardous emissions. Furthermore, electrolysis produces 0.9 tons of pure oxygen per ton of aluminum, instead of several tons of greenhouse gases. A single electrolytic cell using inert anode technology can produce the same volume of oxygen as 70 hectares of forest. According to Andrey Makarov, there is no technology that would produce steel or aluminum while completely eliminating pollutant emissions and discharges. Currently, we can only talk about minimizing these factors—for example, through the use of direct-reduced iron technology. This solution eliminates the two most environmentally unfriendly and problematic processes—coke oven and blast furnace—from the steelmaking process. As a result, both the carbon footprint of the product and its environmental impact are significantly reduced. As we are periodically reminded, censorship is prohibited in Russia. However, this doesn't prevent legislators from regularly narrowing the boundaries of what's permissible, introducing new categories of information that cannot be distributed at all, or can be distributed only with restrictions: only to adults or only with a disclaimer indicating the content. Alexey Byrdin Photo: Ivan Vodopyanov, Kommersant Alexey Byrdin Photo: Ivan Vodopyanov, Kommersant It's hard to say that the industry—the producers and distributors of films, television programs, books, music, and games—is conceptually opposed to this. Following the November 2022 presidential decree on traditional values, no one has any illusions about the direction state content policy will take. Rather, industry GR is attempting to balance the approach to how these bans will be implemented, who and how they will affect, the size of the fine, whether criminal offenses will be included, and so on. It also seeks to determine whether the criteria for "prohibited" content, enshrined in regulations, will allow for sufficient clarity in describing all the nuances of subtle images and meanings so that they are understood equally by the artist creating them, the producer financing them, and the overseeing official. The restrictions from 2022 to 2025 came in waves, first affecting non-traditional sexual relations, then childfree propaganda, while the approach to drug propaganda was simultaneously revised. Starting in March 2026, the Ministry of Culture will review films and TV series for any defamation or denial of traditional Russian spiritual and moral values. What the press and many disgruntled viewers call "self-censorship" by platforms is, in fact, merely compliance with the law, the violation of which is severely punished by Roskomnadzor. Dura lex sed lex. In this sense, it's pointless and naive to expect online cinemas to risk hefty fines and the suspension of a multi-billion dollar business out of protest, just to spite Roskomnadzor by preserving a fragment of a series' plotline whose original version contains LGBT scenes (the "international LGBT movement" is recognized as extremist and banned in Russia) or the use of substances legal in the country of origin. There are cases where even pirated content is edited by a Russian UGC platform, presumably to avoid complaints from Roskomnadzor: attentive viewers noticed that several seconds were cut from a recent foreign hit series. This is the reality of Russia's traditional and conservative unified information space. Only the most notorious pirate sites and torrents are still immune to the law and Roskomnadzor, and even this is likely an oversight, as this hydra is truly difficult to combat. But the price of accessing prohibited material there is quite high. Want a "unique original"? Mess around with flash drives, and for the sake of a few deleted frames, watch a couple of minutes of trashy online casino ads first, and be prepared to catch a computer virus. Compared to how the Russian film industry simply strictly follows the law under given circumstances, Western practices in the 21st century seem harsher: in the wake of MeToo, along with the "cancellation" of actors, the release of films featuring them was also canceled, and the characters they portrayed were suddenly killed off between seasons of series. Meanwhile, American films released in the Chinese market have been and continue to be subject to strict editing, because there are also laws there. So, creative freedom—no matter how you look at it—is exercised within the framework of norms and codes, because the legal field is always smaller in scope than the field of artistic experimentation. Alexey Byrdin, head of the Internet Video Association

Since the beginning of 2025, Russia has been implementing a new national project, "Data Economy and Digital Transformation of the State." Kommersant examined the priorities, initial results, and prospects of the national project: de facto, its main objective is to define unified, simple, and clear rules of the game for transferring relations within the "citizens, business, and government" triangle into a common digital environment. The supporting task is the deployment of the infrastructure on which these rules will be applied, that is, the creation of a system of interconnected platforms, computing power, and data transmission channels that ensure maximum efficiency, convenience, and security with minimal investment in time and money for all participants in digital relations—and the first results have already been achieved. Deputy Prime Minister and Chief of the Government Staff Dmytro Grigorenko at the Digital Solutions Forum in November 2025. Photo: Igor Ivanko, Kommersant. Deputy Prime Minister and Chief of the Government Staff Dmytro Grigorenko at the Digital Solutions Forum in November 2025. Photo: Igor Ivanko, Kommersant. The "Data Economy and Digital Transformation of the State" national project is relatively new; it emerged as part of the second generation of project instruments under Mikhail Mishustin's government and incorporates digitalization ideas that emerged and matured during the first four-year period and were piloted through smaller-scale initiatives. This allowed for a reconsideration of some previous approaches to digitalization, while also scaling up the experience of the first-generation national projects: from organizing project offices in relevant areas to transferring platform initiatives, previously used only by the most technologically advanced businesses, to the government. Although the first "sketches" of the future national project, its curator, the Chief of the Government Staff and "digital" Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Grigorenko, announced back in September 2024 at the Eastern Economic Forum, the project's "skeleton" had already been formed by winter (see Kommersant of December 5, 2024), giving Kommersant a formal basis to evaluate the content and progress of the initiatives launched this year. A common feature of the latest generation of national goals and national projects, developed by the government in close collaboration with Maxim Oreshkin, the "economic" Deputy Chief of the Presidential Administration, is the exclusion of immeasurable "humanitarian" public administration goals from the project horizon and the concentration within the national project system of detailed planning and instrumental support for specific stages of progress toward measurable indicators for addressing pressing issues. The "Data Economy" is designed not only to implement this approach but also to transmit it to all other national projects through the same digital transformation. On a somewhat smaller scale, it should be noted, Dmitry Grigorenko has already implemented this idea as part of the recently completed reform of control and oversight. The change in the rules of the game in this area was then extended to licensing and permitting activities and, more generally, to state regulation of business-government relations in digital channels. The digital control framework was expanded in the KND within the platform logic (when the KND GIS TOR grew into a whole cluster of interconnected information systems: from the batch issuance of all necessary permits for a specific business to systems for pre-trial appeals of government decisions with overall performance analytics). The "Data Economy" project demonstrates the development of this logic—in its platform-based approach to government procurement of digital systems (the "Gostech 2.0" platform) for resource conservation and end-to-end compatibility, its focus on seamless interaction between government and commercial platforms (the marketplace law), its approach to particularly significant IT projects (which emphasizes the shared interests of state-owned companies, state corporations, and private businesses in developing IT products and minimizing costs while maximizing the replication of the most successful solutions), and its deployment of a public service system tailored to the needs of citizens in specific life situations. In this context, the capabilities of government agencies cease to be decisive for the content of the service provided: they, as executive mechanisms, are designed and shaped to suit the task, not the other way around. The project's toolkit is divided into a set of universal and rather specific situational methods. For example, in its approach to addressing Russia's loss of access to a wide range of Western corporate software, the government is implementing both "universal" methods of competitive struggle for state support and specific tools for collecting information on companies' existing IT import substitution developments in their "internal" portfolios. For this purpose, in particular, a registry of corporate software for its own use has been created. It provides the White House not only with knowledge of the software itself but also with insights into how, for example, critical infrastructure requirements should be structured: to determine these, it is necessary to know what the market can offer for deployment. Currently, the range of particularly significant projects already selected and being implemented in the corporate IT portfolio includes two hundred initiatives with a total value of 184.7 billion rubles. Industrial Competence Centers (ICCs, de facto industry think tanks aimed at selecting projects with the greatest market appeal) define software requirements. The winning project receives a grant of up to 50% from the government and the opportunity to refine and implement the idea at the company chairing the ICC. Upon completion of the project, the developer retains the source code for future deployment across the industry. Thus, the software is received not only by the largest company in its industry but also by others. This guarantees IT developers guaranteed orders and funding, while the industry receives reliable and secure code that is not subject to sanctions restrictions and is unaffected by foreign policy upheavals. Based on the results of the first selection wave (2022), 32 projects are being implemented with government grants totaling 19.9 billion rubles, 113 with company funds, and another 6 with the use of preferential loans. The second selection wave included 49 projects worth 14.8 billion rubles, 17 grants worth 3.2 billion rubles were awarded, and 10 projects are being implemented using in-house funds. A total of 97 ICC projects (including 17 grant projects) have been completed to date. The selection results confirmed the effectiveness of the mechanism: most of the solutions are already being implemented in industry, transport, energy, aviation, and telecommunications, reducing their dependence on foreign technologies. One example is import-substituting software for mechanical engineering and shipbuilding, developed to address the extensive modernization of the Onega Shipyard. The brain behind the digital shipyard project was the commercial implementation of the Russian software solution "Global-Marine: Shipbuilding and Ship Repair Management System," which will at least double labor productivity and increase the number of ships built annually from three to ten, while creating at least 500 high-tech jobs. The system includes an AI module that helps create precise digital 3D models of objects, perform calculations, and recommend the most appropriate technical parameters (the decision is always made by a specialist). AI technology integrated into the software is also used to identify potential risks and possible equipment defects long before emergency situations arise. One of the government's fundamental decisions in the industrial software sector is the forced abandonment of blind competition between companies: the lessons of the early years of IT import substitution have been learned, and the government is quite transparently explaining to the corporate sector that developing corporate IT solutions that are similar in purpose but often incompatible and waiting to see which ones will survive in the market is not in its interests. By effectively lifting some of the secrecy surrounding private developments in exchange for access to state support for the initial design project (OSP), regulators are ensuring a systemic approach to IT construction, accelerating the development and distribution of software with the greatest deployment potential and adapting in-house capabilities to serve the interests of entire industries rather than individual companies. Given that the "domestic" market is limited, wasting its resources on full-scale product competition would mean that many would not be implemented—the new system aims to minimize these losses. Building on previous selection processes, the process is being refined: for the third wave of selection, the government placed particular emphasis on product replicability and reduced excessive bureaucracy for participants (see Kommersant of September 27 and October 14). The third wave of the initial design project (OSP) selection began in September 2025, with a state support budget of 8.3 billion rubles, distributed through the Russian Fund for Information Technology Development. The size of a single grant ranges from 100 million to 2 billion rubles, and both individual companies and consortiums uniting to jointly develop and implement solutions are eligible. The results of the third wave of selection will be announced in December 2025. At the government's direction, the OZP selection mechanism has been redesigned to improve transparency and the efficient use of budget funds, with a focus on replicability, scalability, and commercial potential. Support will be awarded only to projects capable of generating projected sales revenue and a tax refund of at least 110% of the grant amount within three years of completion. Priorities in the selection include platform solutions, including product lifecycle management systems (PLM, PDM, CAD, CAE, CAM, CAPP, MDM, ECAD), the use of artificial intelligence technologies (a new criterion that provides additional points), open-architecture systems, domestic CAD systems, and programs for the defense industry and critical information infrastructure. A significant change in digitalization programs after 2022 has been the sharp tightening of information security requirements—for both specific applications for citizens and businesses, as well as for "heavy" server software and information systems. Conceptually, the national project establishes general "infosecurity" rules for everyone—as with the OZP—which envision the shared use of a common secure infrastructure, from data centers and cloud systems to software that supports data transmission channels and dynamic load balancing, instead of building "defensive perimeters" around each individual IT project—a concept that even fence builders in cottage communities on Rublevo-Uspenskoe Highway have not yet mastered. Specifically, the government developed and included in the national project a comprehensive set of measures to create a unified system to combat cyberfraud, which has increasingly become the victim of citizens. This includes technological tools, legislative initiatives, and educational mechanisms to increase Russians' trust in digital services and protect personal data. The "first package" of system solutions aimed at preventing theft and unauthorized access to personal data includes a ban on transferring SIM cards to third parties, except for close relatives, to counter the anonymization of SIM cards as a means of user identification; a self-prohibition on the execution of communication contracts (issued through Gosuslugi and the Multifunctional Center – even if documents are lost, fraudsters will not be able to obtain a new SIM card without the owner's consent); and a self-prohibition on loans and credits (necessary to prevent the transfer of borrowed funds to fraudsters; by September 1, 2025, approximately 15 million people had already taken advantage of this option). An additional safeguard is the "second-hand" mechanism: a person can appoint a trusted person whom the bank contacts to confirm a suspicious transaction, which is especially important for the elderly. The same security perimeter includes the introduction of criminal liability for droppers—those who provide their bank cards or e-wallets for the transfer of illegal funds, helping fraudsters cash out the stolen money (up to three years in prison for those who knowingly provided their details for a fee, up to six years for the organizers of such schemes; however, those who provided the data free of charge, unknowingly, or under duress will not be held accountable). A platform-based approach has also been found in the fight against cyberthreats: the government is developing a set of tools to identify and block phishing sites and fake pages imitating government and banking resources. The system automatically monitors malicious domains, notifies regulators and telecom operators, and initiates blocking of counterfeits. Moreover, integration into a unified technological framework for protecting the digital environment will enable the creation of end-to-end interdepartmental response scenarios: from threat detection to its elimination. As noted by the Ministry of Digital Development, "the creation and commissioning of the system on the GosTech platform will be ensured by March 1, 2026." Among many other projects, the "Data Economy" includes a reform of government services. One of its core elements is the unification of services based on the "life situations" principle. This principle creates a new framework for citizen interaction with the government. While the digitalization of government services is a priority of the national project, the goal of implementing "life situations" (or "zhesok" in government jargon) is to deploy a more people-focused model of government service delivery, making issue resolution simple, convenient, and fast, and forcing government agencies to adapt their services to the real needs of real people rather than simply following regulations. This approach allows for the replacement of dozens of departmental procedures with a single, clear digital process, structured according to the logic of a life event, be it enrolling in a university, having a child, retiring, starting a business, etc. A single "life situation" brings together, on average, 17 government services and services related to a common theme. The user goes through all the steps—from information to application submission and receiving the result—without searching for the necessary agencies or re-submitting the same documents to different system participants. Personal data already in the system is automatically populated. At the federal level, "life situations" have been implemented since 2023 and, since then, have become a flagship of digital transformation, having been accessed over 70 million times. Forty-two federal services have already been deployed, covering key social and life scenarios. The average number of required documents has been reduced by 29% (from 28 to 20), the average time to receive services has been reduced by 35% (from 102 to 66 days), and the number of required visits to agencies has been reduced almost threefold (from 14 to 5). Since 2024, regional services built on the same principle, utilizing federal methodological recommendations, have also begun to actively develop. Now, Russian regions are also reaping the benefits: the number of documents required has been reduced by 40%, the time it takes to receive services by 42%, and the number of visits to government agencies by 67%. At the same time, the range of "life situations" is expanding: by the end of 2025, 70 federal and 425 regional services in this format will be implemented. Recently, the "Gosuslugi" portal has added services such as "Free Legal Aid" (allowing vulnerable citizens to schedule a free legal consultation, find the address of the nearest state legal office, and choose a convenient appointment time—helping citizens avoid legal scams) and "Tax Deduction" (helping them apply for popular tax deductions without leaving the Gosuslugi portal). A single scenario integrates federal and regional government services, providing a unified interface and minimizing data duplication. A feedback mechanism has been integrated into the system: services aren't simply tested in labs at the outset; each user can evaluate the experience and provide feedback, enabling adjustments and improvements. The key goal of the next stage is to make service provision "invisible," where issues are resolved automatically, even before a request, proactively, based on available data on citizens' needs. A person receives a notification or a ready-made service without additional requests, document collection, or visits to government agencies. For example, upon the birth of a child, a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) and a Social Insurance Number (SNILS) are assigned automatically, and the information is displayed in the personal account on the government services portal. Looking at the expansion of digital government systems, one cannot help but wonder who will support, develop, and maintain them. Therefore, developing human resources for the digital economy has also become one of the areas of the "Data Economy" national project, with two focuses on key digitalization technologies. The Top IT and Top AI projects are being implemented by the Ministry of Digital Development, Communications, and Mass Media with the participation of the Government Analytical Center. They are aimed at training highly qualified specialists for the country's technological development. The IT talent market is oversaturated with junior programmers, or simply entry-level programmers, who account for only 11% of job openings in the industry. Businesses and the government, however, need highly qualified specialists at the middle and senior levels. The Top IT and Top AI projects are aimed at training these specialists. The educational programs are being developed jointly with leading employers, ensuring their alignment with the demands of the digital economy and accelerating graduates' adaptation to key positions in technology companies and public administration. The Top-IT project currently includes 26 universities from 13 regions of the Russian Federation, and the scope is expanding: by 2026, at least 28 more universities are planned to be selected. Approximately 3,500 students have already been accepted for training. The project is funded jointly by the state and the market: IT companies account for at least 30% of the grant. Additionally, businesses send their practicing employees as instructors for these programs, participate in the development of the curriculum, conduct student assessments and evaluations, organize internships at companies, and incorporate real business cases into the training. In 2025, the first competency-role model for the IT sector in Russia was developed at MIPT. It defines key competencies and professional roles for specialists that meet modern requirements. The model was created based on a survey of 50 IT companies and proposals from participating universities. The model consists of three role groups: core roles include undergraduate programs for software engineers, business and systems analysts, QA engineers, DevOps engineers, MLOps and data engineers, cybersecurity specialists, BI analysts, systems and network administrators, and telecommunications engineers. "Advanced" roles include solutions architect, product manager, development team lead, and DevSecOps engineer. "Advanced" role models include project or program manager. This breakdown is intended to precisely align training with the most in-demand roles in future positions for IT specialists at technology companies in the industry. Participating universities have modernized more than 50 educational programs using this framework. "Top-AI," in turn, is a project whose stated goal is to "preventively" provide personnel for the growing market for artificial intelligence technologies. By 2030, the program is expected to produce more than 10,200 highly qualified AI specialists (the estimated number of applicants is at least 14,700). Following a university competition for grants in the form of subsidies held in the second quarter of 2025, 22 universities in 13 regions of the Russian Federation were selected to participate in the project. Top AI has two levels of training: Top Data Science, a program for training AI researchers and architects capable of developing new training methods and designing world-class model architectures, and Data Science, a program for training specialists focused on applied tasks: tuning and further training existing AI models. In this project, the training model (developed by ITMO University) combines the competency-role models of the Ministry of Education and Science and the Alliance in Artificial Intelligence, combining current and emerging competencies, making it resilient to technological change. A key condition for universities' participation in both projects is experience implementing relevant programs and collaborating with industrial partners. For the state, as a strong player, business participation offers the opportunity, among other things, to increase the effectiveness of education investments through the expertise of companies that will subsequently hire specialists. A willingness to carefully examine the consequences of decisions and, if necessary, adjust them before the situation gets out of control is one of the key characteristics of Mikhail Mishustin's government. An environment that allows for working with "digital twins" and industry and technology models before transferring hypotheses to the "real sector" has made the "Data Economy" national project an ideal platform for exploring, testing, and fine-tuning new public administration methods. This, however, requires the preparation of a working environment, so one of the key objectives at the project's launch in 2025 was to integrate the disparate stages of "digitization" across industries and departments onto a single digital government platform. This platform consolidates data on the implementation of national projects, state programs, and departmental indicators, and creates tailored end-to-end digital dashboards allowing the White House and regions to monitor the progress of instructions and the effectiveness of measures in real time. The development of the government's digital architecture is being supported by the creation of end-to-end interdepartmental services that facilitate data exchange between ministries, regions, and departmental platforms (and, in the future, also between systems "external" to the executive branch—the model is being tested on marketplaces). The key achievements of 2025 in this area include the unification of data formats and interfaces between agencies, increased compatibility between federal and regional GIS systems, the introduction of API interaction tools, which has accelerated the integration of new government services on the portal of the same name, and the modernization of the interdepartmental document flow mechanism—it was specifically purged of redundant approvals and bureaucracy, replacing the "sequential" review of draft documents with a "parallel" one to expedite decision-making. Models fed by White House data, as well as big data and artificial intelligence analytics technologies, already make it possible to predict the achievement of national project targets—not through a linear approximation, but by taking into account feedback from the entire project perimeter they affect. This makes it possible to identify deviations and bottlenecks at an early stage and adjust management decisions based on objective digital data. De facto, the Russian government is rapidly moving online and building a new work culture based on live data and continuous monitoring of its own work. One of the most interesting findings in this culture is the risk-free principle, which allows for the right to experiment even in sensitive industries. This methodology has been repeatedly tested in the government apparatus, which has become Dmitry Grigorenko's main "laboratory" for self-experimentation. For example, to gain the right to try AI in drafting bills, resolutions, and departmental documents, the apparatus first implemented strict digital tracking of officials' deadlines for implementing regulatory initiatives, then achieved zero overdue deadlines, and only then applied for permission to integrate AI into the "Rulemaking" GIS (two large language models trained on a corpus of digitized documents and protected from the risk of "picking up stupid things online"). This approach—"learn to do it manually, then hand it over to robots"—allows for a seamless return to proven manual work if robots fail. As a result, AI is gradually becoming an integral part of the management decision-making infrastructure. Machine analysis technologies are already being used to forecast demand for government services, identify common user errors and automatically optimize interfaces, analyze citizen requests received through Gosuslugi to improve feedback, and monitor the implementation of national projects and regional economic dynamics. Since citizens had so far limited themselves to social media alerts, the Veliky Novgorod Prosecutor's Office set up a hotline. Anastasia Merkusheva, Senior Assistant to the Veliky Novgorod Prosecutor, reported on its results. "The hotline was prompted by numerous reports from Novgorod residents about the poor quality of their drinking water. People called not only from Veliky Novgorod (specifically, from Korsunov Avenue, Parkovaya, and Khutynskaya Streets), but also from the Novgorod Municipal District (the village of Borki and the settlement of Podberez'e). While most residents of the regional capital reported problems with the water's characteristic color and odor, those from rural areas reported problems with lack of pressure." According to Anastasia Merkusheva, for example, a young mother living in the Western District of Veliky Novgorod reported that for several weeks she has been unable to bathe her child in such water and has had to buy bottled water from the store. The family simply doesn't use the tap water. A resident of the village of Borki, who has four children, has a similar problem. However, it stems from the fact that the water doesn't reach the fourth floor of the apartment building where the family lives. What is the fate of these complaints? All of them have been placed under the personal supervision of the Veliky Novgorod prosecutor. Each of them will be subject to on-site inspections involving representatives of Rospotrebnadzor, Novgorod Vodokanal, and management companies. If warranted, prosecutorial action will be taken. Reports from residents of the Novgorod Municipal District will be forwarded to the Novgorod District Prosecutor's Office, which will conduct a similar inspection. Photo source: author

Nizhny Novgorod Region Governor Gleb Nikitin and Metropolitan Georgy of Nizhny Novgorod and Arzamas presented the exhibition "People of the Church: The History of a Family" in Moscow. The exhibition was shown to Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko and His Holiness Patriarch Kirill of Moscow and All Rus'. The exhibition was prepared by the Autonomous Non-Profit Organization "Management Company for the Development of the Sarov-Diveyevo Cluster and the Nizhny Novgorod Region," the Ministry of Tourism and Industry of the Nizhny Novgorod Region, and the Nizhny Novgorod Diocese. The exhibition consists of two parts. The first includes materials from the Arzamas Museum of the Russian Patriarchate and the "Confessor of the Christian Faith – Priest Vasily Gundyaev" house-museum in Lukoyanov. It is dedicated to the Gundyaev family—the ancestors of Patriarch Kirill, who lived in the Nizhny Novgorod Region. The exhibition features biographical materials, photographs, documents, personal belongings, and examples of church vestments, as well as information about their time in exile. The second part of the exhibition is dedicated to the spiritual centers of the Nizhny Novgorod region and the project to develop the Arzamas-Diveyevo-Sarov pilgrimage and tourism cluster, implemented with the support of Russian President Vladimir Putin and the blessing of Patriarch Kirill. As part of the project, restoration of the central part of Arzamas is underway, including the restoration of the Resurrection and Transfiguration Cathedrals, and the improvement of Cathedral Square and the Monastery Garden. In Diveyevo, the transformation of the Seraphim-Diveyevo Monastery continues, and in Sarov, the restoration of the Holy Dormition Monastery (Sarov Hermitage) continues. Gleb Nikitin noted that the project encompasses virtually all sectors and is the result of joint efforts between the Nizhny Novgorod Region government and the Nizhny Novgorod Metropolitanate, aimed at the harmonious development of secular and religious facilities and the creation of comfortable conditions for tourists and pilgrims. Residents of the Nizhny Novgorod Region aged 18 to 35 with experience organizing patriotic events can participate in the all-Russian "Victory Ambassadors" competition and join the Victory Day volunteer corps. Competition finalists will undergo an educational program where they will learn about helping veterans of the Great Patriotic War, restoring family history, and organizing volunteer support. The winners will traditionally gather in Moscow to prepare for and support the main Victory Day Parade on Red Square from May 5 to 10. Olga Zanko, Chair of the Central Headquarters of the All-Russian public movement "Victory Volunteers," announced the start of registration. She also spoke about volunteer opportunities around the world. "St. George's Ribbon," "Immortal Regiment," "Garden of Memory," and "Victory Dictation" are events that unite millions of people. "This is the 12th time registration for the Victory Day Volunteer Corps is underway and aims to preserve the memory of the heroes of the Great Patriotic War," noted Olga Zanko. Last year, five representatives of the Nizhny Novgorod regional branch of "Victory Volunteers" accompanied the anniversary Victory Day Parade on Red Square. The volunteers participated in the forum, underwent training, visited memorial sites, and met with veterans, including Nizhny Novgorod residents Vazgen Grigoryevich Oganesyan, Vasily Yakovlevich Kuritsyn, and Nikolai Fedorovich Shishkin. According to Maria Samodelkina, head of the Nizhny Novgorod regional branch of "Victory Volunteers," preparations for May 9th bring people together to preserve historical memory and give everyone the opportunity to make a personal contribution. Young volunteers will also be able to join Victory Day events at the Artek International Children's Center and participate in the supplementary general development program "Victory Ambassadors." Artek: Connection of Generations, a project implemented by Victory volunteers in collaboration with a children's center. Detailed information about the projects and registration are available on the website: volonterypobedy.rf.

The Volga Federal District has begun accepting applications for participation in the inter-municipal and regional qualifying rounds of the "MoloT" (Youth Labor) project for working youth. Young professionals from enterprises in the real economy, aged 18 to 35, including young parents with children, are invited to participate. Participants will have the opportunity to prove themselves in sports, creative, and intellectual competitions, as well as gain recognition at the federal level. In 2024, the district finals of the project brought together 420 participants from 14 regions of the Volga Federal District. A total of 16,000 people from 394 enterprises in the district participated in the qualifying rounds. Competitions were held in professional skills, as well as in sports and military disciplines. The project is being implemented under the auspices of Igor Komarov, Plenipotentiary Representative of the President of Russia in the Volga Federal District. Registration is open on the Volga Federal District public projects website: https://proektypfo.ru/?id=7015.

On February 10, Diplomat's Day, Nizhny Novgorod Region Governor Gleb Nikitin congratulated Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, the Russian Foreign Ministry staff, and the entire diplomatic corps. The governor noted the role of diplomats in establishing trusting relationships with foreign countries, developing bilateral contacts, and creating conditions for international cooperation, emphasizing their contribution to the implementation of foreign policy decisions important to the country. According to Nikitin, international cooperation is a significant area of development for the Nizhny Novgorod Region. With a rich history and high industrial and scientific potential, the region is strengthening its position as a center of international diplomacy. The governor reported that in 2025, 324 foreign delegations from 145 countries—approximately 4,000 guests—would visit the Nizhny Novgorod Region, representing almost 50% more than in 2024. The most significant international events were the 10th CIPR-2025 Conference, which brought together over a thousand delegates from 115 countries, and the World Youth Festival, which attracted over two thousand young people from 120 countries. Gleb Nikitin also expressed gratitude to the Russian Foreign Ministry Representative Office in Nizhny Novgorod, the Consul General of the Republic of Belarus in Nizhny Novgorod, and the Honorary Consuls of Abkhazia, Austria, Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kyrgyzstan, and Malta for their contributions to developing the region's cooperation with foreign partners. In conclusion, the Governor wished the diplomatic corps members success in their work, creative energy, health, and strength.

What reward could there be for academic and social success? How about an unusual trip? Specifically, to the Legislative Assembly of the Nizhny Novgorod Region, to meet with its Speaker, Yevgeny Borisovich Lyulin! On December 24, a team of activists from the Movement of the First and the All-Russian "Big Change" competition from Dzerzhinsk visited the Nizhny Novgorod parliament to learn about its work and history. And who could answer these questions? The Speaker, of course. In the cozy atmosphere of the assembly hall, a warm meeting between the Speaker and the schoolchildren took place. Instead of formal speeches, there was a sincere dialogue during which the students were able to ask the most personal questions. The conversation was truly heartfelt: without candid answers, it was filled with smiles, memories, and reflections on life, even with tears, laughter, poems, gifts, and applause. The first thing the students asked was what books the long-time deputy liked. Evgeny Lyulin, without hesitation, named A.S. Pushkin's "Eugene Onegin." Why? "Fall in love—and ask yourself why!" the deputy replied with a wink. He shared that for him, books are alive, teaching us empathy and distinguishing good from bad. The speaker recommended "How the Steel Was Tempered"—one of the most life-affirming books, in his opinion. The students eagerly asked about Evgeny Borisovich's childhood. It turned out that in his school years, he loved literature, history, and physical education, participating in many sports competitions. He was also drawn to nature, which is why he wanted to become a forester. And today, he still loves the forest and physical education: he devotes every day to sports, and for the New Year holidays, he goes to his native village. The conversation smoothly turned to the New Year—a topic close to every child. The deputy said this holiday has always been special for him: "New Year's is a Christmas tree, snow, home, family, and a stove." He comes to his native village, where his entire family gathers: "The holiday gives you the opportunity to return to childhood and seek happiness." The students kept asking new questions, forgetting about time. They discussed many qualities of leaders, the situation in universities, methods of motivation after mistakes and failures... "You need to develop for yourself, for your own happiness, and not for your parents or praise," the students received advice. They also received books and coloring books about Nizhny Novgorod, as well as a pen and notebook with the emblem of the Legislative Assembly. The students left inspired: the conversation gave them not just knowledge, but the belief that their voice matters, and that dreams of a just society are not a utopia, but a goal worth striving for. Evgeny Borisovich said of the students: "I see they have roots!" Text: Alexandra Terskaya, young correspondent Photo: Legislative Assembly press service

You know what downpours are like in the south? A wall of water, with thunder and lightning! A truly Italian, highly realistic thunderstorm erupted on the fateful night when, as the jester wished, supreme justice was to be meted out, but fate cruelly mocked the mocker... Rigoletto has returned to the Nizhny Novgorod opera stage – and returned triumphantly. Many theater regulars remember the evil jester, played by People's Artist of the RSFSR Vladimir Stepanov: terrifying and vile in his moments of triumph, mortally wounded, he moved the audience to tears. But it turns out the title character can be different and no less compelling – almost a romantic figure, with internal conflict and emotional suffering. There are no "minor" roles. The Nizhny Novgorod Opera and Ballet Theatre has been refreshing audiences lately, offering original productions of the classical repertoire, but this premiere is in a textbook spirit. This is a traditional costume production with traditional sets, meticulously adhering to the letter and spirit of Verdi's magnificent opera. The singing, again, is in the original language, but just in case, there's a simultaneous translation into Russian on the stage and on the screens. No "bold interpretations." The orchestra La Voce Strumentale, conducted by Dmitry Sinkovsky, is sensitive and virtuoso. The soloists shine, earning standing ovations. The Duke (Vladimir Kuklev) is more than just a handsome man: he's wildly charming, a true New Orleans favorite, and understandably, all the women are smitten with him. Rigoletto, performed by Vladislav Biryukov, is a tragic hero. He hasn't yet accumulated any venom and retains a vibrant inner dignity, yet he is driven by pain. Galina Kruch is a classic Gilda, a slender blonde with a doll-like face and a captivating voice worthy of the finest operas. All the characters are richly detailed, yet subtly balanced. Even those who receive only a few lines by the composer gain their share thanks to their expressive movements and the excellent direction of the set: the nimble, enterprising Maddalena (Karina Kharunts), the frivolous, full-lipped blonde Countess Ceprano (Daria Pichugina), and the jealous Count Ceprano, who makes no secret of his displeasure with his wife's frivolity (Viktor Ryauzov), the socialite Marullo (Alexei Koshelev), the rebellious Monterone (Kirill Loginov), and Giovanna (Sofia Skhirtladze), torn between duty and the desire to earn extra money—all work beautifully together. Listen and think. "A performance of stunning beauty and richness," is how Airat Tukhvatullin, director of the Nizhny Novgorod Opera and Ballet Theatre, described the production. Besides the aforementioned thunderstorm scene, there's also a mysterious night-time Italy and a palace where everything screams luxury and sensual pleasures—and all of it is vibrant and compelling (set designer Maria Vysotskaya, lighting designer Ruslan Mayorov, video designer Dmitry Ivanchenko). The costumes again feature a lot of black, but the lack of color is a plus. As intended, there's plenty of laughter on stage. The courtiers roar with laughter, the protagonist mocks, the Duke—the darling of fortune—chuckles contentedly, the beautiful Maddalena bursts into laughter... and the audience giggles too, for example, at Sparafucile's line, "I'm not some bandit, I'm an honest killer!" But he who laughs last, after all, laughs best. Following in Hugo's footsteps, director Sergei Novikov delved deep, inviting the audience to reflect. The Duke and Rigoletto are linked by a kind of karmic relationship. No matter what the rich, handsome man does, all the blows and knocks fall on the pathetic buffoon, the perpetually beaten Petrushka. The curse is his, the abduction of his beloved is also his, and even the hand of an honest murderer is directed against him by providence, while the Duke merely plucks the flowers of pleasure. We see Gilda living in a ghostly world: not only isolated from society but also surrounded by lies and omissions. She doesn't even know the true names of those closest to her—her late mother, father, and lover. Raised in an artificial environment, in a convent, she is completely ignorant of life, and, of course, a confrontation with reality will destroy her. Maria Fedotova. Photo by Alexander Volozhanin. Gilda and the Duke of Mantua as a poor student. 3. Gilda (Galina Kruch) and Rigoletto (Vladislav Biryukov). 4. The famous quartet. The scene where Gilda realizes her lover is unfaithful.

Learn interesting facts, master a few ancient skills, concoct a complex fragrance, and much more at the 17th "Volga Standard" Festival of Historical Reenactment Clubs, which took place at the Shchelokovsky Khutor Museum of Wooden Architecture last weekend. To battle under the sign of the lion. Participants, almost jokingly, called this "Volga Standard" a "multi-century festival of all peoples": the event was diverse, colorful, and joyful, pleasing to both mind and heart. Blacksmiths were at work, crafting brooches—fasteners for outerwear—from pure iron. Potters and carvers, weavers, and tailors offered their wares. Napoleonic soldiers fired blanks, and Vikings brandished swords. Historically accurate clothing and paraphernalia delighted the eye, and entertainment recreated in the spirit of bygone times was on offer. Moreover, almost all the festival participants were not just enthusiastic enthusiasts, but also deeply informed about "who they are" and what they do: no matter who you approached, you'd hear a captivating story! A blacksmith explained how to saturate iron with carbon, a peasant woman revealed the secrets of the symbolism on a forehead protector, and a learned calligrapher helped us master the mysteries of beautiful penmanship on real papyrus. Two thousand years ago, when a Roman wanted to write a letter, he would pick up a cera—a wax-coated tablet—and use a stylus to write a message on the wax. After the recipient read the message, he could erase it, perhaps by smoothing it with his palm, and write a reply—in other words, reuse the cera. If the letter was intended to be long, several tablets were bound together, and if the contents of the letter were confidential, the tablets were folded with the written sides inward and sealed. Incidentally, such reusable notebooks were also found in Novgorod: they date back to the tenth century and contain psalm texts. Now, your gaze falls on a lion's skin with a beautifully crafted head and glowing amber eyes, lying among a suit of Roman armor. A free citizen explains: this is no random object! In the glorious days of ancient Rome, the skin of this magnificent predator, worn over a helmet and tied at the neck by its paws, was worn by the aquilifer—the legion's standard-bearer. A journey into antiquity. You could not only ask questions but also touch them, actively participate in anything your heart desires. For example, help the blacksmith blow the bellows. Or pick up a sledgehammer and, using an ancient technique, mint a coin or two as a souvenir. Try on chainmail with a helmet, pick up a sword—and capture yourself in the image. Or even try archery. Fencing lessons—with soft weapons, of course—are out of the question, so the children happily thrashed each other under the watchful eye of their instructors. Amid the general carnival atmosphere, a NN correspondent, feeling a tingle for gambling, played "Pig" for money. Fortune was kind and helped her win, so the heavy, cool coins filled her palm comfortably. Alas, they had to be left on the game board. There's a table on which sheaves of rye and barley ears are laid out in abundance, along with bowls of various flours. "Don't put this in your mouth!" Igor and Nikita, millers from the "Storm" historical reenactment club, shout to the curious children. However, many still manage to snatch a few sips of the coarse, dark flour and immediately taste their spoils: you definitely won't buy something like this in a store! When asked to share a thousand-year-old recipe—what did our ancestors enjoy in the year of the Christianization of Rus'?—the millers, apparently starved in the fresh air, share a recipe for boar's knee. As for flatbreads, everything couldn't be simpler. Flour was mixed with water and left to rise for 24 hours. "Bakers back then had plenty of wild yeast on their hands, so the result was a sourdough starter," the young people share the secret of ancient breadmaking. Then, the required amount of flour was mixed in, and the resulting dough was baked into flatbreads, which were eaten with whatever God provided. Visiting a fairy tale. Simultaneously with the "Volga Standard" festival, another ethnic festival, "Fairy Tales of Russia," was held on the grounds of the museum-reserve. It was a truly wonderful experience, bringing fairy tale characters friendly to mere mortals to the people. The menacing Leshy, for example, contrary to the folklore, wasn't a malicious mocker and even held a master class on wax candle-making. Baba Yaga, having successfully arranged her personal life (that is, married Koshchei), abandoned her alchemy nook and led a fascinating quest to find Koshchei's magical needles: a needle was found, and not just one. And Marya the Craftswoman, a true Russian beauty, weaved woolen belts, patiently explaining the construction of an unusual loom. Tsar Saltan attracted everyone's attention. A handsome man in light "summer" attire—not a sable coat, but a brocade okhabn trimmed with weasel fur—he conversed with a Persian guest. The conversation took place against the backdrop of a discreet display of strength: the Tsar casually waved his pick. The guest was nervous, wiping sweat from his brow and constantly glancing at his weapon. During breaks in conversation, the Tsar graciously received admirers who wanted to take photos with him, and even allowed some to occupy the throne for a few seconds! The throne, though gilded, was wooden. "The real royal throne, the one made of pure gold, remained in the palace," Saltan replied to a question from an NN correspondent. "After all, the Tsar—that is, I—is currently on campaign, and therefore my throne is a travel one. Carrying a real one around is heavy, and unwise." Maria Fedotova. Photo by the author.

According to the Russian Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment, approximately 50 million tons of waste are generated annually in the municipal sector alone. If this waste is dumped uncontrolled in landfills, they will soon overflow, threatening not only environmental problems but also human well-being. What our country is doing to reduce the burden on landfills and their number was discussed at the international forum "SO.ZNANIE," where participants discussed the country's sustainable future and the closed-loop economy without which it would not exist. It's a carrot and a stick approach. As Denis Butsaev, CEO of the Russian Environmental Operator, noted, since 2019, our country has been developing an infrastructure that will enable the recovery of secondary raw materials, including from municipal solid waste. The next stage of reform should be the advanced processing of recyclable materials for their use in the production of other products. But who would want to make anything from recyclable materials if they are inherently more expensive and cheaper primary raw materials are available? Economic incentives are being introduced to encourage waste producers and recyclers. If an organization recycles, that is, returns the materials used to make goods and packaging to industrial use, it is exempt from paying the environmental fee. However, the rates for other market participants are increased. "If we don't have economic and regulatory incentives for the use of recycled materials, then, unfortunately, the circular economy model won't work," says Denis Butsaev. "Economic incentives are embedded in the concept of extended producer responsibility. What does it entail? It's a mechanism requiring manufacturers and importers of goods and packaging to ensure their recycling after use and the loss of their consumer properties." According to Gusein Ibragimov, Deputy Head of the Department of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), by 2027, all packaging without exception must be recycled and reused. As for other types of goods, the recycling rate will increase until 2029. The list of mandatory recycling items includes textiles, paper, cardboard, rubber, glass, plastic, electronic and household appliances, batteries, lamps, machine oils, and more. The environmental fee rate and recycling standards, which have already been adopted, will incentivize this. There are no incentives, no opportunities. The number of companies engaged in recycling will also increase. The deputy head of the Department of Environmental Protection called for more active public involvement in waste separation. Useful fractions collected mixed with food are highly likely to end up in landfills and be lost to recyclers. "A closed-loop economy won't work without a responsible approach, starting with every citizen who sorts their waste," stated Gusein Ibragimov. Meanwhile, Nizhny Novgorod residents complain that plastic waste, even collected in mesh containers (where available!), is often transported to the landfill in the same truck with other trash. Therefore, they see no point in separating it. However, regional operators justify this by claiming that this occurs when plastic is contaminated with organic matter. Some also believe that the culture of recycling isn't solely to blame for residents' reluctance to separate their waste. As Andrei Betin, the leading executive director of the ANO "Russia – Land of Opportunities" and rector of the Senezh Management Workshop, explained at the forum's plenary session, there simply isn't any proper infrastructure for separate waste collection in apartments. For example, there are no three-compartment bins for sorting waste by fractions. Dalia Safiullina, head of the business unit for transition to a circular economy at Kept, also believes that the reform has so far done little to encourage Russian residents to manage their waste responsibly. She notes that in some countries, such as South Korea and France, residents who separate their waste pay less for solid municipal waste collection. "The quality of separate collection directly impacts how much residents pay for it," she explained. "And such a system is called door-to-door waste collection accounting. Incentives for recyclers. To motivate Russians, the expert suggests focusing efforts, firstly, on raising awareness and promoting a culture of conscious consumption. As Dalia Safiullina put it, so they don't rush out to buy the "tenth blouse" on Black Friday. Secondly, the state should introduce economic incentives that will attract residents. When will dual-fraction bins for separate waste disposal, for dry waste and organic waste, appear in every courtyard? And won't they cost more than the current general bin fee? According to Dmitry Biller, Development Director of the regional waste removal operator Nevsky Ecological Operator, until we build a closed-loop economy, separate waste collection will be ineffective. Right now, we need to support and incentivize recyclers. "No matter how much recyclable material we collect, it must ultimately find its own facility where it can be effectively transformed into products and goods," he says. "Even if there were recycling bins in every courtyard right now, they wouldn't achieve the desired effect. But once the closed-loop economy kicks into gear, there's no doubt that businesses will come to every courtyard, and the necessary infrastructure will be in place." Dmitry Biller explained that his company conducted a study tracking the contents of recycling bins. It turned out that the amount of excess waste dropped significantly after environmental education events, and less waste needed to be sorted. Overall, he believes that 80 to 95 percent of recycled materials can be realistically returned to the economy. Meanwhile, as Irina Baibarovich, Advisor for Strategic Communications and Sustainable Development at Siberian Glass, reported, the glass container industry is currently ready to recycle up to 80 percent of cullet, but there isn't enough. "The only way to obtain high-quality glass waste is to collect it from households," she said. "But when, for example, a glass jar ends up in a garbage truck, it compacts it." Ultimately, only the small bottom, where the glass is denser, remains uncrushed; the rest crumbles and ends up in the landfill. Irina Baibarovich explained that collecting cullet requires traveling many kilometers from the factory. This translates into transportation costs, which account for 98 percent of the cost of glass. This also hinders the acquisition of high-quality raw materials and a mixture with organic materials. The problem again stems from an ineffective waste collection system, and reform is clearly overdue. A question from an amateur: What eco-friendly habits can you incorporate into your life, without breaking a sweat? I would start by separating your household waste into organic and recyclable. Organizing your eco-friendly life, which involves separating waste, is as simple as pie: put it in separate buckets (bags). One for food scraps, peelings, and fruit and vegetable peelings; the other for all dry, pre-washed plastic bottles, jars without lids, cardboard and paper packaging, and other items. The second thing I would incorporate into my eco-lifestyle is reusable items – shopping bags, cups… In everyday life, you can limit yourself to these. But! If you want to get more involved with an eco-friendly lifestyle, you can come to our ECOTORIUM environmental education center in Switzerland Park. Here we hold various workshops on the use of recycled materials," said Svetlana Vasilyeva, head of the ECOTORIUM environmental education center of the Nizhny Novgorod Region Ministry of Ecology, deputy director of the State Budgetary Institution "Ecology of the Region," and member of the Nizhny Novgorod Region Public Chamber. Until February 8th, the fair's first and second pavilions will be a riot of color and showcase every conceivable diversity of the visible world. This is the next edition of "ART WORLD." This year, the festival's theme was "Constellation of Cultures": many countries, many nationalities, many schools, all converging in an Apollonian galaxy within the vast expanses of the fair. The opening also featured a "constellation of arts": live music, a performance, and champagne. Artists signed autographs and business cards, while others indulged in creativity. The exhibition brought together 398 artists from 29 Russian cities and 18 countries, both individual artists and members of gallery collections. The galleries, of course, were also very diverse, each with its own identity and concept. Take, for example, St. Petersburg's JeMari—the first Russian gallery of contemporary animal art to bring to the fair portraits of animals in images ranging from the everyday to the cosmic! Among the participants were many familiar names from previous Art Worlds—magnificent, outstanding names—but also many new artists. They presented paintings and graphics, delicate, luminous miniatures and deliberately rough, even brutal, canvases, ceramics and sculpture, designer dolls and objects (including glowing and moving ones)—a vast array of works, many of which make you want to linger, examining the artistic concept. The Shukhov Ornithological Tower proudly rises—you can climb it. The "monsters" of Ilya Spichenkov, a former firefighter from Dzerzhinsk, grin joyfully (incidentally, one of his works adorns the theater area of Philip Kirkorov's mansion). The astonishing "Facets of the Celestial Empire"—a photo project created by a collaboration of Chinese and Russian photographers—is captivating. Landscapes reminiscent of troubling dreams and images seemingly beckon from the heavens are captivating. The Mona Lisa, in a "cubist" style, is stunning. Achromaticism strikes with a powerful blow, and the luxurious palette of still lifes delights the eye. Animals crafted from tightly fused wood and metal, as if smoothed by loving hands, are captivating. Another animalistic work, also made of wood and metal, is a mechanical fish... for some reason, equipped with a sturdy brass door handle. There's plenty to see! However, due to the large number of visitors, weekdays are the most convenient time to visit the exhibition. The festival program also includes many interesting meetings, master classes, tours, and more. The exhibition is open from 11:00 AM to 8:00 PM, and on February 8th from 11:00 AM to 6:00 PM. 6+.
